rows.title: China launches anti-dumping probe into European chemical exports
rows.content:
Edward White in Shanghai and Henry Foy in Brussels

Published October 3 2026

Updated October 3 2026

Beijing has launched an anti-dumping investigation into European exports of a chemical used for dyes and pharmaceuticals as tensions rise over China’s massive trade surplus with the bloc.

The commerce ministry in Beijing said on Saturday that it had started an investigation into p-nitrotoluene, which is also used in pesticide and pigment production, after a complaint from Chinese industry.

The investigation marks the latest tit-for-tat measure between Brussels and Beijing after trade tensions flared again in recent weeks.

The EU opened three anti-dumping investigations into chemicals from China last week. It also began consulting on a new diversification tool that would seek to reduce imports from China.

It comes just ahead of crunch talks between EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, commerce minister Wang Wentao, in Beijing this month.

The EU in June set an October deadline for progress in reducing its trade deficit with China, which is now running at €1bn a day.

Brussels has warned that without any action it could resort to new trade measures, which are set to be debated at a summit of EU leaders at the end of October.

The European Commission declined to comment.

The FT reported last month that among the initiatives proposed, the EU has asked China to restrict its exports of plug-in hybrid vehicles voluntarily, as well as restrain exports of some chemicals.

According to the commerce ministry, from 2022 to 2025 European exports of p-nitrotoluene were at high levels while prices declined by 60 per cent, meeting the grounds for an investigation under both Chinese and World Trade Organization rules.

The Chinese move also follows a warning from Brussels to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham that Britain would need to raise tariffs on Chinese cars and align more closely with EU trade policy if it wants to avoid “made in Europe” barriers on exports to the bloc.

EU officials have argued that Chinese controls on rare earth exports, introduced last year as part of China’s retaliation against US President Donald Trump, have unfairly hit European companies.

Over recent years, the EU has targeted Chinese industrial products with higher tariffs while China has sought to influence EU member governments by hitting agricultural interests, including dairy products, pork and cognac.

rows.title: Europe Express: Lies and statistics
rows.content:
Ben Hall

Published October 3 2026

Welcome back. It’s been a big week in French politics and a tough one for far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in next year’s presidential election.

Let’s start with the statistics.

The sell-off in French debt accelerated this week with yields on 10-year government bonds climbing to 4.9 per cent, a rise of 130 basis points since early July (more than double the increase for UK debt). The surge in borrowing costs only adds to the impossible arithmetic — and impossible politics — of deficit reduction in France.

The higher the yields go, the more the public finances become the defining issue in the campaign. This is not to the Rassemblement National leader’s advantage given the party’s promises of massive tax cuts and flaky plans to cut spending. France’s fiscal squeeze could test its claims to be a responsible party of government — to destruction, its mainstream opponents hope.

I’m at [email protected]

Reality check

“Reality is catching up with us,” said prime minister Sébastien Lecornu, as he warned about spiral debt-servicing costs on the eve of his 2027 budget . The interest bill will rise to €73bn next year, up by a fifth on 2026. That bill will grow to €124bn by 2030, according to a report (in French) by a commission led by four independent economists — Xavier Jaravel, Xavier Ragot, Jean-Luc Tavernier and Natacha Valla — in July. Their calculations are already out of date. But their report provides a lucid explanation of France’s predicament.

On current policies, they say, France’s deficit will keep rising to 6.8 per cent of GDP by the end of the decade because of surging interest rates and the increasing costs of an ageing population. Debt will hit 122 per cent of GDP next year and keep on rising to 131 per cent by the end of the decade. France has to run to stand still.

Achieving debt sustainability by the end of the next five-year presidential term would require bringing the deficit to 3 per cent of GDP (a small primary surplus minus debt servicing costs). The four economists said this would require annual savings of €126bn by 2032, with the effort frontloaded during the term. In the three months since their report, that number has risen to €140bn.

None of the presidential candidates has a plan for savings on that scale. As Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, told La Croix newspaper this week, “when your debt is close to 120 per cent of GDP and not on course to be brought under control, it is a serious matter.”

Time for a rule

Le Pen knows she needs to bolster her party’s credibility on public finances. Having long opposed any budget constraints, such as those enforced by the EU, she has now come round to the idea. Writing in L’Opinion on Thursday, Le Pen said she would seek to enshrine a public deficit ceiling in the constitution (a variable number but probably around 2.5 per cent). To get to that objective from the current level of 5.5 per cent, her “golden rule” would require a minimum 0.5 percentage point reduction each year.

Blaming President Emmanuel Macron for the “catastrophic” state of the public finances, she boasted that the RN was now the only party willing to get to grips with the problem.

But a debt rule matters less than a credible plan for the tax rises or spending cuts needed to meet it. The far-right is expected to unveil its new proposals next week. Previous iterations of its annual “shadow budget” beg a lot of questions. The shadow 2026 budget included tax cuts worth some €47bn offset by spending reductions of €88bn. Many of the proposed cuts were questionable: ending benefits for foreigners and withholding half of France’s budget contribution to the EU are legally doubtful. There was also no indication of where a second year of savings would come from — pensions and welfare remain off limits.

Lost ticket?

Now to the “lies”.

RN president Jordan Bardella, who Le Pen touts as her future prime minister, was engulfed in scandal this week when investigative news site Mediapart alleged he had made multiple antisemitic statements in private messages as a young activist in the party. The claims threaten to undo the leadership’s efforts in recent years to “detoxify” the party by rooting out racist and antisemitic elements.

Bardella vehemently denied the allegations, calling them a fabrication and a political assassination attempt. Le Pen said the claims were a “secret service operation”. But on Thursday Mediapart hit back , publishing a dossier with excerpts from messages and a detailed explanation of how it corroborated the evidence, including a cache of messages from Meta that was certified by a legal officer. Bardella is sticking to his line that the claims are a fraud, but he looks like damaged goods.

With debt markets on fire and a joint ticket with Bardella potentially going up in smoke, it’s been a bad spell for Le Pen. But the real flames this week were burning outside high schools across France, where students protesting against underfunded education, egged on by the far left, clashed with police. Shocking scenes were beamed around the world. It was a perfect addition to the RN narrative of an impotent state before a country in chaos.

Vladimir Putin has personally told his military commanders to abandon the rules of war, Volodymr Zelenskyy tells Christopher Miller in an interview from a bombed-out Kyiv school.

rows.title: Chart of the Week: What’s driving the global bond sell-off?
rows.content:
Hakyung Kim

Published October 3 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

This article is an on-site version of our Unhedged: Chart of the Week newsletter. You sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Saturday, or explore all FT newsletters

Good morning. Sovereign bond yields have been rising all year, and in the past few weeks the pace has accelerated across most developed markets. But there is not a clear consensus about what’s driving the sell-off. Looking at the most cited factors — inflation and indebtedness — across various countries reveals a mixed picture.

Mapping debt-to-GDP ratios against year-to-date increases in 10-year yields reveals a loose positive relationship. But there are exceptions, such as South Korea, which has a relatively low debt-to-GDP ratio of 52 per cent, but a jump similar to that of Italy, whose public debt sits at a staggering 137 per cent of GDP. Adding inflation rates offers only a little extra clarity. Italy and Spain recently both had annualised inflation readings above 4 per cent, yet their yield increases have lagged behind those of French sovereign bonds, despite France’s tamer inflation rate of 3 per cent.

Growth is another part of the equation. The steady expansion in US real GDP helps explain why its yields have risen more than those of Italy, which has higher debt and more inflation. Finally, there’s the unquantifiable variable: political risk. French bond yields have surged to levels near those of the European debt crisis, as election uncertainty comes on top of a worsening fiscal situation.

The biggest outlier is, of course, Japan. The yield on the 10-year JGB has surged by nearly one percentage point in 2026, an increase comparable to that of Gilts and Italian debt. Yet Japanese inflation came in at just 1.9 per cent in August — the lowest on our list. Historical context is important. While other countries would be pleased with a 1.9 per cent inflation rate, decades of deflation in the Asian nation have made these “normal” inflation levels, alongside a weak yen and energy shock, a bigger jolt to the economy.

rows.title: How airlines try to weed out rogue pilots
rows.content:
Peter Campbell in London

Published October 3 2026

Updated October 3 2026

A decade after a Germanwings co-pilot crashed a plane into the French Alps, the aviation industry is bound by safety procedures designed to prevent another pilot from going rogue.

Aviation safety regulators across the world tightened rules after that disaster: pilots seeking to enter the profession now face strict psychological tests, along with annual check-ups that include questions about depression and suicide.

Details are still emerging about the assault aboard Flydubai flight 1073 . UAE authorities have said the co-pilot stabbed the pilot with an axe in the cockpit and tried to take control of the plane in a “terrorist act”.

The incident, which follows millions of safe flights over the years, has raised further questions over how the industry monitors pilots’ mental fitness to fly.

Pilots, instructors and safety experts told the FT that current checks may still fail to catch the tiny number of unsuitable people who apply to join the industry, or who develop severe mental health problems or adopt extreme ideological views over a long career.

“It’s effectively self-reporting,” said one commercial pilot. “There are obviously right answers.”

Flying internationally remains a safe form of transport — “the most dangerous part of any flight is always the drive to the airport”, said aviation analyst Andrew Charlton.

But several industry figures argued that this was down to broader safety procedures, stringent pilot training and the professionalism of those in the industry rather than to the psychological testing system.

Pilots must undergo annual check-ups that determine their chances of becoming medically incapacitated during a flight, including a conversation with a doctor about their state of mind, along with questions about alcohol and drug use.

Airlines also carry out regular background checks, which include looking for signs of extremist sympathies.

“We do psychometric testing and background security checks on a regular basis,” said an airline executive.

But one working pilot told the FT their last full psychological analysis was more than two decades ago. Another said pilots “prepare” for their annual check-up and “answer questions to make them think all is well”.

Andrew McKechnie, who spent 30 years as a pilot and now runs McKechnie Aviation, a safety training group, said: “A pilot’s income depends on holding a valid medical certificate, so pilots may be reluctant to seek help for health issues in case they lose their medical certificate . . . Similarly, there’s a strong incentive for pilots to avoid disclosing mental health concerns to their aviation medical examiner.”

However, tightened checks have in some cases helped to identify people whose mental health has deteriorated or who suffer life shocks, pilots said.

Pilots who suffer bereavements or major traumas are required to make several visits to a therapist before returning to flying, said people with knowledge of the process.

After the 2015 Germanwings crash — which killed 150 people and which investigators found had been caused by the deliberate actions of the pilot — most airlines also introduced extensive schemes to enable crew to report colleagues they believe may be unsafe.

This is helpful in an industry where the fluid nature of rosters means that pilots, co-pilots and crew change constantly. Many will have met each other only hours before take-off. “Being able to form a team quickly is part of the job,” said one longtime pilot.

Interventions that follow whistleblowing are robust, helping struggling crew members get help. Multiple people said the system has led to improvements.

It is also open to abuse: the industry is rife with tales of pilots or crew who report each other to the system after the end of a romantic relationship.

The industry’s focus on safety also makes people reluctant to come forward with genuine concerns.

“You cannot declare a problem,” said one person who works in pilot training, adding that people with autism, attention deficit disorder or depression feel unable to speak out. “You can’t get counselling, other than for eating disorders or marriage counselling,” they added.

Working as a pilot entails broken sleep patterns and near-constant jet lag, while long periods away from home can lead to marital strains. One pilot said: “If you’re not OK with your own company — and watching really bad TV in your hotel room — it can be an overwhelming experience.”

But others said they believed changes in the mental state of pilots were more often caused by life events such as divorce than by the job itself. “The most difficult bit is to assess people who have shocks that then trigger and change them into a different personality,” said one former pilot who runs a training centre.

One long-haul airline pilot described the role itself as “pure escapism”. “You see sunshine every day . . . [and] you go to a different part of the world where no one knows who you are,” they said. Another repeated a well-known industry joke: “The pressure is always highest at altitude zero, ie on the ground.”

Flydubai chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith on Friday reiterated that a “full official investigation” was under way into the near miss on its flight, and added: “It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts . . . Safety is, and always will be, our highest priority.” Flydubai declined to comment on pilot checks, pending the investigation.

Investigators have not released the name of the alleged attacker on the flight, though the UAE on Saturday said the flight’s co-pilot “attempted to carry out a terrorist act”.

The co-pilot was “attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft”, UAE attorney-general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said. The investigation will “establish the full circumstances, motives, and any links related to the incident”, he added.

Andrew Lobbenberg, an airline analyst at Barclays, said it “could lead regulators and airlines to revisit psychological screening, crew vetting procedures and access to flight controls when only two pilots are in the cockpit”.

McKechnie is unconvinced by arguments for more testing. He said the checks rely on the belief “that pilots who plan to commit acts of sabotage and murder will discuss this with colleagues, counsellors or medical examiners”.

He added: “These attempts to use psychological and psychiatric assessments to reduce the risk of sabotage by pilots are ineffective.”

But others in the industry disagree. Arik Arad, former security chief of Israeli airline El Al, told CNN this week that pilots “should also have psychological and background checks not only when they get accepted to become pilots but periodically, maybe every six months . . . just to make sure nobody is going astray.”

rows.title: Co-pilot used axe to carry out ‘terrorist act’ on Flydubai flight
rows.content:
Peter Campbell in London

Published October 3 2026

The co-pilot of Flydubai Flight 1073 attacked the captain with an axe in the cockpit as he “attempted to carry out a terrorist act”, UAE prosecutors said on Saturday.

Authorities have been questioning Smit Machchhar, the captain, and his co-pilot, who has not been named, after Wednesday’s incident when a fight on the flight deck broke out in what has been described as an attempted hijacking.

“The co-pilot began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft,” said UAE attorney-general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi.

The crash axe is a heavy one-handed axe that sits in the cockpit, allowing pilots to break glass or even punch through bodywork in the event of an emergency.

While it was known that Machchhar had been stabbed, it was unclear until Saturday what weapon had been used. Pilots and crew are subject to the same security checks as passengers.

Al Shamsi added: “Investigations are ongoing to establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, as well as to complete technical examinations and analysis of physical and digital evidence. The final results will be announced upon the conclusion of all necessary procedures.”

Although details of what happened are still emerging, the pilot of the aircraft has been praised for unlocking the cabin door, allowing passengers and crew to enter the cockpit and regain control of the aircraft, which had fallen steeply. The plane, which had been heading for Tel Aviv, was then landed at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia.

Passengers were transferred to Tel Aviv, while Machchhar and the co-pilot were both flown from Saudi Arabia to Abu Dhabi on Thursday “accompanied by the UAE security team”, according to Saudi state media.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”. Israel has not released evidence for that claim.

rows.title: Manchester City’s fightback begins
rows.content:
Josh Noble and Benjamin Wilhelm

Published October 3 2026

This article is an online version of our Scoreboard newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Saturday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

It’s been another gruelling few days for executives at Nike. On Thursday the company announced a fresh round of job cuts and gave investors another gloomy forecast for the year ahead. Shares dropped more than 6 per cent yesterday, their lowest level since 2013.

Sales in China, its second-biggest market, fell by more than a fifth in the first quarter of its financial year ending in August. Nike has been seriously squeezed there by local brands and has so far struggled to regain its footing.

The sportswear maker also announced a new campus in Bengaluru, a sign that it sees India as a potential saviour. But if there’s a light at the end of the tunnel, it’s pretty hard to see right now.

So, time to get on to the biggest story in sport — Manchester City’s legal war against the competition it has come to dominate. Plus, the NFL’s international expansion shows signs of overexposure. Do read on — Josh Noble, sports editor

Send us tips and feedback at [email protected] . Not already receiving the email newsletter? Sign up here . For everyone else, let’s go.

At 7pm on Thursday, Manchester City’s attempts to overturn the damning findings of an independent commission formally kicked off. City was judged to have arranged a series of “sham” sponsorship deals that — along with moves to hide costs off the books — flattered the club’s accounts to the tune of more than £900mn over a period lasting almost a decade.

The club, owned by a member of Abu Dhabi’s royal family, said it had lodged its appeal against the Premier League-appointed panel:

The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

The appeal had been widely flagged ahead of time and is just part of the response to the ruling by the club and its allies.

On Wednesday, Abu Dhabi-based airline Etihad threatened legal action against the Premier League, saying its communications around the case had “created damaging implications”. Etihad, City’s principal sponsor, said it “categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements”.

There is a significant political element too. City chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak is an influential figure in Abu Dhabi’s government, and chief executive of the sovereign wealth fund Mubadala. You can read our in-depth profile of him here .

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was forced to backtrack on comments earlier this week after saying he would be “really concerned” if City’s owners were forced out. Downing Street later said: “The initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules.”

English football’s new independent regulator also weighed in with a rather pointed statement:

The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals.

City’s football empire stretches well beyond the Premier League. The parent company has five clubs in Europe alone, with more in Australia, Brazil, the US and beyond. Any suggestion that certain owners or executives are “unsuitable” would have implications across the game.

Legal experts have billed City’s chances of overturning the verdict itself a serious uphill climb. But with the club insisting it will pursue all avenues available, many expect the case to run and run. One lawyer described this week’s events as being more like the “end of the beginning” rather than anything approaching an ending.

This is all pretty miserable for the Premier League. City, after all, are currently top of the league. Bookmakers currently rate the club as the second most likely to be crowned champions and the fourth most likely to be relegated. The uncertainty hanging over the competition will weigh heavily.

In the short term, it’s hard to see much of a knock to the Premier League’s business. If anything, the soap opera may well make the action on the pitch even more enticing for subscription-paying fans.

But if every result against City this season is now going to come with a caveat, the integrity of the world’s most popular football league is going to come under increasing strain.

As the NFL’s footprint spreads around the globe, there are signs of American football fatigue in London, the cradle of the league’s international expansion.

Facing slower ticket sales than usual, the NFL has cut prices down to £79 ($105) for tomorrow’s game between the Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts at Tottenham Stadium. Tickets are available for even less on resale markets.

Excitement was probably damped by initial face-value prices of up to $325 for a match-up of middling teams. The NFL is also playing games in Paris, Madrid and Munich this season, giving fans in Europe options beyond the British capital.

While London remains a hub for the NFL’s global ambitions — it hosts three games this season — the city is just one stop in the league’s ever-growing International Series. This year, that includes a record-breaking nine games spanning seven countries and four continents, with an appetite for more.

The NFL has toyed with the possibility of a Super Bowl in London but more recently backed off the idea. Meanwhile, commissioner Roger Goodell told a German publication last month that he has “no doubt” that there will eventually be an NFL team outside the US.

Such an idea faces significant logistical barriers. A more realistic outcome of the NFL’s global expansion is Goodell’s vision of a 16-game international schedule, which would mean every team plays one game abroad each season. In typical NFL fashion, the league could then carve out a lucrative broadcast rights package to sell to a global streamer like YouTube or Netflix.

The NFL views the Premier League’s global reach as inspiration, as Kansas City Chiefs president Mark Donovan told the FT in June:

It might have been eight years ago now, we sat in a league meeting, and the NFL put up a map of the EPL, and said, “If you look at the EPL, one of the most successful leagues out there, 20 per cent of their franchise fans are in the country. Eighty per cent are around the world. If you look at the NFL, 80 per cent of our fans are in the country, 20 per cent are around the world.”

The league’s efforts to change that include its Global Markets Program, which awards franchises marketing rights to countries to build their own fan bases. The NFL has also invested in the development of flag football around the world, and successfully pushed for the low-contact sport to be added to the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

Time will tell if global audiences embrace American football, a game that mystifies even a few Americans. Last month’s NFL debut in Australia — a San Francisco 49ers blowout of the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne — drew a modest 3.2mn viewers outside the US on Netflix, where it was broadcast globally.

On the other hand, 100,000 fans filled the Melbourne Cricket Ground for that game. Another 72,792 packed Rio de Janeiro’s legendary Maracanã Stadium for last Sunday’s match-up between the Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens and erupted when the Ravens won in dramatic fashion .

The NFL played its first game in Brazil just two years ago, compared to the dozens held in London since 2007. The novelty may have faded in the UK but there is still massive room for growth there and beyond.

The board of Madison Square Garden Sports, which owns the NBA’s New York Knicks and the NHL’s New York Rangers, approved the split of the two franchises into separate publicly traded companies.

The NBA is expected to select the winning bid for ownership of a Las Vegas expansion team in the “very near future”, according to ESPN, with a price of at least $12bn to $13bn for the franchise and a new arena.

The US Senate passed legislation that aims to regulate college sports — primarily American football and basketball — which have rapidly professionalised after a series of court rulings allowed revenue sharing and for athletes to profit from their “name, image and likeness”. The bill, which still requires approval from the House of Representatives, would grant the National Collegiate Athletic Association an antitrust exemption to enact rules that cap player pay and limit transfers.

The Chicago White Sox won their first playoff series since 2005 with a sweep of the Houston Astros this week. During the booze-fuelled celebration, Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami sidelined his translator and gave an interview for the ages .

rows.title: Capital gains tax rise would deter equity investors, wealth bosses warn
rows.content:
Emma Dunkley in London

Published October 3 2026

Updated October 3 2026

Chief executives of the UK’s largest investment sites have warned against increasing capital gains tax in the upcoming Budget. They say it could deter savers from investing in the stock market, creating a conflict with one of the government’s stated aims.

CGT is charged on profits from selling assets such as shares, businesses and second homes. The main higher rate was increased in the 2024 Budget from 20 per cent to 24 per cent. The annual allowance — the amount exempt from CGT — was also cut in half to £3,000.

Concerns that CGT could rise further have intensified in recent weeks, as it sits outside the Labour government’s commitment not to increase taxes on working people.

But wealth management bosses urged the Treasury against making the tax more punitive, noting that it could undermine the government’s attempts to encourage more people to invest and back the UK’s equity market.

Matt Benchener, chief executive of Hargreaves Lansdown, told the FT: “The government wants to get more Britons investing, but raising capital gains tax would work directly against that goal.

“By some estimates, more than £600bn sits in excess cash , its value being eroded by inflation. Taxing investment returns more heavily would be another deterrent for cautious savers who need to be encouraged to take the next step and invest.”

“They say they are trying to foster a retail investing culture, but their policies are doing the opposite,” said Michael Summersgill, chief executive of AJ Bell. “The chancellor should be looking to encourage long-term investing by simplifying tax rules instead of continually layering on complexity and cost.”

Richard Wilson, chief executive at Interactive Investor, said: “You cannot build a nation of investors while increasing the tax on investing. Higher capital gains tax reduces the incentive to take risk, back businesses and build long-term wealth.

“At a time when the government says it wants growth, raising CGT would send entirely the wrong signal to millions of savers and investors whose capital helps power the economy.”

Investment sites tend to charge dealing fees when investors make trades — such as selling their shares.

Other wealth managers point out that increasing CGT will not necessarily generate more revenue for the government.

Steven Levin, chief executive of Quilter, noted that investors could end up deferring the sale of assets as a result. “Any changes to CGT therefore need to be assessed not only through a fiscal lens, but also through their impact on investment activity, entrepreneurship and the UK’s attractiveness as a destination for capital.”

Higher CGT could also lead more people to invest in gilts, which do not incur CGT, instead of shares. Peter Hargreaves, co-founder of Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “If there is less advantage in investing for growth, [people] will change, they will look at low-coupon gilts, which are CGT free.”

rows.title: The right and wrong lessons to learn from Spain’s housing crisis
rows.content:
John Burn-Murdoch

Published October 3 2026

Although housing crises have been smouldering across much of the high-income world for a decade or more, they have generally tended to rank some way down the political agenda.

That may be about to change, with reports suggesting Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez is considering calling an early election in a bid to resolve mounting public and political discontent over spiralling rents and prices after his flagship housing bill was rejected by parliament on Friday.

Mass protests were sparked recently by the case of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal. She was served an eviction notice after her previously rent-controlled flat was bought by a corporate landlord which sought to increase the rent to a level well above her monthly pension income.

Much of the anger has centred on the role of so-called “vulture funds” in the rental market — Sanchez’s party has proposed banning large-scale investors from buying homes until 2028. But if policymakers and tenants alike want to see durable improvements and to avoid unintended negative consequences, it’s worth taking a step back and looking at what is, in truth, a much deeper problem, both in Spain and in other countries.

Consider the many recent cases in the UK and Ireland where protesters have similarly rallied in opposition to evictions — often not by greedy corporate landlords but by local councils seeking to move rent-controlled properties on to new low-income tenants. These happen after the former tenant passes away or moves out but their family members refuse to leave.

The specifics of such cases are very different but they all speak to the same problem: acute housing shortages. A landlord — whether the corporate or “mom-and-pop” variety — increases rents only when they are confident they will find someone willing to pay the higher price. The bidding wars resulting from shortages provide fertile ground. Spain has built fewer homes per capita than virtually any other high-income country over the past 10 years . More than 50 per cent of its young adults now live with their parents, up from 33 per cent in 2005, and rents have risen more steeply than almost anywhere else.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The reason the children of British and Irish social housing tenants are desperate to keep hold of the homes after tenancies expire — and why waiting lists for those cost-controlled homes are so long — is the acute shortage of properties in these countries. The UK and Ireland each lack roughly one in seven homes they need to adequately house today’s populations.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Spain’s problems are on both the supply and demand sides. Its housebuilding crunch has coincided with a population boom fuelled in large part by a conscious effort by Sánchez to boost immigration . On top of that, surging inflows of tourists and digital nomads mean the market-clearing rent is often set not by local incomes but by those of affluent visitors. Courting workers and high-spending visitors from overseas is sound economic policy, but it requires a joined-up approach on the supply side in the form of much greater housebuilding — some of which could be funded through increased tourist taxes.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The government’s proposals so far amount to a patchwork of sticking plasters that address some of the symptoms but not the underlying cause. Stronger protections for existing tenants and bans on investment will not ease shortage-driven pressure on rents and prices. Nor will they house the millions of young adults whose lives and careers are on hold while they are forced to share a roof with their parents.

In this regard Spain may want to look to Ireland, where policymakers last year watered down rent controls over concerns they were contributing to weak rates of new construction in the rental sector, exacerbating the underlying causes of the disease whose symptoms they were intended to treat.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Fixing housing crises is far easier said than done. If mounting costs and worsening shortages were simple to reverse sustainably, they would not be afflicting so many different places with a wide variety of policy and economic environments.

But to stand any chance of lasting success, policymakers must ensure they go beyond shallow and often counter-productive regulations or selective protections for those lucky enough to already be renting, and wrestle instead with the more challenging reforms that could put downward pressure on rents and prices for all and for good.

rows.title: Rising gilt yields attract retail investors hunting for tax-efficient assets
rows.content:
Steve Johnson

Published October 3 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

A surge in UK government bond yields to multi-decade highs is luring more retail investors into the market, with buying heavily concentrated in short-dated gilts, investment platforms say.

At the same time, concerns that global inflation and borrowing pressures could keep interest rates higher for longer have made investors reluctant to take on longer-duration risk.

“We are seeing some pretty considerable activity,” said Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at Hargreaves Lansdown, who said the UK’s largest DIY investment platform had seen a 38 per cent year-on-year rise in the number of clients holding individual gilts.

The increase comes as benchmark 10-year gilt yields have jumped to 5.4 per cent, the highest level since July 2007, and 30-year yields climbed above 6 per cent for the first time since 1998.

Alongside fears over rising energy prices, yields in both the UK and other developed markets have been pushed up by concerns over rising government debt levels and mounting competition for capital, as AI hyperscalers such as Meta, Alphabet and Microsoft borrow huge sums to finance their data centre rollouts. Bond prices fall when yields rise.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said that short-dated gilts had become the most popular asset held in the platform’s DIY investor dealing accounts, adding that higher- and additional-rate taxpayers were being drawn to shorter-dated bonds because capital gains from gilts are tax free, while coupon payments are not.

Rising gilt yields have pushed down the market price of shorter-dated bonds, issued with historically low coupons, to comfortably below par value, meaning that, if held to maturity, the overwhelming majority of the return will be in the form of tax-free capital gain when redeemed at par.

“That’s a key attraction for investors, particularly those who have used up their Isa allowance and are looking for alternative tax-efficient ways to make money,” Coatsworth said. The attraction has only increased, he added, thanks to the speculation that CGT rates could be raised in this month’s Budget.

Macdonald said many HL investors were now selling out of a 0.375 per cent coupon gilt due to mature on October 22 that has essentially now returned to par, and instead are buying a 0.125 per cent coupon bond running until January 2028, currently trading at £94.78, giving a yield to maturity of 4.2 per cent, with the bulk of the return being tax-free.

Jason Hollands, managing director of wealth manager Evelyn Partners, said it has seen “strong interest” in its Cash & Cautious Bond strategy, which blends money market instruments such as US Treasury bills and short-dated gilts.

At Bestinvest, Evelyn’s DIY investment arm, Hollands said clients “have largely ignored fixed income for many years”, but that the fourth most popular ETF in September was the iShares UK Gilts 0-5yr Ucits ETF, “which indicates that at least some clients are starting to see the rise in yields as an opportunity”.

Despite the market ructions, Macdonald had a simple recipe for investors seeking shelter.

“Over the long term the best way to protect yourself against inflation is to buy real assets, so equities are going to be the best way to protect yourself from that,” she said.

rows.title: Does the EU want Britain back?
rows.content:
Peter Foster , George Parker and Ben Hall in London

Published October 3 2026

It was a balmy late September day in New York when Andy Burnham, Britain’s new prime minister, first gave a clue of his plan to reopen the UK’s Brexit debate, 10 years after the country’s vote to leave the EU.

In a private meeting on the margins of the UN General Assembly, Burnham told Ursula von der Leyen, European Commission president, the UK was ready to look again at closer relations with Europe, including possibly rejoining the bloc.

“I think public opinion in Britain is way ahead of the political elite at Westminster,” he said, according to people briefed on the talks. “I’m not sure how far I’m going to get, but I’m going to try to close that gap.”

No one had seen it coming. After years in which Britain’s Brexit negotiations with Brussels have been stuck in a rut, Burnham has dared to reopen the debate on Europe. But EU leaders are clear that any discussion about closer ties will be conducted on their terms, not the UK’s.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

A week after the UN meeting, the prime minister received rapturous applause when he told his Labour Party conference in Liverpool he wanted a debate on Britain’s “long-term relationship” with the EU, including possible membership of a customs union and the single market. Or, as he put it later, he would look at going “all the way”.

“Welcome back,” responded French President Emmanuel Macron, breaking into English at a press conference alongside his Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez this week.

Sánchez said that “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms”. EU diplomats expressed delight at the new strategic vision from Burnham, even if the final destination remains far from clear.

But Macron was quick to issue a reminder that Europe would still call the shots: “You cannot pick and choose among the Union’s freedoms, nor can you decide to take only what suits you while leaving the rest,” he said, indicating that the fundamental choice remained one of in or out. “So, come back.”

Still to be determined is whether British politics is really capable of accepting that improved access to the EU’s single market will mean opening up to more EU migration, paying money into EU coffers and living under laws made outside Westminster. But finally a British prime minister has got Brussels’ attention.

“It’s a breath of fresh air in a hitherto stagnant debate,” said one senior European Commission official. “But whether the UK can accept the trade-offs, well, that is the billion-euro question. But at least Burnham appears to have the balls to find out.”

Even if agreement can be reached at home, Burnham will also have to convince the EU that he is serious when the bloc is rethinking how to bring its trusted partners closer in an era of geopolitical upheaval.

Some member states would welcome the UK back as a liberal counterweight to France, but Paris itself remains wary of a country with Atlanticist, free-trading, low-regulation instincts.

Since the 2016 Brexit referendum ended Britain’s four-decade membership of the European club, a succession of both Conservative and Labour prime ministers has promised a cherry-picked relationship with Brussels but with very limited success.

“I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough,” Burnham told his conference, quietly accepting that Labour’s own attempt to finesse the Brexit choices after the election of Sir Keir Starmer in 2024 had hit the same roadblocks encountered by his Conservative predecessors.

Starmer had promised his party would “tear down” the barriers to trade with Europe while sticking to the same “red lines” that had underpinned former prime minister Boris Johnson’s post-Brexit trade pact with Brussels: no return to the single market, the customs union or free movement of people.

“Starmer thought he could ‘make Brexit work’, but Burnham is saying that he fears it cannot,” says Anand Menon, director of the UK in a Changing Europe think-tank.

But Michel Barnier, the EU’s chief Brexit negotiator, warns that the new conversation will not be fundamentally different from the last — even if the geopolitical landscape of 2026 is very different from a decade ago.

“One thing is sure: the more the UK diverges, the harder it will be to rejoin,” Barnier says. “There will be no cherry-picking. The single market is not à la carte. The British government perfectly knows the rules and the conditions.”

From the perspective of many in the EU, US President Donald Trump’s antagonism towards Europe, the Russian threat and a desire for like-minded liberal democracies to club together are reasons to bring Britain closer to the bloc.

“There is a strong strategic case for bringing Britain back into the European fold,” says Georg Riekeles, associate director at the European Policy Centre think-tank in Brussels and a former official in the EU’s Brexit negotiating team.

He adds that a UK decision to drop its red lines “opens the possibility of a much more serious conversation about common interests” but warns that “appetite for closer integration and readiness to reopen membership negotiations are two different things”.

In particular, he thinks that EU governments want reassurance that any UK move would “survive a change of government if negotiations were to be opened”. With the Conservative Party and Reform UK deeply committed to Brexit, “that still seems rather far away”.

Berlin and other northern European capitals have always been open to rebuilding ties with Britain.

But the country that would need most persuading is France, which has long seen Britain as an economic and ideological competitor within the EU.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The UK was traditionally a proponent of widening the bloc to new members rather than Paris’s vision of deeper integration among a core group of countries. Other EU governments saw Britain’s refusal to join the euro as a sign of its detachment from the bloc’s political project; any suggestion of ditching the pound remains political dynamite in the UK.

Over the past decade, the EU has also adopted much of Macron’s thinking on “strategic autonomy” in terms of security, technology and trade, especially with China.

“Since Brexit, the bloc has changed and is more about building its own independent capacities,” says Sébastien Maillard of the Jacques Delors Institute think-tank.

“Member states, especially France in its Gaullist tradition, would test whether a rejoining Britain would fully support this objective or if it just wants to use the EU to boost its own GDP.”

Paris has been the EU government most anxious to prevent the British from selectively enjoying the benefits of membership from outside the bloc.

It has demanded London pay a high price for accessing any EU programmes, such as the EU’s €150bn so-called Safe loans defence scheme — to which London has failed to negotiate access.

Were Britain to rejoin the bloc, it would have to be ratified like any accession by three-fifths of French MPs and senators or in a referendum, a high bar to clear.

Then there is the possibility that far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who has vowed to block further EU enlargement, wins the French presidential election next year.

She plans to confront Brussels by slashing France’s contribution to the EU budget, pulling out of parts of the single market and reasserting the primacy of French over European law.

Conflict with one of its most important members might consume the EU’s bandwidth. It could also give Britain pause for thought about rejoining.

Philip Rycroft, who served as the top civil servant at the Department for Exiting the EU from 2017 to 2019, argues that the referendum 10 years ago was the worst possible moment Britain could have picked to strike out on its own.

“It turned out that 2016 was spectacularly poor timing for a liberal open economy to launch itself on to the rough seas of the global trading order just at the time it was fracturing and the security situation was deteriorating,” he says.

A decade on, Burnham’s fledgling government has found itself coming up hard against those realities. China is exporting often heavily subsidised goods at a scale, cost and quality that poses an existential threat to some sectors of European manufacturing. In response, the EU is adopting a defensive “made in Europe” agenda that could itself hit Burnham’s own ambitions to “reindustrialise” the UK.

The fear in London is that new EU rules requiring cars to be assembled in the bloc will stifle investment in an industry vital to the West Midlands and North East regions of the country.

This has helped crystallise the choices facing the UK — as have similar threats to the chemicals, nuclear and green hydrogen industries, according to Anton Spisak, a former UK Brexit negotiator now at the Centre for European Reform think-tank.

It also highlights problems with Starmer’s idea that accepting “dynamic alignment” with some EU rules and regulations would unlock privileged access to the EU single market.

Rycroft argues that the experience of the past decade shows that none of the options namechecked by Burnham at Liverpool this week — a customs union or rejoining the EU single market — are workable.

“Burnham has the credibility to open the debate. And he’s accepted the outcomes range from ‘where we are now’ to ‘rejoin’, but you quickly find the way stations between those points are not very comfortable,” he says.

“The UK is too big an economy to be bound into a reality where it takes trade deals and rules from Brussels with no say over how those deals and rules are put together.”

Although the 56-year-old Burnham has said he would like Britain to rejoin the EU “in my lifetime”, the European cause has never been a big part of his political identity. Asked whether the prime minister was interested in the EU, one ministerial colleague says: “Not hugely.”

The minister adds that Burnham is worried about Brexit’s long-term economic impact, as well as the China import shock and the EU’s response to it.

Burnham returned to Westminster in June as MP for the staunchly Leave-voting working-class seat of Makerfield near Manchester and told voters in that by-election campaign that he did not want to rerun “divisive arguments about rejoining the EU”.

His calculation appears to have changed. His strategists believe that by flirting with “Rejoin”, Burnham can win back voters from the Green Party, which is responsible for the overwhelming majority of defections from former Labour supporters.

But some colleagues fear the UK prime minister risks playing into the hands of Reform, particularly in working-class seats. The rightwing party’s leader, Nigel Farage, said this week that by reigniting the Brexit debate, Burnham had “opened the door to Reform in the most extraordinary way”.

Another longtime Labour colleague of Burnham says the prime minister is “conflicted” on Europe. In 2019 as Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said he would vote Leave in a second Brexit referendum if Labour could secure a better exit deal.

“He understands why people voted Leave. He gets that white working-class alienation,” this person adds. “He won’t want to gift Reform a lifeline by embracing the evangelical crusade to rejoin.”

Stella Creasy, chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, adds that “Labour now has to win the case across the country and with its own membership for why and how to rebuild our relationship with the EU”.

On the face of it, polling is encouraging for pro-Europeans. Since 2021 public hostility to Brexit has grown; YouGov found last month that 59 per cent favoured rejoining the EU with 32 per cent against. However, surveys also suggest that popular support wanes when people are given more details.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

YouGov found in June that only 35 per cent favoured Rejoin if Britain had to give up all of its old “opt-outs”, including being required to join the euro and the Schengen passport-free travel zone area.

“People think Brexit has failed, and feel cheated,” says Luke Tryl, of the More in Common think-tank. “They are happy to look at going back in but they are really worried about a return to ‘Brexit wars’ — people are exhausted — and that we end up with a crappy deal.”

Burnham has developed a habit since becoming prime minister of opening up debates and then quietly retreating in the face of hostile fire, and any reversal of Brexit will require huge amounts of diplomatic acumen and political willpower both at home and in the EU.

A test of his seriousness and of Europe’s response may come next week, when he travels to Berlin for his first meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

“The EU wants a strategic sense of direction,” says Mujtaba Rahman at Eurasia Group, a consultancy, who contrasts Burnham’s bold gambit with Starmer’s incrementalism. He adds that senior figures in Brussels are “all talking about” the British prime minister’s overtures. “There’s no plan, no detail but he has created the political space to have a conversation.”

rows.title: Struggle to handle Fairford plot shows need for reform, local police chief says
rows.content:
Robert Wright in Quedgeley

Published October 3 2026

The head of the police force first on the scene of last week’s suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford says that its small size, limited finances and decrepit IT systems make it a suitable target for a “merger-acquisition”.

Temporary chief constable Maggie Blyth cited the incident near Fairford — which has led to the arrest of six men on terrorism charges — as the sort of event small forces like hers struggle to manage.

Blyth was speaking as police forces across England and Wales await publication of a report by Lord Bernard Hogan-Howe, a former Metropolitan Police commissioner, setting out his proposals on how best to cut the number of forces in England and Wales from the current 43 to around 20 or fewer.

Hogan-Howe’s report — commissioned by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood — was handed to ministers in September following further consultation with elected mayors to ensure the recommendations fit with the devolution plans of Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

With only 1,200 officers, Gloucestershire Police is one of the UK’s smallest police forces — which Blyth said caused problems coping with incidents like Sunday’s apparent attempted attack at RAF Fairford.

In an interview at Gloucestershire Police’s headquarters in the town of Quedgeley, Blyth said: “I cannot resource some of the specialist capabilities that I might need to have access to when a large, important incident happens or when there’s a pattern of crime and offending that requires specialist capability.”

The Gloucestershire force handled many aspects of the response to the Fairford incident, Blyth added. It also has responsibility for policing other sensitive sites, including the headquarters of the GCHQ security agency in Cheltenham, which is situated in the county. “The force would receive no additional resources to cover the cost of the Fairford operation,” Blyth said.

Neighbouring forces sent officers to help Gloucestershire under “mutual aid” arrangements.

Five men were arrested by armed officers in Whelford, near RAF Fairford, on Sunday, September 27 on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing a terrorist act. They were released on bail the next day. A sixth man was arrested in London on October 1 on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.

The main criminal investigation into the Fairford incident is now being led by Counter Terrorism Policing, a unit of London’s Metropolitan Police.

It is not yet clear what the Hogan-Howe report will recommend and whether ministers will endorse its findings in proposals expected to be published before Christmas.

Blyth, who plans to retire when a permanent replacement is chosen, has long been in favour of her force disappearing in the merger process even before Sunday’s incident.

Blyth said the force had told the government that to balance the books on its current budget would mean cutting critical parts of its operation. Such an outcome would be “nonsensical”, she said.

“It doesn’t make sense to me that you maintain a police force that cannot perform as well in some priority areas as other parts of the country because it’s trying to do everything itself,” she added.

The aim of policing reforms is to ensure forces can develop more specialist teams to tackle hard-to-investigate crimes such as domestic abuse. A new National Police Service will take charge of investigating terrorism and some other complex cases, for example.

Mergers should also help forces make better use of IT — a particular problem for Gloucestershire, which Blyth said was suffering a “technical debt” because of the failure of previous chief constables to invest sufficiently in modern technology.

Blyth said she had already held talks with several neighbouring forces. “We have been very clear and open publicly . . . that we would be a good case for a merger-acquisition,” she added.

The chief constable’s stance contrasts with that of some police leaders elsewhere. The City of London Corporation, local authority for the Square Mile of the City of London, has argued vociferously that it should retain its independent police unit instead of merging with the Met, which Hogan-Howe is expected to recommend.

Tim Passmore, Police and Crime Commissioner for Suffolk, has warned that a potential merger with the neighbouring force in Norfolk would be an “unmitigated disaster”.

Any eventual mergers would be the first in England and Wales since 1974. Most of today’s forces emerged in the wave of consolidation that followed the 1964 Police Act.

The Home Office said it was considering the structure of police forces to ensure every part of the country had “excellent neighbourhood policing” alongside access to the specialist capabilities that communities needed.

It added: “We have received Lord Hogan-Howe’s report and will set out further details in due course.”

Blyth said she hoped that as part of a larger police force, those living in Gloucestershire would reap the benefits of having specialist teams to tackle crimes such as rape and domestic abuse.

“It would be much more sensible to co-ordinate that at a regional level,” Blyth said. “You need to be able to harness specialist investigators and specialist knowledge where you need it.”

She said that such teams could be part of tackling a new policing landscape, in which local incidents, such as the alleged Fairford attack, might have far wider ramifications.

“These days policing goes from the neighbourhood to the regional to the national to the global,” Blyth said. “Policing doesn’t have the need for the boundaries that were set arbitrarily in the 1960s.”

rows.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked Donald Trump to block Russia and China’s Starlink rival
rows.content:
Christopher Miller in Kyiv

Published October 3 2026

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has asked Donald Trump to impose sanctions on Russian and Chinese companies that the Ukrainian president says are involved in developing a rival satellite network to Elon Musk’s Starlink.

Musk earlier this year blocked access to the Kremlin’s forces after they began using SpaceX’s Starlink satellite system to guide drones hitting Ukraine . This has prompted Moscow to accelerate plans to develop its own satellite network, Rassvet, with China’s help, Zelenskyy said.

He told the FT China was working with Russia on the technology and that Rassvet could become operational by “the end of the year, beginning next year”.

“We know that China works on satellites, works on the possibility of helping Russia with a similar Starlink,” Zelenskyy said.

He warned the capability would allow the Kremlin to improve air-strike precision, as Vladimir Putin escalates his aerial campaign against Ukraine in an effort to pummel it into submission this winter.

Zelenskyy said he asked Trump “several times” for his administration to impose sanctions on the entities involved, including in New York last month when he met the US president on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

China’s foreign ministry, the Kremlin and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. Beijing has previously denied Zelenskyy’s allegation that it supports Russia’s army with weapons.

Rob Lee, a Kyiv-based military expert for the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said “Rassvet won’t be as effective as Starlink but Russia could begin to use it to stream [aerial drone] footage to command posts” as a better alternative to WiFi bridges.

He said the satellite network could be used for ground, sea and mid-range strike drones .

Before being blocked, Russian forces used Starlink on their Molniya and Italmas BM-35 aerial drones, which they used to strike high-value targets in Ukraine, Lee said.

Russian brigades still use Starlink inside occupied regions of Ukraine to stream the footage from Mavics — small drones often used for reconnaissance — to command posts, but they lack enough whitelisted terminals to place them on drones, Lee said.

Rassvet could also give a significant boost to Russia’s sabotage campaign against Ukraine’s European allies, according to Lee.

“Drones could be piloted from Moscow using Rassvet in other countries,” he said. The Kremlin’s forces could mirror Ukraine’s own Spiderweb operation that used dozens of small first-person view attack drones against Russian air bases.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said Europe was preparing for “severe” Russian hybrid attacks , as Putin threatened that his conflict with the west could reach a “fatal point of no return”.

Zelenskyy has also lobbied Trump to allow his forces to launch Starlink-equipped drones up to 200km inside Russia against ballistic missile launchers and drone launch sites. Ukraine’s military is currently restricted to using the system within the country’s borders.

Zelenskyy said Trump told him Musk needed to make the call, while Ukraine’s former defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, has said Musk had already agreed and that it was up to the US president to decide.

“President Trump told me that he supports it,” Zelenskyy said on Thursday, and that the US leader added: “Ask Elon.”

SpaceX and Musk did not respond to requests for comment.

Trump in recent weeks has pressed Zelenskyy to halt drone strikes on Russian refineries , which the US president has blamed for driving up American diesel prices, even though the Iran war has been a more significant factor in the increase.

Still, Zelenskyy insisted Starlink-guided drone attacks in Russia could lead to “real de-escalation” and even peace because they would force Putin back to the negotiating table. If the Trump administration or Musk developed concerns, he noted, the system could be easily “switched off”.

Additional reporting by Katya Arenina and Will Langley

rows.title: The ever-shrinking case for expanding Heathrow
rows.content:
Published October 3 2026

To lift his spirits, Hugh Grant’s character in the film Love Actually pictures the joy of those reuniting in Heathrow’s arrivals hall. The UK airport itself is going through much glummer times: its long-discussed £33bn third runway is once again in doubt after Prime Minister Andy Burnham declined to back it last week.

Airports the world over are prone to getting bogged down in arguments over planning, pollution and profit. The debate over the privately funded expansion of the world’s second-best connected airport is all the more emotive because Heathrow is so closely associated with London’s status as a global financial centre. But at this point, whether it goes ahead or not matters more to the national psyche than the UK economy.

Heathrow still has a case to make in favour of its giant infrastructure project. It would create tens of thousands of jobs. Full-service airlines — and not just British Airways, which operates about half of the airport’s slots — grumble at the cost but really want the additional capacity, particularly for hugely profitable North American flights. The third runway also has wide business support. Airports do add more than tourist dollars to their surroundings: the recovery in corporate travel since the pandemic shows that business cannot or does not want to survive by Zoom calls alone.

Yet the extra £2.6bn, or 0.05 per cent, that the runway would add to the UK’s annual GDP by 2056, according to government estimates , could be considered a rounding error in the grand scheme of forecasting.

Besides, the need for giant hubs is being challenged by the rise of long-range narrow-body planes that go to places their bigger predecessors couldn’t. Airbus reckons its A321XLRs could open up more than 1,000 currently unserved routes worldwide. The ability to fly direct between, say, New York and Birmingham International — only two hours’ drive from the capital — would be a reasonable alternative for many passengers.

Even that won’t fully remove the bottlenecks at Heathrow, where about 40 additional airlines are at present seeking access. But political capital and planning capabilities are limited, while Heathrow’s relative position in the pecking order has deteriorated.

Love Actually is, by now, an oldie: it was released in 2003. That’s the same year a third runway at Heathrow, which then handled one in three UK passengers and now caters for about one in four, first won initial government backing. Of the two, the Hugh Grant classic has aged rather better.
