rows.title: The coming futures market in AI compute
rows.content:
Marc Rubinstein

Published October 3 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

The writer is a former hedge fund manager and author of the Net Interest newsletter

You can trade all sorts on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange: soyabeans, precious metals, lean hogs, crude oil, interest rates — all the staples that underpin the world’s economy. Now, CME Group plans to introduce a new commodity to its roster: compute, which it dubs “the new currency for the AI economy”.

“Just as oil fuelled the 20th-century economy and evolved from spot trading into a global derivatives market, our futures contracts will now turn compute into a standardised, tradeable commodity,” said Pete Keavey, the CME executive responsible, when the product was announced in August. Others on Wall Street are equally bullish. “A new asset class will be buying futures of compute,” said BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink in May.

For an exchange, it makes sense to tack on new products, and compute is a potentially large one. Boston Consulting Group estimates that the market for AI compute will climb from $360bn in 2025 to roughly $2.3tn in 2030. If the CME can capture even a fraction of those flows, it will add a lucrative revenue stream.

But just because a market is large doesn’t make it ripe for trading. Research on the origins of futures markets finds that between two-thirds and three-quarters of new contracts fail to attract and sustain a profitable level of trading volume. For compute derivatives to flourish the way oil derivatives have, they must satisfy a number of conditions.

First, underlying prices need to be volatile enough to make hedging worthwhile. Speculators may supply liquidity to a futures market, but it is commercial hedgers that give them their economic purpose. On this test, the case for compute is fairly strong. Long lead times bringing new capacity on stream can make pricing quite volatile.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Oracle’s Project Jupiter data centre build illustrates the point. The facility is due to come online in 2028 but has faced setbacks, ​including delays to a planned natural-gas pipeline and legal challenges over water and air-quality permits. More generally, when chip bottlenecks were tightest at the beginning of 2024, hourly rental rates for one of Nvidia’s H100 chips spiked as high as $8, before falling below $2 in late 2025. That kind of variance is something participants may want to hedge.

Second, participants need to agree on a standardised contract. When oil futures listed in 1983, they were designed to reference West Texas Intermediate, with Cushing, Oklahoma chosen as the physical delivery point. Although WTI accounts for only a small percentage of global crude output, it serves as a pricing benchmark for the rest of the market. In contrast, pioneers of bandwidth trading in 1999 struggled to converge on a standard. Reliability, quality and bandwidth services varied too widely and attempts to fashion a market collapsed with its champion, Enron.

Working with index provider Silicon Data, CME Group has chosen Nvidia’s H100 and B200 chips as the reference for its contracts. According to Silicon Data, capacity on a B200 can be rented for $5.86 per hour; $2.77 on the older H100. CME plans to list contracts that reflect the future value of these rental rates, going out 36 months.

But even a GPU-hour is not fully standardised. Performance varies with cluster configuration, networking, software and location. Rapid obsolescence fragments the market further: an H100-hour is not interchangeable with a B200-hour, which is why CME needs separate contracts for each. Nor is there consensus over how to measure even those rental rates. Another index provider, Ornn, has its own benchmark, and the two do not always align. Until a consensus forms, a derivatives market may be slow to build.

Finally, a vibrant derivatives market requires a diverse group of buyers and sellers. Onion futures were explicitly banned in 1958 in the US after two traders cornered the market. Compute is unlikely to be cornered in quite the same way, but it is already highly concentrated. Nvidia dominates chip supply, hyperscalers control much of the available capacity and a handful of AI laboratories account for much of the demand.

CME Group’s compute futures will attract plenty of attention when they list. The price of compute increasingly bears on the economics of AI, the value of its infrastructure and the vast investment boom surrounding it. This gives investors good reason to want a benchmark for it. Bears may recall the ABX subprime index, which illuminated a previously opaque corner of mortgage finance — and became a focal point for the unwind that followed. Whether it validates the boom or punctures it, compute futures may ultimately matter more as a signal than as a market.

rows.title: Record 12,000 complaints made against Lasting Powers of Attorney
rows.content:
Aliya Shibli

Published October 3 2026

The number of complaints about alleged financial misconduct by those acting under a Lasting Power of Attorney has risen to a record level, new data shows.

Complaints of financial misconduct rose to 11,910 in the year ending March 2026, up from 10,240 in the previous 12 months and 9,538 in the year before that, according to data from the Ministry of Justice obtained under a freedom of information request by law firm TWM Solicitors.

In response to complaints, just 263 attorneys had their authority revoked or partially revoked by the Court of Protection during the year, according to the law firm.

Stuart Downey, partner and head of will, trust and estate disputes at TWM, said the figures highlight the potential for financial abuse where an attorney misuses the authority given to them under an LPA.

“The record number of complaints about financial misconduct is concerning, particularly where the donor is elderly or otherwise vulnerable. An LPA gives an attorney considerable authority over another person’s affairs, so there needs to be confidence that appropriate safeguards are available when that authority is abused,” Downey said.

An LPA enables someone to appoint a person they trust to make decisions on their behalf if they are unable to do so themselves, such as in the case of illness or loss of mental capacity. There are two types: an LPA for a person’s health and welfare and one for their property and financial affairs.

The roles can include managing bank accounts and other finances, as well as making decisions such as selling the person’s home, and are often held by family members or other people known to the donor rather than professional advisers.

Problems involving LPAs can include financial fraud or mismanagement, as well as unauthorised decisions relating to residential property.

Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, said: “Inheritance is now the mechanism by which most people are able to transform their standard of living in our country, so the stakes are incredibly high.”

“It would be nice to think that we were all more high-minded than that, but at a time when living standards are so constrained that is probably asking too much,” Abrahams added.

Where there are serious concerns about an attorney’s conduct, the Office of the Public Guardian and the Court of Protection can intervene.

However, the process can be complex and daunting for families, Downey said. “Unfortunately, my experience is that protecting the vulnerable against financial abuse is not as easy as it should be.”

He added that unexplained withdrawals, unusual transfers of money, changes to property arrangements or an attorney preventing family members from seeing the donor could all warrant further investigation.

“It remains a very good idea to have [a Power of Attorney], and really the earlier the better, but it is certainly important to think carefully about who you choose,” Abrahams said.

“What matters most in this context is what is objectively best for the older person, but this can be hard to disentangle from family relationships and emotions. Taking expert advice can help.”

rows.title: A senate race runs through the Maine woods
rows.content:
Siona Jenkins

Published October 3 2026

On a bright morning in late September, there is little sign of the political storm that has rolled in and settled over Maine. Driving south on East Ridge Road towards the village of Harmony in Somerset County, the sky is a deep, cloudless blue and the air is tinged with a crisp chill that presages the changing season. The area’s famous foliage is just starting to change colour, with bright red spots appearing in the mass of green along the roadside.

I turn left at the Harmony gas station, where Maga paraphernalia is sold alongside chainsaw parts, and follow a road which takes me into the forest. At a clearing in the trees I find the house of Kathryn Thompson, a gravel-voiced 79-year-old. She is with her friend Mary Stuart, a former primary school teacher in Somerset County who lives in the nearby village of Canaan. Both arrived here in the 1970s as part of the back-to-the-land movement that saw groups of young Americans leave cities in search of a simpler life, subsistence farming in rural communities.

“We ended up here because the land was cheap,” says Thompson, laughing, as we sip coffee on the deck. She tells me how she and her husband built their home, which I later discover still has no indoor plumbing. For $9,500 they bought 70 acres. “The locals said we got ripped off,” she says.

The two women saw Somerset County as a chance to change their lives. When they got there they found a farming community in decline. Once thriving farmland had, in much of the area, gradually been taken over by forest. “The old-timers were delighted we were here,” Thompson says. “They were happy that there were younger people coming back and farming, because, you know, their kids didn’t want that life.”

Logging was a mainstay of the county’s economy and there were jobs in sawmills and leather factories on the nearby Kennebec River. Still, the women were struck by the poverty in the area. “You would hear the old-timers say, ‘You know, the Depression came and we didn’t know the difference’,” says Thompson. Stuart nods: “The one thing I really noticed was that so many women had missing teeth. And the men often had a full set of dentures.”

Over time, the area would change politically too. In the 1970s and ’80s, Somerset County leaned “more Democratic”, according to Thompson. The mill workers belonged to unions that were Democrat-supporting back then. But things changed when the mills closed in the 2000s, and “it really shifted with Trump”. He has won the county in each of the past three presidential elections, while narrowly losing the state overall.

On a previous visit last autumn, however, there were signs that a populist Democrat could be changing minds again in Somerset County. Cycling along East Ridge Road, I was struck by the roadside signs supporting Graham Platner, a charismatic oyster farmer campaigning to become the Democratic candidate for Senate in the forthcoming midterm elections. Then, this July, his campaign blew up spectacularly after he was accused of sexual assault. (Platner denies the allegations.)

With the deadline for the party to choose a candidate just weeks away, Troy Jackson, a former logger from a long line of loggers, and a longtime representative in the state legislature, was hastily chosen to replace Platner. Jackson goes up against the Republican incumbent Susan Collins, a five-term senator who has maintained support by positioning herself as a moderate in a state evenly split between “red” and “blue” counties. The Republicans’ thin majority in the Senate could be lost if the Democrats take at least four seats without losing any they already hold. Before his downfall, it appeared that Platner could have won over Republican voters in places like Somerset County. But could Jackson reach them too?

I ask Thompson and Stuart what they make of the situation. Neither is a fan of the president but, they tell me, they don’t know much about Jackson either.

To find out more, I head to his home county of Aroostook, a 17,280 sq km expanse with just 66,600 inhabitants, which includes Jackson’s home settlement of Allagash. To get there, I drive north on the interstate through 140 miles of forest. Township names are often numbered designations, such as T9-RS, denoting little or no human habitation.

I turn off just before the town of Houlton, near the Canadian border, and head to Wood Prairie Family Farm to meet Jim Gerritsen, a 71-year-old seed potato farmer who has lived in the area for 50 years. He hands me a catalogue of the potatoes he grows as we sit at a table outside, the air cooler than further south. “We’re usually a week or so ahead on leaves changing up here,” he tells me.

Aroostook, like other parts of rural Maine, is “Trump country”, Gerritsen tells me, which he blames partly on the national Democrats for “not knowing how to run a party” and doing “a terrible job of communicating”. But he thinks Jackson, who represented the district for several years, can cut through. An articulate and outspoken advocate of organic farming, Gerritsen has worked with Jackson to draw up Maine’s organic food standards and described him as “courageous”. “He’s always sacrificing himself for the common good, and if there could be a better litmus test in politics, I don’t know what it is,” he says.

Gerritsen also knows the Collins family, who are from the area and run the local “building supply monopoly”, as he calls it. “There’s nothing more working class in the state of Maine than a logger,” Gerritsen says. “Susan Collins is from the other end of the spectrum… There’s this idea that she’s a moderate . . . but she’s a moderate that votes 96 per cent of the time with Trump.”

Like many other small businesses, Wood Prairie Family Farm is being hit by high fuel costs, which Gerritsen blames squarely on the White House. Even on a family farm that is not highly mechanised “there are things that need to be done, and whether diesel is $3 a gallon, $6 a gallon, or $10 a gallon, you’ve got to do it. You’ve just got to take that on the chin,” he says. He is hopeful that Jackson’s strategy, as he sees it — “putting yourself behind working people and their interests” — is a winning one.

In Somerset County I meet a logger who disagrees. The fact that Jackson is a fellow logger is “kind of irrelevant”, says Kyle Morrison. “I just don’t agree with most of the Democrats’ policies.”

Morrison is a softly spoken 41-year-old Harmony native who works in the family business and spends most days in the forest. His grandparents were Democrats, like many older people in the area, but he is a Republican. There are pros and cons with Trump, he says, but “the biggest pro was that he made me pay attention”. Morrison admits the price of diesel , which has soared to record highs since the president launched the war on Iran in February, has made life harder. “I support Trump, but I’m not a big fan of the war going on,” he says. “It’s taking a pretty good chunk of the profits.”

We’re sitting in his airy kitchen on a Saturday morning, as Dexter, his black labrador, lies patiently nearby. Morrison drops the dog at Kathryn Thompson’s house early each morning before heading into the forest to work. The two are family friends and he usually loads logs into her wood stove as the labrador trots into the house. “We look after each other around here,” Thompson tells me later. But they’ve had to steer clear of politics lately. They’ve argued “many times”, Morrison says. “I don’t think it’s healthy for our relationship to talk politics.”

Brad Farrin is also taking a step back from politics. He’s about to retire as Somerset County’s state senator and return to his home in the village of Norridgewock, where he has a full-time job working for a construction equipment supplier and can spend more time with his children and grandchildren.

We’re chatting in the handsome State House in Augusta, Maine’s capital. Farrin, a former national guardsman, has done a 12-year stint here, also serving in the state assembly. “When I first started serving down here, I felt there was a lot more common ground,” he tells me. “People still were willing to serve, to try to do good for the constituents, and good for the state of Maine. Some of my dearest friends and relationships I built down here have been on the other side of the aisle.” Now, he says, the spirit of compromise seems to “really have diminished”. Farrin, a Republican, says he is as frustrated with the far right as the far left.

He hopes the strong sense of community in Somerset County and the state as a whole will keep at bay the partisan divides that have riven much of the country. “It doesn’t matter whether you’re a Democrat or a Republican or an independent, that sense of community that you don’t get in a lot of the bigger places, I think is really important.”

Farrin believes Susan Collins, whom he considers a friend, will win a sixth term because she “truly loves the state of Maine”. Platner’s rise was “more a testimony to the Trump factor than the Susan factor”, he adds. Having worked with Jackson at close quarters, Farrin blames him and the Democrats for higher labour and energy costs in the state. “I hope common sense prevails in the midterms,” he says.

Two hours east of the Somerset County woods is the pretty coastal town of Blue Hill. I pass through its picturesque main street, with its clapboard shops and restaurants, before reaching the home of Nina Milliken, the district’s Democratic representative in the state assembly. It’s mid-afternoon and we sit on her deck in the sunshine.

Milliken tells me that Hancock County, where her district sits, straddles rural and urban areas, which has given her an insight into Maine’s political divisions. “Sometimes policy arguments seem partisan, but what they are is urban-rural,” she says.

Milliken knows Jackson well and believes that he can also appeal to voters. “Troy didn’t inherit [Platner’s] platform; he’s had that platform this entire time,” she says. “He’s a phenomenal legislator. He’s not as charismatic as Graham but he’s got the same message.”

She believes moderate Democrats, many of whom have supported Collins in past elections, will desert her this year. She also worries that the resources being poured into Collins’ campaign could tip the race: nearly 100 billionaires and their spouses had already donated to her re-election campaign, according to The Maine Monitor, a local news site, in June.

Back in Somerset County I drive through the small hamlet of Athens to meet John Alsop, the county commissioner for the towns of Skowhegan and Cornville, through which East Ridge Road runs. Commissioners are non-partisan and they mostly decide budgets, he tells me as we sit on his porch, looking out over fields and trees. “It’s kind of a management job; it’s not really political.”

A retired lawyer, he has lived here for nearly 50 years, serving as an assistant district attorney and a probate judge, as well as working in private practice. Alsop doesn’t think the area has changed that much over the years. “It’s always been a pretty conservative place . . . of what are now described as ‘Rinos’ [Republicans in Name Only] but used to be old-fashioned centre Republicans” – although “some people on the right have become more vocal than they’re accustomed to being”, he says, smiling.

He thinks Platner was “the right man or person at the right time to express what a lot of people are feeling”. Collins will be hard to beat now that Platner is out, he says.

As November draws closer, the campaigning in Maine has become fierce and polls show a close Senate race. But there is little sign of Jackson’s message reaching crucial voters in Somerset County. A Jackson town hall meeting scheduled for Skowhegan in the final week of September was moved to the Democratic stronghold of Portland in the south of the state.

Before I leave Maine I drive along East Ridge Road one more time, to meet another logger at his cabin near the village of Solon. More of the trees are starting to reveal their autumn colours, but this time there are few political signs on the verge.

Peter Pfeifer is a Maine native who left for university then returned and settled in the woods, where he has lived for nearly 50 years. His cabin is off-grid, with solar panels and a wood stove, but it contains a well-stocked library and he’s a keen observer of local politics. “Graham Platner was like a prairie fire,” Pfeifer tells me. “We’re all very disappointed.” He also believes that while the Democratic Party’s chances of taking the Senate will be helped if Jackson can rekindle some of that excitement in rural Maine, it could come down to the candidate whose name is not on the ballot.

“It’ll be a vote about Trump,” says Pfeifer. “Either for or against.”

Siona Jenkins is the FT’s US political news editor

rows.title: China, America and the new Great Game
rows.content:
Rana Foroohar

Published October 3 2026

You know the US-China relationship has reached a low point when the best that can be accomplished during a major bilateral summit is the loan of two giant pandas. That was Xi Jinping’s gift to Donald Trump last week. The two leaders took the requisite photos overlooking the White House Rose Garden and issued statements about long-term co-operation after a meeting that Trump called “very productive”. But the truth was plain to see.

Whatever happens next, no amount of trade concessions over soyabeans or rare earths will change the fact that the two countries are in a strategic conflict that will shape the global political economy for years to come. The fact that there was so little news from the summit doesn’t mean there isn’t much to say. It means that there is no resolution in sight to what will be a generational stand-off.

It’s not a new problem. The idea of a Thucydides Trap — the notion that a rising power inevitably challenges the incumbent, with a subsequent war often leading to a shift in the global order — goes back to the ancient Greeks. Xi Jinping referenced it at the September summit, optimistically offering that the “trap can be overcome”.

Possibly, but while the Thucydides Trap is a nice metaphor, it may not be the best practical historical analogy for what is happening between the US and China. The Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta was won and done in 27 years. The geostrategic competition between the US and China has been — and will be — with us for many decades.

In that sense, it has much in common with the Great Game between Britain and Russia in the 1800s — a century-long struggle that drew allies and adversaries alike into multiple regional conflicts involving both competition and collaboration. Then, as now, mercantilism was the driving force. Britain’s 19th-century wealth and influence had been built off the back of colonial dominance, particularly in India. Finding a passage to India, with its enormous mineral and trade riches, had been a dream of Russian leaders for a hundred years. Thus ensued decades of moves and countermoves by both empires to control the Caucasus, Afghanistan, Persia, Tibet and ultimately India.

The same paradigm exists today in the US-China relationship. Both countries look to secure and increase their wealth and power in a world that has moved beyond the Washington Consensus era of free trade, open borders and decreased conflict. Like the Great Game of the 19th century, the US-China conflict today is both economic and political, geographic and virtual, a battle about territorial spheres of influence but also broader systems dominance. Then, as now, middle powers and vassal nations are drawn into the larger conflict, shifting positions and changing sides as it suits them.

The Great Game, a term popularised by Rudyard Kipling, pitted an incumbent global power — Britain — against Russian tsars eager to extend their growing empire into new territories. For Britain, the battle was somewhat defensive; it was about making sure that Russia did not acquire a route into India or make Afghanistan a Russian dependency. For Russia, it was about imperial expansion and self-determination. Just as Russian tsars wanted to dominate (rather than be dominated by) their Asian and European neighbours, so the Chinese look to shape the post-neoliberal world order, rather than be reshaped by it.

Today, the US is of course the established hegemon, and China the challenger trying to move into new territory. Consider how Beijing is exerting more control, both within and beyond its own territorial waters of the South and East China seas, causing alarm among members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). As early as 2013, China began a series of dredging operations to build seven islands in the South China Sea, all of which support military logistics.

By creating more coastline in the territorial waters of other countries, China could claim sovereignty over one of the world’s most important trade channels. It’s a classic Great Game-style land grab, mirroring the way in which Russia eventually absorbed the Kazakh steppes and various Turkmen territories and used infrastructure builds (such as the Trans-Caspian railway) to move ever closer to the Afghan and Persian frontiers.

China is also extending its trade and payment systems into regions such as Africa and Latin America. Indeed, Trump’s ousting of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in January was in part a reaction to Beijing’s growing influence not only there but in places such as Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Peru.

China is South America’s leading trading partner, surpassing both the US and EU, as well as a major investor in infrastructure projects via the Belt and Road Initiative. Consider the Peruvian megaport at Chancay , envisioned as a future “Shanghai of South America”. China owns 60 per cent of the facility and has exclusive operational rights for what will eventually be the largest of its kind in Latin America.

In the domain of infrastructure and maritime power, one could argue that China increasingly occupies the role that Great Britain once did. The US may still have the world’s strongest navy, but China owns the shipbuilding and maritime industrial complex , which is arguably more important since 90 per cent of military combat vessels’ equipment and supplies are delivered by commercial ships. Not only is the US Navy not able to police the entire world, but the US maritime industry lacks the logistical capacity required to get around a blockade of, say, Taiwan — whose future sovereignty has become a major question in the new Great Game.

China owns commercial shipping, a major advantage in its strategic competition with the US. As Carlos del Toro, President Joe Biden’s former secretary of the Navy, who pushed hard for the US to build commercial ships again, puts it: “No great naval power has long endured without also being a maritime power — a commercial shipping and shipbuilding power.”

Shipping is as important as it ever was to global supply chains; so are ports. Today, almost half the leading container ports outside China have some Chinese ownership or operations. In the western hemisphere, that includes three locations in Mexico, a stake in the Panama Canal, and ports in the Caribbean and Argentina as well as Peru.

In the 19th century, British naval power was the silver thread that connected industrial production, trade, imperial communications, colonial natural resources and London finance (sterling was then, like the dollar today, a global currency, albeit in a far less expansive way). Today, China’s maritime dominance functions in much the same way, allowing Beijing to dominate global supply chains, increase manufacturing capacity abroad and lay claim to new natural resources.

This is apparent even in places as far-flung as the Arctic , which has become a new zone for great power competition thanks to its gas and mineral resources, and new trade and transit routes. The US is building icebreakers with Finland to expand its limited reach into the High North, even as the Chinese have opened a weekly transpolar shipping route across Russian territorial waters.

China’s efforts to forge a “Polar Silk Road” reflect deep thinking about global chokepoints, which will be ground zero for this new Great Game, as they were in the old one. Just as control of chokepoints such as the Khyber Pass or the Caspian Sea was crucial to British and Russian strategy, so the Northern Sea Route has become a Chinese hedge against blockage of the Suez and Panama canals, and global ports and agricultural land (China has been buying it globally for years) a hedge against trade wars.

What’s more, the chokepoints today aren’t just geographical, but also virtual. The British controlled 19th-century communications via telegraph. Today, both the US and China are squaring off to control AI and financial systems. While the US still holds advantage in terms of the latter, China is gaining with the former, offering to train developing countries in its own open-source AI models through “application co-operation centres”. A new 29-member World AI Cooperation Organization will put forward Chinese AI solutions around the world, much as US-based organisations did for American standards in the 1990s.

In the 1800s, as now, the great powers staged their war for supremacy across buffer states. India and central Asia were the 19th-century focus. Today, however, nearly every country in the world has skin in the game when it comes to US-China great power competition. In the east, countries such as Japan, South Korea and Australia look to form new trade and security alliances — sometimes with the US, sometimes not — to offset Chinese influence. In the northern hemisphere, Canada, Finland and others are allying to protect themselves against both Chinese and US pressure. In Europe, China warns of retaliation against EU efforts to fight back against Chinese dumping, even as Beijing courts individual member states such as Spain and Germany, as well as others like the UK.

Some countries in conflict areas are themselves trying to pit the superpowers against each other as they look for the best deal. One case in point: Greenland is using its position as a security linchpin in the High North to draw investment from Europe (which looks to offset Trump’s obsession with the territory). Canada is doing more trade with China in the wake of Trump’s bizarre trade war with America’s northern neighbour. Iceland’s electorate recently rejected the idea of opening talks to join the EU. But it is strengthening European security ties, signing a new defence partnership last spring that covers Arctic affairs.

Then, as now, countries could be “frenemies” amid the power struggle. In the 19th century, Russia and France fought together and against each other at different times. The Afghans and Persians frequently changed their allegiances. Today, China and Russia are partners in the Arctic. China, Russia, Iran and North Korea also represent a kind of anti-American axis. But the alliances are fragile, as are US relationships with allies such as Canada, the EU, Japan and South Korea.

The new Great Game could well last as long as the old. One could draw a direct line from the British and Russian battles over Afghanistan — the “graveyard of empires”, as Milton Bearden, former CIA station chief in Pakistan, dubbed it in a 2001 article for Foreign Affairs — to the conflict between the US and Russia, which is arguably a Chinese vassal state today (albeit a very large one). As the British journalist Peter Hopkirk wrote in 1990, “Some would maintain that the Great Game never really ceased, and that it was merely the forerunner of the cold war of our own times, fuelled by the same fears, suspicions and misunderstandings.”

Of course, there are many differences between then and now. Climate change is a huge driver of the new Great Game. This is most evident in a literal sense in the Arctic, where melting ice has opened the new trade and commerce pathways being exploited by both sides. But it is also part of China’s core strategy to own the clean energy future.

The fact that the EU exists as a third pole between the US and China today creates some pushback to both nations’ most rapacious tendencies. Although we think we are living through a breakdown of institutions, the 19th century was a Wild West in that respect. Legal frameworks and multilateralism are still much more solid now than they were two centuries ago.

This means that buffer states have real power — witness how “middle powers” such as Canada can broker new trade and security alliances. Europe’s “open door” offer to Canada to become an associate member of the EU is the best case of an anti-Great Game dynamic in play today. In the 19th century, Afghanistan, Persia, Tibet and Central Asian khanates were typically too divided to stand against Russia or Britain.

So what lessons should we take from history as we think about the outcome of the new Great Game?

Getting ahead of the battle is key. Russia and Britain preferred to beat each other to a given territory, control a chokepoint or be the first to exploit resources and alliances, rather than engage in direct combat. This “forward strategy” avoids outright war but also leads to all sorts of intrigues, minor battles and shadow conflicts. The war in Ukraine, the weaponisation of the Strait of Hormuz and the simmering tensions over Taiwan are all part and parcel of the new Great Game.

Which country wins — and indeed whether there can be an ultimate winner — depends on how you define the terms of engagement. In the 19th century, Russia accumulated more territory and influence in Central Asia, but Britain retained systemic control over global finance, maritime pathways, communications technology and Indian natural resources. As Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, put it in a speech at the Economic Club of New York this summer, “the next era of economic competition will not be confined to the movement of goods across oceans and ports. It will be shaped by the platforms, systems and protocols through which commerce flows in the 21st century.”

In that framing, one could make a strong argument that the US is still in a good place. It retains the advantages of the dollar as the world’s global reserve currency (though that place ebbs a bit with each new Treasury auction), as well as the world’s richest and most powerful technology companies. Global waterways, while increasingly filled with Chinese ships, are still free. Global commerce still flows, on Chinese ships perhaps, but mainly priced in US dollars. Territorial disputes over Taiwan and Greenland have been held at bay for the time being.

Viewed another way, China could also seem to be in pole position. Not only does it control the physical infrastructure of the economy (in the form of industrial capacity, supply chains, transport logistics and key raw materials such as rare earths), it controls some of the highest-value technologies, such as clean tech and electric vehicles. Renminbi-based electronic payment systems are where the most financial innovation is being done. Chinese political and economic influence is extending well into America’s own backyard.

But one thing to remember from both the old and new Great Games is that outside nations can swing the battle. Afghans and Persians repeatedly foiled the plans of both Britain and Russia. And it was ultimately the rise of Germany that ended the Great Game, by shifting the entire geostrategic chessboard westward. Today, India, Japan, Canada, Turkey, the Gulf states, Nordic nations, Asean and the EU are hardly passive. Their choices, not just the aspirations of America and China, may decide our 21st-century power struggle.

Rana Foroohar is the FT’s global business columnist and associate editor. Her book ‘Sea Change: America’s New Great Game in the Arctic’ will be published in the US by Crown on October 6 and in the UK by Swift Press on October 12

rows.title: Trouble in Auroville, India’s ‘City of Dawn’
rows.content:
Chris Kay

Published October 3 2026

The bulldozers came as the mid-afternoon sun filtered through the lush green canopy of the Darkali forest in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu.

It was December 9 2021 and trouble had been brewing for days in Auroville. The previous weekend, the first yellow JCB had arrived in the community in the dead of night and rolled towards the youth centre. Along with hundreds of trees, the centre, which had hosted workshops, festivals and pizza nights since the 1990s, had been marked for clearance to make way for a new road.

As the word spread, residents rushed out into the darkness to protect the building. By dawn, Auroville was on high alert. Some people sat on the deep red earth in front of the rumbling diggers, organising round-the-clock watches for the days to come. Tempers flared and scuffles broke out. What was happening felt to many like a profound rupture.

Frederick Schulze-Buxloh was among them. Tall and lean, with clipped grey hair, light-blue eyes, tanned skin and thick hands, the German was known to nearly everyone in Auroville: he had spent much of his life fighting for the survival of this strange utopian community, tucked beneath a dense tropical forest of some three million trees — acacia, banyan, neem — planted by its inhabitants over the past half century.

But Frederick was now in his eighties and recovering from cancer. Better, he had thought, to leave this fight to younger Aurovilians. Then, as he sipped his coffee at home that sunny afternoon a few days later, his son-in-law arrived with alarming news: “Frederick, you better go there because your daughter is standing in front of a running JCB.”

When he arrived in the forest, the scene was chaotic. A crowd of Aurovilians surrounded the machines, bodies damp with sweat, facing off against a group they accused of being hired goondas or thugs. One woman screamed repeatedly: “No violence!” Another pleaded: “You are brothers. Please don’t fight us. We love you.”

Frederick did not know what possessed him as he moved through the crowd. He suddenly felt an overwhelming compulsion to climb into the digger’s scoop. As the stand-off cooled, a number of people locked hands and a gentle chanting broke out. When an official from Auroville’s governing body eventually arrived, Frederick calmly confronted him. “I know you have to follow orders,” he said. “But we also have to follow our inner order . . . We will make it impossible for them to enter.”

Auroville is an anomaly in India , more so than any ashram, commune or cult. Its residents, about 3,000 people from more than 60 nations, are a mix of spiritual idealists, elderly hippies who arrived decades ago, younger generations born of those pioneers and new arrivals searching for inner truth. Founded in 1968 as an experiment in human unity and social evolution, it has governed itself through painstaking consensus for nearly 60 years. The community has no private ownership, a semi-autonomous economy and has historically been able to secure long-term visas for its foreign residents. It is also home to one of India’s most remarkable rewilding efforts. Over the decades, as the rest of the country has rapidly urbanised, Auroville has moved in the other direction — become greener and wilder. Darkali, where the bulldozers were now advancing, was part of that achievement. Now, it was under threat.

Tensions had been building over the months since the appointment that year of Jayanti Ravi, a senior civil servant, as the secretary of the Auroville Foundation, part of the settlement’s complex governing structure. Since her arrival, some residents had been alarmed by what they saw as a reckless and increasingly dictatorial approach to development. It felt as though the outside world had broken in and was encroaching on the community.

Critics accused Ravi of orchestrating an unlawful takeover of Auroville’s institutions, installing loyalists in key positions and overriding the community’s group-driven decision-making. They said Auroville’s founding ideals were being hollowed out and that a planned expansion would transform it into a “spiritual Disneyland”.

Some saw the struggle as emblematic of a broader effort by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to take control of India’s cultural, religious and philosophical institutions and extend its reach. Tamil Nadu is one of the few major states that has never been governed by the party. But beneath the confrontation lay a deeper unease about privilege and belonging in postcolonial India.

Ravi and her backers saw Auroville as stagnating. They said it was no longer functioning effectively to fulfil the dream of its founders. One of Ravi’s supporters accused the crowd at Darkali that day, which included many white foreigners, of being “guilty” of living on large tracts of land in an overcrowded country. Neither Ravi nor the Auroville Foundation responded to requests from the FT for comment on this story.

The events in December 2021 marked the beginning of a battle that would consume Auroville for years, triggering lawsuits, expulsions and allegations of land grabs. More than 100 residents are estimated to have left since then, and many foreigners who remain fear they will have to leave India. “Until then, people were living in a bit of a bubble,” said one Aurovilian, of the moment the bulldozers came. “We were naive.”

Frederick was one of Auroville’s founders . His childhood was overshadowed by the second world war. Heir to a family fortune built on industry and mining, he was shaken by Germany’s wartime legacy and the horrors of the Holocaust. In the wreckage of Europe, he recalled feeling “like an alien”.

He was 20 when he headed east, unsure what he was searching for. In 1959, he reached Bombay by boat and joined a group of hippies and privileged dropouts drawn to India by ideas of mysticism, freedom and adventure. On his travels, Frederick became intrigued by the teachings of one Indian sage: a Calcutta-born, anti-colonial revolutionary who had moved to the French territory of Pondicherry on the south-eastern coast to evade British authorities. His name was Sri Aurobindo. In 1960, Frederick travelled to his ashram where he encountered an elderly woman: Blanche Rachel Mirra Alfassa, known simply as The Mother.

Alfassa had been born in Paris in 1878 to a wealthy Sephardic Jewish family. She practised occultism in Algeria before visiting Pondicherry in 1914. When she met Sri Aurobindo, she identified him as the “dark Asiatic figure” of her visions. Aurobindo regarded her as a spiritual equal. When he retired into permanent seclusion in 1926, The Mother became his link to the outside world and the administrator of his growing ashram. After Aurobindo’s death in 1950, Alfassa inherited its leadership and, by the end of the decade, the ashram had expanded into one of India’s largest spiritual communities, with about 1,200 members. “She became this goddess if you will,” said one person connected to the ashram.

Alfassa did not seem especially divine to Frederick: a frail old woman with kind eyes and a drooping face. Yet during their first meeting, his knees buckled. Frederick felt as though he were being “turned around” and forced to look inward. He devoted himself to one of The Mother’s grandest ambitions: building Auroville, the “City of Dawn”. On the harsh red earth north of Pondicherry, she envisioned a new international society, where labour would be spiritual practice and money would no longer reign. The project’s charter declared: “Auroville belongs to nobody in particular. Auroville belongs to humanity as a whole. But, to live in Auroville, one must be a willing servitor of the Divine Consciousness.”

Those ideals captivated the young hippies who had begun arriving. Johnny Allen, an Australian architect, was one of them. He toiled alongside roughly a hundred other foreign settlers as they built homes from bamboo and thatch, dug wells and tried to coax life from the brutally parched landscape. “We were very disorganised,” Allen recalled. “We hadn’t got a clue what we were doing.”

The anti-materialistic experiment was sustained partly by wealthy “Trustafarians”. Frederick says he passed much of his own inheritance to The Mother. And, at least initially, funds flowed freely.

The Mother commissioned French architect Roger Anger to give form to her vision. He conceived a swirling “Galaxy” plan for a future city of 50,000 people. At its centre would stand the Matrimandir, a spheric golden meditation chamber surrounded by radiating roads. In practice, however, Auroville’s early inhabitants were less concerned with grand urban blueprints than their immediate survival, and they set about planting trees to protect themselves against the fierce sun.

The project captured the mood of the era. Unesco endorsed it, and Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, who had visited the ashram and developed a close relationship with The Mother, gave her backing too. Months before its official launch, Frederick’s first child was born. The boy was regarded as Auroville’s first child and The Mother christened him Auroson.

The township’s inauguration in February 1968 was attended by some 5,000 people. Representatives of 124 nations and 23 Indian states gathered around an amphitheatre, each depositing a handful of soil into a giant urn as a symbol of unity. Frederick delivered a speech broadcast on All India Radio, brimming with utopian confidence.

“Ten years from now Auroson will have a city-in-the-making as his playground . . . A planetary city,” he declared. “Computers will answer his questions, televisions and radiotelescopes will narrate the cosmic stories.”

Weeks later, Auroson drowned in a pool in Pondicherry. The accident lanced Auroville’s early optimism. The Mother told his heartbroken parents that the child had been sickly. “Make a new body,” she told Frederick and his Swedish partner. He would later write in his authored recollections of The Mother that she told others that Auroson was with her and she would reinsert the soul.

The Mother’s own death in 1973, when she was 95 years old, had devastating ramifications. Without her authority, the experiment entered one of its darkest periods. A power struggle erupted over Auroville’s governance. The Sri Aurobindo Society, the non-profit organisation that owned Auroville’s land, was led by Indian ashramites, accustomed to deference and respect. The young western settlers, by contrast, were deeply suspicious of centralised control. As relations deteriorated, the society started to withhold visa recommendations and financial allowances unless residents fell into line. Many refused. Supplies dwindled and food shortages became commonplace. Some Aurovilians embraced zealous interpretations of Sri Aurobindo’s teachings, rejecting conventional medicine and education in favour of yoga and Ayurveda. Serious illnesses went untreated. Cult-like behaviour spread, including mass head-shaving and book-burning.

Frederick became one of the leading figures resisting the society. One night he slept inside the township’s auditorium to assert Aurovilian control. At dawn, half a dozen shirtless, drunken men beat him severely. Photographs of him lying bloodied, his face cut and swollen, circulated through the community. He and others lobbied politicians in New Delhi relentlessly for support. Some of the friendships Frederick forged came from unlikely quarters. At an exhibition about Auroville in Bombay, he struck up a conversation with JRD Tata, the chairman of India’s largest industrial conglomerate, who used his influence to support Auroville’s cause.

By 1980, the government took control of the community by force, leading to the 1988 Auroville Foundation Act, which established a hybrid governance structure comprising political appointees, an international advisory council and a residents’ assembly. The City of Dawn developed at a snail’s pace but in 2008 the gold-panelled Matrimandir, its spiritual nucleus, was finally complete. As Frederick sensed soon after the legislation was passed, “Auroville has suddenly been propelled on to a totally different scale.”

In February 2018, Modi entered the Matrimandir. Barefoot and dressed in a white short-sleeved kurta, the prime minister climbed a spiral ramp bathed in golden-pink light into its hushed inner chamber. Visitors to the temple are warned that even the slightest cough can echo like an explosion in the white-carpeted sanctuary, illuminated by a shaft of light falling on a crystal globe. After meditating inside, Modi descended to pour water collected from three of India’s sacred rivers, the Ganga, Kaveri and Narmada, into a lotus-shaped marble pond.

At the auditorium where Frederick had been attacked four decades earlier, Modi praised the philosophy of Sri Aurobindo and The Mother in a speech to mark Auroville’s 50th anniversary. “The progress of humanity calls for continuous thinking and rethinking, so that the human mind does not become frozen into one idea,” he said.

Not everyone welcomed his visit. The BJP had become increasingly interested in Sri Aurobindo, seeking to claim the philosopher as a supporter of their Hindu nationalism, despite his warnings against communal politics.

Three years later, a new civil servant took charge as secretary of the Auroville Foundation. Jayanti Ravi charmed many residents when she arrived in the summer of 2021. Her credentials were impressive: degrees in nuclear physics, as well as public administration from Harvard and a PhD. She had published several books, including one endorsed by Modi himself. She spoke with an ever-present smile in the measured cadence of a university lecturer. Frederick was impressed and touched when she told him, “We two can now realise The Mother’s dream.”

Krishna Devanandan, an Indian Aurovilian who has helped organise arts festivals there, recalled that honeymoon period. “Everybody was kind of cuddling up and rabbiting around and thinking they could get along,” she said. “She sussed us out before she came and she already obviously had clear ideas.”

Those soon became apparent. Ravi began pushing to implement Auroville’s master plan, based on Anger’s original Galaxy outline, despite criticisms that it was outdated and prioritised infrastructure over ecological restoration. According to complaints from the community, during one walk around the area, Ravi allegedly shouted at some residents: “Encroachers, I will make an example of you.” By late 2021, community representatives claimed she had sidelined them and installed her own appointees in key positions. In one meeting, Auroville’s governing board, made up of political appointees selected by India’s Ministry of Education, endorsed plans for growing Auroville’s population from about 3,000 to 15,000 people within four years.

Then the bulldozers arrived. The conflict almost immediately went before India’s courts in a series of legal cases accusing Ravi of over-reach. The diggers were temporarily halted by an environmental tribunal order, but not before much of the youth centre lay in rubble and some 900 trees had been felled. In court, the Auroville Foundation argued that they and the governing board are the main authority and they are implementing the approved master plan to expand the township for more habitation.

Days later, hundreds of Aurovilians packed into one of the largest residents’ assembly meetings in years. Uninvited, Ravi walked calmly to the front and asked for silence. When the room quietened, she accused the gathering of obstructing the development of a city intended to house 50,000 people. “Can we be less selfish?” she asked.

Over the next few months, community representatives say they were locked out of their email accounts, while power was cut to buildings that they refused to vacate. Control over finances was shifted to those aligned with the foundation. Police complaints were filed against those protesting the foundation’s moves. Some, including Frederick, were accused of obstruction.

When the governor of Tamil Nadu, who also chaired Auroville’s governing body, made his first public address to its residents in November 2022, he doubled down on the secretary’s message. He laid into the community’s “boisterous opposition” and media coverage he said made Auroville look like it was “being destroyed by totalitarian control”. Their commitment to Sri Aurobindo’s teachings was “grossly deficient”, he said.

Some residents began scrutinising the foundation. One dossier accused outside contractors of using substandard material to pave new roads. Other audits alleged millions of dollars’ worth of inflated and wasteful spending, as well as the felling of 20,000 trees since 2021. One area, equivalent to roughly two football fields, had been cleared to make way for a VIP access road and a parking lot, which were absent from the master plan. Exchanges of farms and other prime Auroville real estate were also probed. The foundation was alleged to have signed land transactions that resulted in estimated losses of more than Rs2.4bn ($25mn) in value. Particular alarm centred on Annapurna farm, one of Auroville’s most productive agricultural sites, earmarked last year for demolition to make way for a proposed campus of the Indian Institute of Technology Madras.

As the opposition to Ravi intensified, more than 200 residents found their stipends cut and experienced lengthy visa delays, according to a community-authored report. For decades, Aurovilians from abroad had assumed they would receive five-year visas as part of the community’s social contract. Many had invested in building homes with no legal title, working in Auroville’s service for modest allowances.

The first expulsions followed. Satprem Maïni, a French architect who compiled many of the investigative dossiers, was ordered to leave India in 2023. “The previous conflict with the Sri Aurobindo Society was like a sibling rivalry,” one Aurovilian told me. “This is much worse. You are fighting the government of India. It’s a losing battle.”

As anxiety spread through the community, some wrote letters to the government and travelled to New Delhi. Late one morning in September 2024, a handful were granted a short audience with Amit Shah, India’s home minister and Modi’s right-hand man, at his residence. Rotund, gruff and with an unnerving gaze behind his rimless glasses, Shah did not push back on the idea that Ravi’s campaign had been sanctioned from the top, one attendee said.

“Aurovilians need to be taught a lesson, and they have to understand that they are living in India, they have to follow the law of the land,” the attendee recalled Shah saying. “That phase is over, now it’s time for collaboration.” India’s home affairs ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

Just over six months later, Frederick received news that he said felt like “somebody had injected a bit of poison”. At the age of 86, and after almost a year of waiting, he had his visa renewal denied. “My home is here. I live here. My children are living here. My grandchildren are living here. I have no other place to go, I have no money,” he pleaded in a video broadcast posted across social media.

“I wish I could respond to what I am accused of. I don’t know anything. I have given an apology for everything I might have done wrong, for all my shortcomings,” he added. “Every evening when I go to bed I ask The Mother, ‘Please forgive me.’”

The once sleepy French enclave of Pondicherry, officially renamed Puducherry in 2006, has become a popular tourist destination. At the weekends, crowds wander the cobbled streets of the old colonial quarter, still known as White Town. Visitors stroll the seafront promenade and sip beer on hotel terraces overlooking the Bay of Bengal before dining on French cuisine in restaurants stocked with Auroville-made cheese.

On a humid morning in March, I met Peter Heehs at a bakery a short walk from Sri Aurobindo’s ashram, where people still throng to meditate around the courtyard tomb where he and The Mother are interred. Heehs, an American historian who works in the ashram’s archives, came to Pondicherry in the early 1970s. “It was pretty dead, but nice. I mean quiet, virtually no motor vehicles,” he said. “Now all the old buildings are getting turned into Airbnbs or restaurants.” That development has started pressing at the borders of Auroville. Private housing developments and half-finished estates now encircle the community.

In Auroville itself, the signs of the internal crisis are impossible to miss. Felled trees, piles of rubble, a cavernous moat dug around the Matrimandir and unfinished roads to nowhere scar the landscape. One such project had threatened to cut through Solitude Farm, one of Auroville’s best-known agricultural ventures. Krishna McKenzie, a British Aurovilian who arrived in the 1990s and helped build the six-acre farm and café, has become something of a social media star. As he strode barefoot through the farm, dressed in a dark turban and white south Indian veshti while speaking fluent Tamil, McKenzie expressed infectious enthusiasm about everything growing around us, lamenting that more nearby restaurants did not use locally sourced ingredients.

For McKenzie, Auroville’s greatest achievement was not architectural or even spiritual, but its ability to create unexpected possibilities. “It was amazing because you came here and you just found a place and you built a hut and you just started living,” he said. “The Mother said, ‘This is a place of non-ending experimentation.’ That’s Auroville.”

“Whatever you think of The Mother, and the spirituality and all that . . . she had a vision,” McKenzie said. “That vision was based on an intelligence and a wisdom, and people responded to that, and now it’s being suppressed . . . It’s kind of heartbreaking, frankly. It’s really, really tough for all of us.”

The next day, I met with a group of Aurovilians, including Frederick. The decision to deny his visa had sparked uproar. A petition requesting his application be reconsidered garnered 4,000 signatures. A few weeks later, he’d received an unexpected call from an Indian official asking him to reapply. He was granted a three-year visa, though it was backdated and would expire this July.

Despite the reprieve, the shock has taken a toll on Frederick, he told me. But the situation had also caused him to reflect on his own privilege as a foreigner in India. “I have taken a lot of advantage of the fact that I’m a white person . . . and I’ve stepped on quite a lot of toes in the process, and maybe I have to look down at those toes.”

While Frederick won a respite, control over Auroville’s future seems tipped in the foundation’s favour. The dispute reached India’s Supreme Court last year, which sided with the foundation’s argument that Auroville’s governing body was the “supreme authority”. After that verdict, in November 2025, Auroville Today, an independent monthly magazine, announced it was closing after nearly four decades. Its editors said they could not operate under new rules placing the community’s media under a centralised hub intended to project a more unified image of Auroville.

A month later, a glimmer of hope came after an Indian parliamentary committee called for closer consultation with Auroville’s residents, as well as greater transparency over land transfers. It criticised the plan to turn the Annapurna farm into a university campus and recommended alternative sites be considered. Instead, in early September 2026 the resident farmers received an eviction letter from the foundation, ordering them to vacate the land within 10 days. Pointedly, the political committee advocated the preservation of Auroville’s international character and urged that five-year visas remain the norm for its non-Indian residents.

“The international character of Auroville is not just a matter of pride but the very intent of Auroville,” the committee wrote in its report. “As the Honourable Prime Minister has noted in his visit to Auroville, ‘Anyone who is willingly in service of the Divine Consciousness is entitled to live in Auroville.’”

Late one afternoon in March, Arun Ambathy took me on a walk through Revelation Forest, one of Auroville’s oldest, handing me a slow-burning stick of incense to ward off the mosquitoes.

Ambathy is a 39-year-old former special forces commando, who served in counter-insurgency operations in Kashmir until an accident forced him to slow down. During his recovery, he began questioning the path he was on. He felt there must be better ways to serve his country and eventually he quit the army and found his way to Auroville in 2018, working on the reforestation project.

We stopped beneath a 40-year-old banyan tree. A snake was climbing the trunk towards a nest of baby squirrels while their mother darted frantically around it. We stood watching the stand-off before moving on. “I don’t know which one won,” said Ambathy, sounding disappointed.

Ambathy is not a man who shies away from confrontation. “In some perverse ways, that drives me,” he told me with a grin. Over the past few years, he has become one of the biggest thorns in the side of Auroville’s leadership. He has filed complaints alleging illegal soil mining, timber theft, corruption and inflated construction contracts and has repeatedly challenged foundation officials in meetings and in person. A few months after we spoke, he was briefly arrested following a minor altercation with Ravi’s supporters.

“In some ways, I like a fight, but it’s not a good thing. I came to Auroville to transcend that,” he said. I asked Ambathy whether he felt able to be so combative because he did not need to worry, like Auroville’s foreigners, about being expelled from India. In fact, the opposite was true, he said. “You can still go back to Britain and have a life there. I am taking on the powers that be, which are going to be in power for some time, and I have to face them.” Last year the foundation declared Ambathy persona non grata, barring him from entering or residing in Auroville and cutting him off from various services. He has refused to leave and is challenging the order in court.

Frederick is making plans of his own. Last August, after receiving his visa, he decided to travel back to Munich to visit his remaining friends and family there. At Bengaluru airport he made his way over to the immigration counter and handed over his passport. The officer examined it carefully, called over a superior and passed it on to them. Watching the exchange, Frederick grew nervous. Was something still wrong with his residential status?

The second official looked at the passport, studying the photograph before handing it back to the junior officer. Looking up at Frederick, he asked: “You have been in the Auroville ashram for the last 60 years or so?”

“Yes,” Frederick replied, bracing himself. There was a pause. Then the officer asked: “Can we have your blessings?”

Chris Kay is the FT’s Mumbai bureau chief

rows.title: Dethroning FICO won’t much help US homeowners
rows.content:
Published October 3 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

If you don’t like your exam result, how about requesting a different examiner? The US government thinks this might be one answer to the pressing problem of US housing affordability.

American housing has become increasingly expensive since 2022, when the Federal Reserve started raising short-term interest rates. Persistent inflation has pushed up long-term yields, and 30-year home loans now cost an eye-watering 7 per cent . Unsurprisingly, mortgage lending has plummeted — the $200bn of loans originated in the latest quarter is half what was seen in 2021.

For individual homeowners, the obstacle isn’t just the benchmark rate, but their own credit score. Hence a proposal from federal housing tsar Bill Pulte to push for more competition among consumer credit agencies. This knocked a quarter, or $4bn, off the market capitalisation of Fair Isaac, whose FICO credit scoring system currently reigns supreme in the mortgage market.

Under the new plan, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which buy, guarantee and securitise mortgages at the behest of the government, will now be able to take ratings from VantageScore on an equal footing with FICO. Under the current system, using the alternative system results in a loan surcharge.

The theory is that VantageScore, backed by credit bureaus Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, may be better able to detect some of the “credit invisible”. It uses a slightly different algorithm with different weights for factors like credit utilisation and payment history. Its backers cite research saying this reveals at least 5mn mortgage-ready borrowers FICO would have missed.

It’s plausible that this would give more Americans access to mortgages, and at slightly lower rates. Home loan providers including Rocket Mortgage have publicly shared their enthusiasm. Some asset managers are less thrilled, worrying that the net result might be a reduction in underwriting standards. After all, they are the ones who end up holding the mortgage-backed securities.

One analogy might be credit rating agencies. The US securities regulator recognises 11 of them today; back in 1975, there were just three: S&P Global Ratings, Fitch and Moody’s. Fragmentation raises the risk that borrowers shop around for the most lenient provider, but it also addresses the homogeneity that led the financial system into danger ahead of the 2008 financial crisis.

The trouble is that introducing competition in haste undermines the case for a broader use of data. And if asset managers think the White House is simply trying to jack up mortgage volumes, they will start pricing asset-backed bonds — possibly including those that rely on FICO — at a discount. That would send Washington’s housing strategists back to the drawing board.
