rows.title: Protests from the City about bank tax ring hollow
rows.content:
Philip Augar

Published October 3 2026

The writer is the author of several books on the City and Wall Street

Are banks too big to tax as well as too big to fail? That is the question arising from the industry’s vigorous lobbying of government, hoping to avoid an increase in bank taxes.

The sector’s case as it attempts to head off such a move in John Healey’s first Budget on October 28, is that it is already overtaxed relative to both the rest of the UK corporate sector and global competitors. The post-crisis banking windfall tax and UK balance sheet levy, although reduced, remain in place. The banking lobby reckons that the UK’s banks pay 47 per cent in total taxes compared to 28 per cent in the US and under 40 per cent in some EU competitors.

More taxes, this argument runs, would lead to a loss of business to other financial capitals. In what looks like a co-ordinated campaign by global banking chiefs, JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon warns of “adverse consequences” from further tax increases. Dimon, whose bank is planning a new £3bn head office in Canary Wharf, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham on a recent visit to London. The threat is clear enough.

But it is the British banks that have the most skin in this game — and the most to say. Increased taxes, they protest, would reduce their capacity to fund small and medium-sized enterprises lending, be passed on to customers and impair their own contribution to domestic GDP. The City of London Corporation, the Square Mile’s local authority, urges the Chancellor to “do no harm” to the financial services industry. “That means,” it says bluntly, “no more sector-specific taxes.”

Whether to take this advice requires delicate judgment from Healey, who has a fiscal gap to fill and a growth plan to deliver. Would a populist tax grab really cut the banks’ capacity to lend? Would the cost of loans go up? Or are there other ways the banks could absorb such an increase?

Would more banking taxes really drive business away from London? Perhaps the banks are just playing the Stuart Gulliver card: Gulliver became HSBC chief executive having previously said his bank would consider moving its HQ out of London if retail banks in the UK were ringfenced. The banks were duly ringfenced but HSBC stayed.

The sector’s case is weakened by its extraordinary profitability since the interest rate cycle turned in 2022. Higher interest rates improve banks’ net interest margin (the difference between what they pay to depositors and charge borrowers). The benefits flow through to their UK ringfenced banks, businesses for which Barclays and NatWest reported high returns on equity of over 20 per cent last year.

Together with Lloyds, these three returned nearly £12bn to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks from their 2025 profits. Reducing capital returns to shareholders would give banks the capacity to absorb moderately increased taxation and sustain lending. Bank shares would probably give back some of their recent gains — the FTSE 350 Bank index is up 30 per cent year-on-year — which would increase their cost of capital. But the industry is distributing rather than raising capital at present, so this is a theoretical cost.

Context is important. The banks received a massive taxpayer bailout during the financial crisis of 2008 on the unarguable grounds that a banking failure would be devastating for the whole economy. Arguing that further bank taxation would jeopardise recovery from the crisis that they created looks like a classic “heads we win, tails you lose” scenario, especially since post-crisis policy interventions are currently costing the exchequer dear.

The BoE pays what is known as the bank rate to the commercial banks on their reserves. This rate is now higher than the yield it receives on the Asset Purchase Facility [APF] — gilts bought from financial institutions during Quantitative Easing. This “cost of carry” on the APF is covered by quarterly cash transfers from the Treasury to the BoE, forecast by the OBR to have been an astonishing £11bn in 2025-26 and to be £5bn-£6bn per annum over the next few years, eroding prior gains.

This is a direct cost to the current budget deficit and is in effect an unearned subsidy to banks and other financial institutions. It’s not surprising that the chancellor may be tempted to get some of this back either through direct bank taxes or by engineering a cut in the interest rate paid to banks on part of their reserves.

Burnham has said that the tax burden should fall on those with the broadest shoulders. With the banks enjoying boom conditions, mostly not of their own making, their shoulders are indeed broad. No one likes to pay more taxes, people or corporations. But this is a time of national need. As beneficiaries of taxpayers’ largesse and having already had their say, the banks should now do the gracious thing and back off. Over to the chancellor.

rows.title: SkyNet satellite battle tests UK pledge to ‘buy British’
rows.content:
Sylvia Pfeifer in London

Published October 3 2026

A battle between two of the world’s leading aerospace and defence groups to build the next generation of satellites for the British armed forces has become an early test of Labour’s stance on military sovereignty.

The contract for the new SkyNet satellites, estimated to be worth up to £2bn, has pitted European aerospace group Airbus , which has overseen SkyNet for decades, against a rival bid from Lockheed Martin of the US.

Ministers who have pledged to “buy British” are being lobbied to stick with the European company, whose presence has helped make the UK a centre for military satellite communications. But they must also navigate an increasingly unpredictable relationship with Donald Trump’s administration in Washington.

The FT reported this year that officials had questioned whether the UK should be entrusting such a key military capability to a US company.

The decision on SkyNet will be one of the first big-spending choices taken by Wes Streeting , appointed defence secretary by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July, at a time when the UK has promised to bolster its military capabilities.

It comes as the war in Ukraine has underlined European nations’ reliance on space-based communications, with Kyiv leaning heavily on satellites to provide intelligence to repel Russia’s armed forces.

Douglas Barrie, senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies think-tank, said the government would face criticism either way.

“Go with the US and your defence industrial policy looks like it’s getting off on the wrong foot. Go with the incumbent Airbus, and you need to minimise any blowback from the White House,” he said.

SkyNet is the UK’s military satellite communications system that has been in operation since the 1960s. The Ministry of Defence is upgrading the network through its SkyNet 6 programme, with the contract worth up to £2bn covering two geostationary satellites that will provide secure communications into the 2040s and beyond.

Final offers submitted late last year are due to expire in the middle of November, according to two people familiar with the situation, and a decision is due in the next few weeks.

Airbus’s work designing and building satellites helps to support about 2,500 jobs at its sites in Stevenage and Portsmouth and a further 18,000 in the wider supply chain. Some 650 Airbus employees work directly on SkyNet.

Supporters of Airbus, which has been involved in SkyNet since 1974, have urged the UK to award the contract to the European group.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, said the government needed to “ensure that it makes good on its promise to invest in British industry and buy British in defence”.

Kevin Bonavia, Labour MP for Stevenage, said SkyNet 6 was vital to retaining “the skills, expertise, supply chains and freedom of action that underpin a genuinely sovereign UK space capability”.

Failure to win the contract could also put up to £10bn worth of potential Airbus exports at risk, according to people familiar with the situation.

The competition is being fought against the backdrop of wider European consolidation in space.

Airbus is in talks with France’s Thales and Leonardo of Italy to create a pan-European space champion capable of taking on Elon Musk’s SpaceX as well as rivals from China and Russia. The companies are discussing where to locate different centres of excellence.

People close to Airbus fear the UK could lose its position as a centre of military satellite communications if the company does not secure the SkyNet contract. “If you’re not a space power, you’re not in that conversation,” said an executive close to Airbus.

Lockheed Martin, for its part, has said it would build a new manufacturing facility in north-east England if its bid wins, and promised to create a “national space ecosystem” in the UK, with about 2,000 jobs, of which just over 400 would be direct.

The US defence giant has also said it would use the UK as an export hub for future space programmes, with about $15bn in potential export opportunities identified. Industry experts said the potential for close integration with the US military’s significant space capabilities should not be discounted.

Critics, however, have questioned how “sovereign” Lockheed’s factory would be, suggesting the company would rely on US intellectual property.

Lockheed has stressed that the “design authority” for its technology, the company or organisation that creates and can modify a particular weapon, would reside in the UK.

Several defence industry executives attending this week’s Labour Party conference in Liverpool said there was still a lack of clarity around what exactly constituted “being British” in procurement decisions.

Airbus and Lockheed both declined to comment.

Francis Tusa, editor of Defence Analysis, said the SkyNet contract should be awarded to Airbus, arguing there were “strategic implications” to consider at a time when there were “concerns over whether the US is a trusted partner”.

The Ministry of Defence said both bidders were “subject to full evaluation of their proposals and must offer satellites that are assembled, integrated and tested in the UK”. The “design authority must be based in the UK and a range of critical components must be provided from UK sources”, it added.

rows.title: Who let the dogs out? Please put them back
rows.content:
Emma Jacobs

Published October 3 2026

Meeting my 90-year-old aunt, visiting from Canada, was a rare chance to catch up in person over lunch, talk about what was happening with my cousins, share my news and reflect on her late brothers (my dad and uncle).

That was the aspiration, anyway. As we tucked into our eggs hollandaise, a small dog at the next table started yapping, shrill barks reverberating around the dining room. Its owner studiously ignored our glares. How I wished the pair were somewhere more suitable. Knee-high in mud in the middle of nowhere, ideally.

Restaurants are for humans to eat, drink and converse — not dodge excitable puppies while desperately snatching a word in the brief silence between the howling of hounds. Yes, I know that children can be more annoying than Labradoodles; that’s why the restaurant chain Giraffe, with its balloons and crayons, was invented. But this view is out of favour.

This week at Musée Carnavalet in Paris, a gastronomic event was held for 40 dogs, who were served shredded pot-au-feu, pan-fried basmati rice with crushed carrots and poultry jus jelly from platters on white tablecloths. Devised by Michelin-starred chef Thierry Marx, footage shows a variety of enthusiastic hounds tucking in, with one particularly happy sausage dog dressed in a red beret and striped outfit chowing down, its paws on the table.

A marketing stunt for a premium French pet food market, it nevertheless symbolised an irksome trend: the doggification of human leisure activities. Nowhere is safe from the tide of Shih Tzus and spaniels. Once relegated to country pubs and outdoor terraces, they are now embraced by hoteliers, restaurateurs and even cinemas .

The online Michelin Guide encourages users to search for dog-friendly restaurants: over 100 in the UK, including Pied à Terre and Brutto. The Athenaeum five-star hotel offers a premium pet package with a goody bag. Even at home, this spoiling is evident in pet food upgrades that can be hazardous: a friend’s dad bolted down three handfuls of kibble, believing it was Bombay mix.

The late Pope Francis took a harsh line on emotional investment in pets. “We see that some people do not want to have a child,” he said four years ago. “They have dogs and cats that take the place of children.” He described it as a “form of selfishness” — a bit rich coming from someone who did not have children (nor a pet), and whose whole schtick was care beyond the family.

Nonetheless, the anthropomorphism of pets is a trend that industry has seized on. Sam Nguyen, senior retail analyst at the market researchers Mintel, says that about 40 per cent of pet owners buy seasonal gifts for them, including on Valentine’s Day and Halloween; a third shell out for designer clothes and luxury grooming. Others even co-ordinate outfits.

Some experts worry that a lack of boundaries creates separation anxiety — though it’s unclear if that is for the dog or the human.

Look, I’m not a beast. Some of my best friends love their dogs intensely — I’m very fond of many. And if they refer to fur babies and dog parents, happily they do it out of earshot. But everything has its place. And Rover’s is not in a fine-dining establishment. If I’m splashing my cash on an overpriced piece of fish, I would at least like to hear my companion and not worry about canine competitors for space and tidbits.

Nor do dogs belong in the workplace. No matter what dog-friendly employers like Amazon (not for delivery drivers, just white-collar workers) or Ben and Jerry’s insist. It’s fine to bring them in for a drive-by “hello” when you’ve forgotten your laptop. But no canine co-workers, please.

Sure, watching your line manager ruffle Fido’s fur might reveal their softer side, but a “thank you” would work just as well.

rows.title: Polymarket’s Alpha traders
rows.content:
Niamh Rowe

Published October 3 2026

For his mother it was a dream come true, watching him in a cap and gown wander through cobbled streets. She sat through an hour of Latin that the audience could not understand, but they all knew what it meant to hear it. That his diploma bore a grade so mediocre hardly seemed to matter. The dreaming spires looked the same. “Is earning three-quarters of a million dollars while at Oxford worth a 2:2?” she’d asked Google’s Gemini after he opened his results. The chatbot’s verdict: a good trade. That was all his mother needed to hear. As for him, the graduate with a second identity as a prediction-market trader called @sigh, and three-quarters of a million dollars in the bank, well, he had never doubted the bet.

Studying often got in the way for @sigh and his trading brethren, who gathered in a secretive and selective group chat known as Alpha, an invitation-only venue for some of the world’s most successful Polymarket traders. “I had two math exams,” one member explained, scrambling to get up to speed after an attack on the Ukrainian city of Kurakhove had prompted a debate about whether it would fall to the Russians.

A message arrived showing drone footage of a crumbling apartment block, released by the Russian military. The sender needed help locating where in the city the explosion took place, and help watching closely for even faint silhouettes of any military personnel in the area. In less than a minute, a recipient in the chat confirmed they had begun the search, starting with the house next door. Military co-ordinates and aerial images flew back and forth. Two words were translated from Russian to English, based on sounds made by the camera operator in the first seconds of the explosion.

Appeals like this are constantly made in the chat as traders race to quantify the world. Sometimes they are for assistance with a task. Other times to solicit a specific skill set or expertise. Often to corroborate or falsify a thesis, or gauge opinion. Frequently to pitch a trade to collaborate on. On rarer occasions, money is loaned. But unlike a junior colleague, or ChatGPT, or a bank, access here is free and 24/7. It’s not only a service but a meandering discussion. The requests maintain the chat’s momentum, alongside the more casual moments shared. Breaking news brings reactions. Memes fly, jokes are forged, lore builds.

The group has hallmarks of a codependent family or friendship group, with an urgent need for boundaries. But most of its members haven’t met and probably never will. They’ve not seen each other’s faces nor do they know each other’s real names. So why would a group of strangers choose to experience life together anonymously?

Polymarket and its rival Kalshi launched during the pandemic. They offer traders binary contracts on real-world events: will this thing happen, yes or no? The platforms emerged as fringe sites for political betting, and went mainstream during the 2024 US presidential election.

The 30 or so members of Alpha meet in the shadows of Discord, a messaging platform often used by video gamers. Technically it’s a “server” rather than a group chat — a private virtual space to hang out in, built to stream videos and share media. No matter the hour, an Alpha is online. More than a cabal of gamblers, it is a fraternity, oceans apart but bound by an ambition to master their own fates. They are intoxicated by winning. The vast majority are Gen Z, an internal survey revealed, including at least three teenagers. Their number one rule, according to one member, is “don’t talk about politics”. Collectively, they’ve profited an estimated $40mn on Polymarket since 2024.

When I started introducing myself to Alpha members on Discord in April, a poll was created in the chat tallying who had been approached by Niamh Rowe about “his” story. There was once a member who claimed to be female, but the group “had arguments about whether she was a real woman or not”, a veteran Alpha told me. After the person left the group, their biography mattered little as history became legend.

Most members of Alpha ignored me. Eight didn’t. Among them were the Oxford undergrad; a mathematics PhD in Moscow who trades seven days a week; and an Ivy League political science PhD candidate who monitors the world across escalating screens: phone, laptop, desktop, monitor and projector playing Al Jazeera in his living room eight hours a day. All but one are in their twenties. They span five continents. Their name for their activity toggles between trading, gambling and gaming. Almost all of them are hiding it from someone.

I got to know them over several months. They are introduced here by their Polymarket handles, and the FT has verified their trading activities.

I wanted to know what brought them together and what kept them there. And ultimately, why has a group of highly intelligent, ambitious young men chosen to sit far from the world instead of living and working inside it? Why have they decided that watching it collapse is a better bet?

Polymarket and Kalshi combined averaged some $1.6bn in daily trading volume in August — about as much money changing hands as does in shares of Wells Fargo or McDonald’s. That’s up nearly 2,000 per cent from a year earlier. Trading volume on prediction markets is forecast to double by 2030, reaching $1tn annually, according to Bernstein analysts.

This is a turning point, say the platforms’ founders: institutional decline paving the way for a more democratic era. Prediction markets are a new financial system, and the new infrastructure of information for a generation who scrolled into adulthood.

Prediction markets offer a way to profit from the world that priced this generation out; the chronically online are recast as “smart money” and screen time is their edge. “They’ll be bigger than the stock market,” Kalshi co-founder Luana Lopes Lara told CNBC earlier this year. “If you’re very into music or politics or cars, you’ll find a lot of prediction markets that will give you a better understanding of the future and exposure to it.” That interview aired in March, shortly after Lopes Lara was crowned the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire just ahead of her 30th birthday, an age not yet reached by Polymarket’s founder, Shayne Coplan, nor most of either’s employees.

But prediction markets aren’t everyone’s game. A study published in June by the Centre for Economic Policy Research found that two-thirds of Polymarket users have lost money, based on trading since 2022. The study found that among the profitable traders, just 1 per cent captured more than three-quarters of profits — and just 0.1 per cent captured half. Can it be that fortune favours a few while everyone else remains at its mercy?

No, it cannot, the 0.1 per cent would respond. Most traders pick “yes” or “no” based on the articles they’ve read, or what they’ve seen on social media — educated guesses. The 0.1 per cent play a different game. This is not because they’re insider-traders (although a few may be) or prophets, but because they try to calculate events’ fair values to exploit mispricings.

Polymarket and Kalshi were founded not long after the US Supreme Court lifted a ban on sports betting in 2018, unleashing an explosion of legal wagering across the country. But prediction markets aren’t gambling, the companies insist. Federal regulators and certain courts agree. For more than three decades, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has recognised their products as financial derivatives known as “event contracts”.

Political prediction markets have been a fixture of American history — the country has bet on elections since George Washington. Despite a record of accuracy, the New York Stock Exchange banned these markets during Prohibition, when gambling flourished underground, and their predictive power was later replaced with scientific polling. Now scientific polling is in crisis and the markets have returned.

The CFTC had until very recently resisted political markets on such exchanges. Event contracts that are “gaming” are banned by federal regulations; the entire predictive project hinges on the meaning of that word. For years the main American offering was PredictIt, which was tiny and operated with special and narrow permission thanks to its academic affiliation. The CFTC at first fought Polymarket’s and Kalshi’s election markets. But under the Trump administration the regulator dropped these legal battles, and has launched new ones against states seeking to ban the markets on the ground that they violate local gambling laws.

“Luck” did not feature in the vocabulary of any Alpha I met. They used a Discord bettor’s lexicon, as if it were a native tongue, my fluency assumed. “Dumb money” refers to most of the traders — the casual, uninformed users who gamble using vibes, statistically likely to lose. They’re also called “fish”. They supply liquidity and mispricings to feed the advanced traders like themselves who are known as “sharps” — like Wall Street “sharks” who hunt retail investors.

Blending in among the sharps are professional algorithmic traders and suspected insiders. But the Alpha members I spoke to estimate that those groups are a small fraction of smart money. They’ve found that quants stick to volatile live-sports and 15-minute crypto markets, which their algorithms can ruthlessly exploit. And it can be difficult to know if accounts acting suspiciously — created specifically to place a large bet despite unfavourable odds — know something we don’t, or are misinformed and reckless.

I met one Alpha while he was visiting New York City for a night before jetting off to another US state. His previous stop had been South Korea. The trip was for “business” but he wouldn’t tell me anything else. It was a warm spring evening, one of the first after a relentless winter. A native of Moscow, he was visiting America for only the second time, both trips related to trading. I’d chosen a bustling wine bar with tables that spilt on to a leafy cobblestone street lined with brownstones — the Brooklyn from movies. I knew very little about whom I was meeting.

I only had a Polymarket profile. It belonged to @gopfan. When combined with his @gopfan2, it showed profits of $1.7mn in two years.

A young man in tracksuit bottoms and strappy sandals approached with a look of caution. There was something boyish about his unruly eyebrows, wispy moustache and mild acne. He ordered a black tea and spoke softly, rarely making eye contact. Not long into our conversation, he asked to go outside, annoyed by the tumult. We shared a cigarette and wandered the affluent streets of Brooklyn Heights. By the age of 25, @gopfan said, he had received a PhD from one of Russia’s renowned institutions for mathematics and programming. From early childhood, he said he competed in chess tournaments and All-Russian Mathematical Olympiads — prestigious national competitions dating back to the early Soviet Union.

“I can’t imagine a life without competition,” he said. “That doesn’t make any sense to me.” He said his grandparents recall that as a young child he had to beat his personal best and the top scores of everyone around him. To this day, beating other people motivates him more than money. After graduating, he worked as a crypto developer but it didn’t last a year — he couldn’t see trading tokens as anything but gambling, with money laundering on the side. Unsure what career would combine the rigour of his PhD with the need to beat an opponent, he found himself playing around with Polymarket in 2024. He traded mostly on the weather and US elections. His strategy: building probabilistic models from vast, historical datasets.

He made nearly $80,000 trading weather in what became the hottest July on record. And he didn’t simply bet on candidates to win races — he traded Trump’s margin of victory in Michigan and South Carolina, and whether he’d win every swing state. He cashed in on markets mispricing Trump, which made him “sort of famous” in the Polymarket community, he told me. He received an invitation to join Alpha before the year’s end. When I asked which market felt best when it was resolved, he said the presidential election. I asked why. “I’m ‘gopfan’ because I wanted Trump to win,” he said, looking confused. I laughed, confessing that I had thought the name was ironic.

Alpha started with a few Discord users huddling together as the presidential campaign accelerated in the spring of 2024. Polymarket was flooding with recreational bettors wanting to gamble on the race. All this “dumb money” brought more mispricings and higher margins. Some nascent sharps lacked the liquidity to maximise these opportunities, so they pooled their capital and their expertise. For example, a whale once bid for $1mn of “yes” shares on the market: “Will Trump create Bitcoin reserve in first 100 days?” Alpha swarmed to gobble them up — half the order in under a minute. They profited $250,000 in total, according to Polymarket data, which also shows that @gopfan and @sigh were among the quickest to the trade.

The embryonic collective gradually invited others to join, looking less for big bankrolls than for success rates and specific skill sets. Recruitment, I’m told, always looks the same: a member nominates a “rising star” whom they’ve spotted, then a plenary vote.

The Kurakhove explosion that Alpha had raced to locate happened in November 2024. Locating it was easy, but a debate dragged on for hours, requiring input from their Ukraine-war guru in Australia. He woke up, finally. The market was pricing Russia to capture the city by December. But Alpha knew the real question: what’s fair value that this explosion meets the criteria for Russian-controlled territory, according to the Institute for the Study of War, the American think-tank whose map adjudicates the front line. The Australian was given strict orders: find the fair value but do not read any of the chat. His edge was best when pure.

He arrived at a 70 per cent chance that Kurakhove would not be captured before December, contrary to others in the group who predicted it would fall. He realised that he wouldn’t change any minds by talking more. He’d have to put his money where his calculations were. He plugged 0.7 and the market price into the Kelly criterion, a mathematical formula used by investors and gamblers to calculate the optimal size of a bet as a fraction of bankroll. He shared the answer: half. An opponent in the debate urged him not to bet so much, or perhaps not to bet at all. He decided not to bet so much.

When December arrived at the end of the week, Ukraine was still holding Kurakhove, as the Australian guru had predicted. Polymarket deposited just over $7,000 into his account. Had he ignored the group’s caution, it would have been double that.

Scenarios like this raise questions about Alpha’s premise and glue. Could strangers scattered across the world ever share one view of reality — and of risk — however determined they were to see it clearly? Maybe not. But perhaps the times when they cannot are part of Alpha’s value: a guardrail constructed of the fact that subjectivity can never be eliminated. To that view, Alpha did not cost him $7,000; it prevented him from losing more had he been wrong.

The mother of @sigh, the Oxford graduate, might have had an “irrational fetish” for the grandeur of that ancient university, as he described it, but she wasn’t delusional about his prospects. As a child her son read constantly. There was a book in his hand throughout adolescence, most often about science or military history. By the end of high school, he wasn’t sure what career he’d end up doing, but it would be humanistic, he knew that. Study social sciences somewhere impressive and he could figure it out from there. “I low-key wanted to be an academic weapon,” he told me, laughing.

His family wasn’t poor but they were also not rich relative to the residents of their East Asian metropolis. They were comfortable enough to scrape together the international university fees and aspirational enough to believe that an Oxford degree was worth the cost.

He left the dense skyline, the only view he’d called home, to land among the green quads and romantic turrets and pictured all the books he would read beneath them. But the mystique faded fast. The future seeped in through the ancient walls. Many of his peers arrived on campus having already applied to finance societies, networked on LinkedIn and formulated the criteria for entry. This would help them land a spring internship in finance. Firing off dozens of applications was the norm. Then came multiple rounds of interviews and personal essays. Hopefully you’d end up with a spot. But that only got you inside the building, where the real battle for a job began.

He found it all profoundly depressing. Academia or maybe journalism was the future he wanted. But where he came from, making money was the priority. No, it was the reason for existence. So the stampede beckoned. He secured an internship with a small investment bank. It dawned on him that whether it was a bulge-bracket bank or a boutique, the job came down to figuring out how to extract money from the next schmuck. He could’ve explored quantitative trading, consulting or private equity, but none felt intrinsically valuable. Everybody’s just trying to take some money out of everyone else’s pocket, he thought.

“Soul-crushing and alienating” was how he described the internship he’d fought for. The slow march towards the City or Wall Street had begun. He needed an escape. It was 2022 and some of his friends had recently made money from the NFT frenzy and were jumping between pump-and-dump tokens named BONK or Fartcoin.

There was also chatter about a new site called Polymarket where you could bet on elections. From his desk at the bank he created an account. He chose the username @sigh in reference to a Karl Marx quote: “Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature . . . It is the opium of the people.” His Polymarket profile displays the line but swaps “religion” for “gambling”. He played around on the site. At least they were pricing a real outcome, he thought. There was something grounding their value.

After @sigh’s first year at Oxford, a summer with no internships stretched before him. He had time to kill and Polymarket was booming. He bet on elections, invasions, diplomacy, interest rates, tweets — winning time after time. His strategy was fairly simple. He wasn’t spending hours conducting deep research and he didn’t build statistical models. He didn’t need to know the future; he needed to know behaviour. Sometimes traders would leave up orders, then the situation would evolve and they’d be too slow to react, or may have simply forgotten about it altogether. He’d sit on X and wait for things to happen.

Stale liquidity accounted for the majority of his wins. Other times dumb money. His only deep research: hunt for big orders on outcomes favourable to Trump, then sleuth the counterparties’ politics. He was hoping to find bettors with no strategy beyond pro-Maga. Striking gold was finding $TRUMP memecoins in their crypto wallets. Polymarket didn’t feel like trading stocks. It felt like a computer game.

Then @sigh returned to Oxford in October to begin his second year. The presidential election drew closer. Studying no longer felt like an investment in his future; it felt like foregone profit. Sometimes keeping up with election markets required all-nighters. He’d only break to restock on Tesco meal deals or a kebab. He’d walk through empty streets, past the lit window of a cramming student or a drunk collegiate herd pouring out of a nightclub, deep in contemplation of his trades.

It was during this time that he received an invitation to join Alpha, recruited after a member spotted him debating something in a market’s comment section. The term ended in December. He left campus $75,000 richer. The US elections were over, but he was just getting started. At any time, somewhere in the world there’d be a political race or conflict or disaster for him to monitor. When he returned after Christmas, he spent most of his days in his college bedroom, sitting at his desk, eyes glued to his laptop, infinitely looping X, Discord and Polymarket.

“There’s free money on the floor,” he said. “But you have to be there. And you have to be very fast at clicking.”

Another Alpha remembered precisely the moment he noticed the money lying at his feet. It was the week of New York City’s Democratic mayoral primary in June 2025, when voters would rank their choices. He’d placed a bet on the number of rounds of municipal tabulation that would follow. He’d quickly reasoned that the number predicted on Polymarket was almost certainly wrong. Another count, nearly guaranteed to be correct, was priced at rock bottom. He bid for those shares, tens of thousands of them, but he felt guilty about the suckers filling his orders. In the comments section below — the trading pit — he urged his counterparties to stop. When they accused him of flagrant deceit, he fired off paragraphs of legal explanation with links to his sources, but he was unable to convince them that he was taking their money.

“I know how ridiculous I sound,” @jep-g, a political science PhD student at an Ivy League university, told me. “Thousands of dollars made off of people’s stupidity.” He hesitated. “Various moral quandaries.”

Amid the commotion of mayoral technicalities, over on Discord, he received a private message from @gopfan. Stop posting on the market and delete your comments, @gopfan urged. Then he sent an invite for a private group. Pour the alpha here, @jep-g was told, where it will pool instead of drain away. He deleted the comments, wiping away the knowledge he’d spilt. He’d later meet @gopfan in person in the US — by this time he’d come to know him as Alpha’s Russian maths prodigy who could accurately model elections all over the world. His superpowers even allowed him to forecast when and where earthquakes would happen. “But I don’t really understand why he’s good at that,” @jep-g said.

Alpha was educational, and after all @jep-g was at his elite graduate school to learn. In one class, a renowned Bayesian statistician had taught him election forecasting and political polling.

The students’ project: recreating Trump’s aggregate approval rating as published on Silver Bulletin, the blog of Nate Silver , the poll aggregator and gambler.

Just a few weeks before that, a friend had showed him a “funny, bizarre” site called Polymarket. His friend had dabbled with cryptocurrency back in 2010 — “you know, for anarchist reasons” — long before today’s Wall Street Bitcoin reserves and presidential memecoins. Drunk enough by that point, the pair were ready to indulge in the degeneracy of it all. His inaugural bet: $10 on Trump’s not ending the Ukraine war in his first 90 days. “It definitely scratched an itch,” @jep-g said.

Betting on Trump’s weekly approval ratings hadn’t been part of the syllabus in stats class but there was surely no better way to optimise his studying. At the start of his spring term, he had a net loss of $100. By the time term wrapped in June, it was a profit of $10,000. By the end of the month, he’d reached $40,000 — a steady churn of approval ratings and a windfall from the Democratic primary. He’d done his homework. His grade: A, α, alpha. He gave himself a new username, taking inspiration from a character in Paolo Sorrentino’s film The Great Beauty .

When I first spoke to @jep-g in April , more than a year had passed since his stats class project. This trading life was not something he would’ve imagined himself doing a year ago. He told me that anyone trading on prediction markets who denies that at least some of it is addiction-driven is being dishonest, regardless of how successful they’ve been. “It sucks you in, especially if you’re capable,” he said. “It definitely consumes my life in a way that is not positive.” He hinted at a relationship breakdown before changing the subject.

The passage of his time could be measured through his staring at screens. Or his net profit: around $200,000. Surely few poli sci PhD students sit at a trading desk full-time. His rationale was to make enough money for the next few years while he searches for postdocs, rather than scrambling to take the first job he can get. Just like every other Alpha I spoke to, @jep-g saw prediction markets as a cheat code — the smartest career move they could make. But he was the only one to call it an addiction. He didn’t think every sharp was addicted, but it wasn’t just competence and a desire for a good life that united them — they each liked to win and craved the rush of the chase. The mundane reality of making a living versus getting paid to play a video game of reality? To them, it was a no-brainer.

When @jep-g first joined Polymarket, he put about $300 into his account. He promised himself: not another dime. Blockchain records show he kept his word. But it didn’t matter: his pockets were soon deeper than he could’ve ever imagined, yet he still felt like he’d lost control.

When we spoke on the phone in August, he’d been attending meetings for gambling addiction. Once more, he found himself in a room of strangers. “I’m trying to cycle down or whatever,” he said. He wanted to prioritise his dissertation and rebuild his relationships, but he didn’t rule out returning. He seemed concerned about the companies “hawking this until everybody in America is gambling”, under the guise it’ll make us more rational. “But the biggest harm isn’t the bets themselves,” he said. “It’s the story that this is democratised, meritocratic finance.”

The amount of time @sigh spent on Polymarket continually grew. The better he got, the more opportunities he saw and the bigger his trades became. He adapted to a new way of being whereby, at any point, Trump could tweet something forcing him to drop whatever he was doing and run to his computer. Hours multiplied, not only those recorded as screen time, but the ones lost in thought. Any time looking away from markets would be spent thinking about what he was missing, all the positions he’d not taken but still could. Silence only fell while he was asleep. But going offline every night felt not peaceful but like a liability. He sometimes awoke to painful losses because he’d not risen in time to click.

His final year at Oxford coincided with the beginning of the war in Iran. After the US-Israeli air strikes in February, what felt like obsessive dedication began to unravel into something that looked more like addiction. “I have been begging Trump to end the war on Iran,” he said in May. “Like, please, just let me study, just let me have a holiday. But no, it just keeps coming.”

At the time, @sigh had recently returned from an Easter break in Cornwall with his girlfriend, taken at the height of air strikes and the escalating crisis in the Strait of Hormuz. He spent around five hours daily jumping between Polymarket and Discord. He hadn’t scaled back this routine when we spoke, even though he was in the midst of his finals. “Terrible,” he shrugged.

But the problem wouldn’t be solved simply by prioritising his degree. It was past the point of a scheduling fix. His brain had evolved for a rhythm of clicking, prompting, scrolling — which felt irreconcilable with the deep focus his essays required. “I don’t have thoughts any more,” he said. “I can’t write anything. I don’t yearn any more.”

The money on the floor continues to cripple @sigh with anxiety because he doesn’t think it’ll last long. Democrats will likely “end prediction markets” should they win in 2028, he said. The spectre of a recession is omnipresent. Dumb money dries up. “It feels almost irresponsible not to take this money,” he told me in May. “There’s this desperation. Just get as much as you can before it might or might not disappear.”

Meandering around Brooklyn, @gopfan and I found a bench to sit on. As soon as he discarded a cigarette, he would light another. I wanted to know what his daily routine looked like, after a life spent in front of blackboards dense with equations, growing up inside brutalist Soviet campuses and palatial towers — whichever premier institution would host the Olympiad.

Polymarket has become his full-time job: eight hours a day, seven days a week, including on vacation. Most of that is spent on election modelling, the foundation built from polls, historical results and local heuristics. This trip he was on was an experiment in collecting real-world data too. “But the key to winning is how you compile it into one number,” he said.

When I asked how he celebrates big wins, he paused. “I mostly just feel relief,” he said flatly. With no days off to spend his money, life looks similar to before, though his social life has shifted.

“It really affects my standing around my friends,” he said. “They know that I’m a millionaire. It changes relationships by increasing inequality. They see the success story and want to repeat it. But not everyone can.” Friends often ring him for Polymarket advice. He answers those calls, for now at least. I asked what his biggest purchase had been. He took out his phone to show me a gold shisha pipe costing $1,500 that he’ll sometimes treat friends to during nights off in Moscow’s hookah bars. The best in the house, he said.

I offered him a ride in my Uber. We spoke about his future. He doesn’t envision this as a long-term career because he’s unsure he can sustain such wide margins as markets grow in efficiency. Nevertheless, he’s confident he can rely on lower-risk trades for another five years, comfortably supplying six figures. His plan is to use Polymarket as a stepping stone to traditional finance, where he believes the real money is.

Family members — or any older adult he meets — don’t understand what he does online, and dismiss it as childish. But dreaming of his future never lasted long before the war jolted him awake. He’s navigating this the only way he knows. He calculated probabilities of emergencies and thresholds beyond which staying in Russia wouldn’t be safe.

He wasn’t wearing a seatbelt, I noticed, and I probed for the odds of a fatal crash without it. It was a Russian custom not to wear one, he said, and some drivers take offence if you do. As we crossed the Brooklyn Bridge, he craned forward to witness the Manhattan skyline — unbelted, but with a weight around his neck. “It feels like everything is gradually falling apart in Russia,” he said. “It really doesn’t feel good. But American taxation is also pretty ugly.”

In August I spoke with @sigh again. He was spending the summer travelling Europe by train. The route included Venice, Slovenia and Vienna, where he could step inside the military history he’d devoured pages of, and where I found him. He’d been taking Claude with him to the sites of Napoleonic battles and front lines of the first world war, he said, prompting the chatbot at every step. He’d allowed himself to take his foot off the gas when it came to prediction markets, though he still traded the Iran war from train carriages and hostel bunks, surrounded by sleeping people.

Soon he would fly to Thailand to reunite with his girlfriend for a few months. He still planned to trade there full-time but craved a healthier rhythm. He seemed eager to prove that, at least for him, “sharp” could remain a job title but not a diagnosis. He spoke with a degree of distance about those final months at Oxford, acknowledging they were unsustainable. None of it sounded like he’d undergone a paradigm shift. Rather, he’d come to see his extreme habits as a “leak” — poker slang for a recurring flaw in your approach that’s losing you money — because he’d burn out. The next few years would be about “locking in” to maximise an opportunity that felt fleeting, he said. This required finding the formula for being “mentally stable”. So he was complicit? Weak-willed? Maybe. There’s a dissonance between @sigh’s disdain of capitalism as a system of exploitation and alienation — unapologetically Marxist — and his acting in a way that so neatly embodies his critiques of the system. (He has also used the handle @yungstalin.) It wasn’t bad faith as he was acutely aware of what he was doing.

But @sigh didn’t seem to view prediction markets as part of the financial system. He spoke about them as if they were a glitch within capitalism that would eventually be rectified — a momentary escape rather than an exit. Eventually he’d return to being exploited like all the other fish. Cashing in as much as he could in the meantime would allow him to resist for a bit longer. He was a mercenary because that was the only role available.

“A parody of capitalism” is @sigh’s verdict on prediction markets. “But it’s not actually creating any value,” he said. “Prediction markets simply accelerate the contradiction that was always going to be fatal. We’re living through capitalism’s last day.”

rows.title: Renoir’s reputation restored at the National Gallery
rows.content:
Jackie Wullschläger

Published October 3 2026

“Renoir: who can fathom that most inconsistent of men?” asked his friend Pissarro.

His fellow artists knew that Renoir struggled, doubted, changed tack and sometimes spent years on a picture, though he strove for the opposite effect. Impressionism depends on illusions of spontaneity, and Renoir wanted to look effortlessly, happily alluring: “Why shouldn’t art be pretty?” he said. “There are enough unpleasant things in the world.”

In the past half century, that prettiness, and especially the fleshy nudes and portrayals of women posed to seduce, led to accusations of misogyny, or simply that the art was vapid, and gradually cost Renoir his position in art history as the questioning, serious artist he undoubtedly was. The last full retrospective was in 1985. Renoir and Love , which arrived this week at the National Gallery from the Musée d’Orsay, compellingly revives his reputation.

Opening with a “Self-portrait” whose nervy features, anxious penetrating eyes and agitated marks banish all thought of easy achievement, the exhibition covers the years of his boldest, most original pictures, 1866-87, and presents a contradictory artist: essential to impressionism yet ambivalent about it, innovative yet besotted with tradition, as often sentimental as experimental.

One day he is in Monet’s garden, dashing off the intimate, silky “Madame Monet and her Son” lounging for a moment under a tree; then he is in Naples and the same motif of mother and child, in the lucid, pared-down “Young Mother”, is influenced by Raphael. Paintings of couples — “Secrets”, “The Promenade” — are saccharine clichés, but the well-worn subject of young women at the opera bursts into charismatic life in the bravura brushwork and velvety red, black and white chords of “A Box at the Theatre (At the Concert)”.

Anchoring the exhibition is the first-ever UK loan of “Dance at the Moulin de la Galette”, the greatest impressionist leisure scene, which renders at an ecstatic pitch a Montmartre Sunday afternoon ball. So enveloping is this monumental picture that in the large second gallery, we too bask in the glow of its clustered gas globes as Renoir’s bohemian artist friends waltz with teenage seamstresses, milliners and florists. Every fluid, darting stroke conveys the energy of the twirling couples. Together, interlacing glances and gestures, rhyming poses and arabesques of groups and darker and lighter hues — blue and purple threading through pinks and golds — build a pictorial harmony declaring social cohesion, continuity, cheer.

In smaller vignettes, Renoir amplifies Montmartre as a voluptuous modern paradise. Fabrics, jewellery and glassware scintillate, a diner lights a cigarette and lilac blooms waft across a café in “After the Luncheon”. Evoked in staccato dots and splashes, sunlight through trees in Montmartre’s gardens casts coloured shadows on white dresses and illuminates a lavender-sprinkled path in “The Swing”: the fête galante — Watteau and Fragonard were Renoir’s heroes — reinterpreted for democratic late-19th-century France.

These pictures’ optimism — the one aspect which never varies — chimed with the hopeful spirit of France’s young Third Republic and, according to art historian Robert L Herbert, with Renoir’s “own history, the working-class boy who was climbing out of poverty by aspiring to a life of ease and beauty: the delusion of the street waif”.

At 13, Renoir was an apprentice in a porcelain workshop copying rococo figures. At 21, he met Monet and the upper-class Frédéric Bazille: “The sort” who has “his valet break in his new shoes for him”. Bazille wears slippers, their bright red threads adding vivid notes to the grey-white tonality of Renoir’s tender 1867 portrait of his lanky, awkward friend painting a heron. A Monet snowscape hangs on the wall; “Frédéric Bazille” affectionately records the trio’s closeness.

Opposite is Renoir’s breakthrough, “La Grenouillère”. In 1869, he and Monet, working en plein air at a bathing club nicknamed “the frog pond” for its partner-hopping clientele, dissolved forms — boats, sails, bobbing swimmers, fashionable day trippers — into blurs and dabs of light and colour in watery reflections: the invention of impressionism.

Through the 1870s, Renoir bathed city and country in the sparkle and decorative brilliance learnt from porcelain painting. The uniform blocks of Haussmann’s Paris in “The Grands Boulevards” soften beneath light-pierced foliage as people chatter in the midday sun. “The Seine at Chatou” is a springtime flutter of breezy long grasses, pink-flecked blossom and, blending into the riverbank, a young girl picking flowers.

The show’s title Renoir and Love refers to courtship and flirtation, but what stands out is not anecdote but the paintings’ all-over sensuous warmth. Features, eyes and lips are delicately modelled with finely tipped brushes. Costumes and wisps of hair are feathery touches. Figures and nature fuse within webs of quivering luminosity: “Lunch at Restaurant Fournaise (The Rowers’ Lunch)”, set against melting oranges and blues of boats and river; “Near the Lake”, father and daughter on a waterside terrace engulfed by long streaking vine leaves.

Then, suddenly, what Renoir called his “gentle and light” manner stops. Facing “Near the Lake” is another spectacular first UK loan, Philadelphia’s “The Great Bathers” (1884-87): massive, audacious, disconcerting. In this internal debate on how to build impressionism into something more substantial, Renoir based the classicised figures on a Versailles bas-relief; they are strongly sculptural yet irreverent and playful, one nude threatening to splash another while a third, pulling a towel around herself, looks on amused. This trio have a crystalline cut-out solidity; background figures are still depicted in impressionism’s sunny indistinctness.

Renoir, in crisis in these years, continued to surprise. Berlin’s little-known “Children’s Afternoon in Wargemont” (1884), for example, places three sisters, each individualised, in profile, three-quarter and front view. In its classical linearity, transparent tones and formal patterned surface, it defies expectations of sugary idealism about childhood.

The show’s weakness is that a thematic (“Intimacy”, “Family”) rather than chronological arrangement limits the engrossing story of Renoir’s painterly twists and turns in the 1880s in favour of an argument about portraying “sociability”. This feels forced. Renoir can’t be recruited as a feminist or gay advocate, and it’s absurd to suggest two women innocuously rowing in “The Skiff” are in “a romantic encounter” because “boating resorts on the Seine were popular for same-sex as well as heterosexual liaisons”. Or that the sensitive portrayal of the dreamy gazing group in “At the Milliner’s” is enlightened because milliners “were widely suspected of being casual sex workers. Renoir . . . avoids such condemnation.”

Never mind. The masterpieces are here, proving Renoir pivotal to impressionism and a visionary who brought the 18th-century French tradition of elegantly orchestrated figures on to the streets of modernity. In “The Umbrellas” (1881-86), a fur-clad bourgeois mother and daughters are conveyed with impressionist haziness, while a milliner’s assistant and the youth offering her shelter are delineated in reserved, dry style, but all jostle together under the black canopies glinting in the rain. “Women pass in the street, different from the ones we used to see, because they are Renoirs,” Proust wrote. Renoir created a new world.

National Gallery, London, October 3-January 31, nationalgallery.org.uk ; Museum of Fine Arts Boston, February 28-June 13, mfa.org

rows.title: Kristin Scott Thomas and Stephen Mangan take on The Cherry Orchard
rows.content:
Sarah Hemming

Published October 3 2026

“Let’s sit here,” says Kristin Scott Thomas, sinking into a sofa in the rehearsal room kitchen. “Beside the bin.” Stephen Mangan heads straight for the kettle. Both actors look . . . bushed.

Chekhov will do that to you, says Mangan, with a broad grin, once he’s plonked himself down next to Scott Thomas, cup of tea in hand.

“It feels like Brownian motion: there’s all these molecules bumping around,” he says. “People’s whole worlds falling apart unnoticed by the other people in the room; everyone just missing each other or wanting stuff that’s incompatible. Life is a mess — that’s what he captures so well. It can be knotty to untangle in the rehearsal room. But joyous at the same time.”

The Chekhov in question is The Cherry Orchard , about to open in London’s West End with Scott Thomas as Ranevskaya and Mangan as Lopakhin. The Russian playwright’s supreme final drama, it combines all his forensic brilliance about human foibles — in this case an aristocratic family on the brink of losing their ailing estate — with an astonishingly prescient portrait of a society on the verge of seismic change. Thirteen years after its 1904 premiere, Russia would erupt in full-scale revolution. Now it lands with remarkable resonance in our own turbulent age.

“You can think of it as a play about loss,” says Scott Thomas. “But thinking about it as a play about change is more interesting.”

So much in it feels familiar, adds Mangan — the myopia, the nostalgia, the intergenerational conflict: “Change is frightening. Some people cope with it; some people see an opportunity; some people are scared by it. And we’re living through more change than ever.”

Just watching the pair of them, side by side on the sofa, you get an inkling of the chemistry they might bring to the stage. Both sharp as tacks, they are opposite in manner. Scott Thomas — contained, watchful and drily funny — can’t help projecting that effortless elegance she’s brought to dozens of screen roles, including her superb portrayal of the steely MI5 chief, Diana Taverner, in Apple TV’s Slow Horses .

Mangan, a brilliant comic actor (famous for his obnoxiously funny anaesthetist in Channel 4 sitcom Green Wing and recently a chronic liar in Florian Zeller’s play The Truth ), is all wiry energy and infectious humour. When Scott Thomas maintains that she’s struggling to find her character’s charisma, he shakes his head: “She’s providing it in spades .”

In The Cherry Orchard , the two find themselves either side of the drama’s great political divide. Scott Thomas’s Ranevskaya is the feckless aristocrat, refusing to contemplate her dire finances or the privilege that has sustained her lifestyle. Mangan’s Lopakhin is the wealthy businessman, who has hauled himself out of poverty and spends much of the play trying to convince Ranevskaya that by selling the orchard she’ll save the estate.

“I feel like Saffy in Absolutely Fabulous ,” he says, referring to the exasperated teenage daughter of the hit TV comedy series. “He has the right answer, but he’s totally ignored. He just can’t get through to them. It’s very bruising to play!”

The genius of Chekhov, of course, is that both parties are instantly recognisable and both are caught up in something far bigger than themselves. For all his wealth, Lopakhin remains an outsider who yearns to belong — he reminds Mangan of his father, an Irish labourer-turned-businessman who endured the prejudice of 1960s London — but he also fails to read the room.

Ranevskaya might be infuriating, self-absorbed and hopelessly impractical, but she’s also paralysed by grief and confronted with change that is almost incomprehensible to her. The cherry orchard, for her, is steeped in memories, not least of her beloved son who drowned on the estate. Scott Thomas, who lost first her father, then her stepfather, at a desperately young age, knows about the long shadow of loss.

“She’s been through the wringer,” she says of her character. “I have sympathy for that. It’s very difficult to imagine what she’s gone through. It’s also difficult to imagine the life of privilege that she felt entitled to. We’re talking thousands and thousands of acres. And she has zero idea of where this is going.”

The play endures, she adds, partly because Chekhov reaches through his characters’ frailties and dilemmas into something much more fundamental and timeless: “[Ranevskaya] is constantly searching for something. There’s all this trying to get to that moment when you were just loved. We’re all looking for that place. And that runs throughout [Chekhov]’s plays. People do not change . . . I think he loves his characters. Even the annoying ones. I think he loves human beings.”

“He had so much experience,” agrees Mangan. “As a doctor, a writer, a local landowner. He set up schools and charities. I think he saw how daft and pointless people’s actions can be, but there’s a fundamental empathy there. There’s warmth to it . . . It’s so funny. Because life is desperately sad and ridiculous and hilarious at the same time.”

We peel ourselves off the sofas and head into the deserted rehearsal room, where the rest of the company has just broken for lunch. En route, we pass dozens of books that director Ian Rickson has brought in as background. Rickson is something of a Chekhov maestro: he directed an exquisitely moving Uncle Vanya in 2020 (with playwright Conor McPherson, who’s also adapted this Cherry Orchard ) and an excellent Seagull (2007), in which Scott Thomas played Arkadina (a role she’d love to reprise).

Stage is a fairly rare treat for her, she says: she got “swept up” in making movies at an early age. She became awfully good at it — particularly as women concealing heartache or wrenching loss beneath an inscrutable surface. Diana Taverner is one such — a character she describes as “very, very lonely”: “She has no other life. And it’s all about self-preservation. She’s solitary. She doesn’t trust anyone.”

But in film, she misses the immediacy and camaraderie of theatre. “Working for a camera is extremely lonely,” she says. “And working with a company, you just feel completely invigorated. And with this, the end-product is ours. Once you’re onstage, you’re onstage . . . You can keep trying things all through the production. It’s alive and pliable.

“That is something that I really, really love and that you don’t feel at all when you watch a film. I’ve always called [film acting] raw material. You give your stuff to the director and the editor, and they do what they will with it. It belongs to someone else.”

“Yes, you’re providing ingredients in film, I think,” agrees Mangan, who, in contrast, deliberately favoured stage over film work in his early career. “Someone else puts it together.”

They talk about the specifics of screen and stage: the satisfaction in focusing on just one scene all day for film; the electricity of performing live; the fear about doing a great play justice; the terror of seeing your face on the poster (Scott Thomas’s Ranevskaya is currently all over the Underground).

Then there are the perils of working with a live audience. The two trade examples of audience misbehaviour — phones, food, fights. “I had a ready meal in the front row once,” says Scott Thomas, laughing. Even so, says Mangan, looking around the room where the rehearsal props sit ready for action, “what a joyful way to earn a living”.

“People say, ‘Why do you prefer theatre?’” says Scott Thomas. “For me it is telling a story to live, breathing, coughing, eating people and trying to drag them along with you. Which I find incredibly thrilling.”

‘The Cherry Orchard’, Harold Pinter Theatre, London, October 3-January 9 2027, thecherryorchardplay.co.uk

rows.title: Meet the new movie villains: Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman
rows.content:
Danny Leigh

Published October 3 2026

This coming January will mark 100 years since the great Austrian director Fritz Lang unveiled his deathless science fiction story, Metropolis . The movie was set in 2026, foreseen as a brutal world of gleaming robots and disposable humans. Above ground, the wealthy frolic in skyscrapers. Beneath it, the masses tend the machines that run the place. All this is the design of a ruthless industrialist, Joh Fredersen. The lot of the have-nots doesn’t trouble him. They are where they belong, he says.

You can imagine the response in the kinos of Weimar Berlin. Now, in the actual 2026, more boos may greet a trio of new movies about three men often seen as modern Fredersens: Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Sam Altman. First up is The Social Reckoning , sequel to 2010’s The Social Network , updating that movie’s caustic portrait of Zuckerberg. Then — in theory — comes the scalding four-hour documentary Musk . (Uncertainty has concerned the plans of international distributors Universal.) Finally there is Artificial , an account of Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI in 2023.

Early feedback from the subjects has been on brand. Musk reacted furiously on X, insulting director Alex Gibney while describing the movie named for him as “a hit piece that misses”. (Nothing says that louder than enraged posts on social media.) Altman has kept his counsel, though his brother Jack may have spoken for the family by giving faint, backhanded praise to star Andrew Garfield for nailing his sibling’s walk. And Zuckerberg has not publicly acknowledged The Social Reckoning . In the wake of The Social Network , the Facebook co-founder admitted to finding it “hurtful”. Now, haughty silence speaks for the imperial CEO of Meta.

Yet even the most hostile movie can only be so frank. The famous dictum of French director François Truffaut was that it was impossible to make an anti-war film because just putting violence on screen made it a spectacle. A similar thought came to mind watching The Social Network . Zuckerberg was played by Jesse Eisenberg, jumpy but magnetic as movie stars are. By contrast, every time its real subject has appeared in public, his awkward, eerie affect reminds you why he more often doesn’t. To different degrees, the same applies to Musk and Altman. In a medium built on characters that audiences like and want to spend time with, these are films about men of which neither is generally true.

With Eisenberg choosing not to return, the lead in The Social Reckoning now goes to Succession star Jeremy Strong, a still more compelling actor. The script again comes from Aaron Sorkin, a writer whose signature is the killer line amid sexy backstairs intrigue.

For the audience, meanwhile, the story offers a charismatic bad guy equal to our current peril. Because, with the timing producers pray for, all three movies meet the zeitgeist head on. Early in Metropolis , an accident in the “machine hall” kills a swath of workers. Now AI is said to have the potential to wipe out all humanity. What more could be asked of the supervillains that represent it?

Scale matters. The Social Reckoning would feel less urgent if we knew it only led to the pathos of Meta’s “pervert glasses”. Instead, at this moment of impossible high stakes, Zuckerberg is reported to have privately urged Donald Trump to block calls to regulate AI.

We will see which side of history that puts him on, assuming someone is left to keep score. In the short term, US cinema clearly wants to be seen as speaking truth to power — a public defender in dark times, with popcorn thrown in.

To some, that will look like just the latest flashpoint in the long, mutual distaste between Hollywood and Silicon Valley. In the same moment Zuckerberg confessed to being wounded by The Social Network , he alluded to a basic lack of understanding from the filmmakers as to what drove a tech leader. Musk being Musk, his recent attacks on Gibney only followed a niche, racially fixated campaign against Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey .

But the reality is two industries much closer than appearances suggest. Since the end of 2023’s Hollywood strikes, the film business has quietly embraced AI in countless ways, across pre- and post-production, and all points between. Despite the oppositional vibes, ever rarer is the movie that can truly claim to have been made without it.

Or, indeed, to have been made by companies not also in the AI business. Witness the tech boss no one has yet made a film about, Jeff Bezos, whose journey from online bookseller to gym-jacked potentate might otherwise seem ripe for it. At the same time as hugely expanding its presence in AI, Amazon’s role in film dramatically enlarged on buying legacy brand MGM. The company has had one of the year’s biggest hits with feelgood sci-fi Project Hail Mary . A large, starry autumn slate includes the movie comeback of Ali G. And once a new James Bond is finally announced, he will be making films for Bezos.

Off-screen, Amazon’s own AI products now include tools for filmmakers, as well as cloud infrastructure used by other studios. A person seeking conflicts of interest might point to Artificial , a movie that was originally an Amazon production. Then, earlier this year, Amazon agreed a $50bn investment in OpenAI. The film was dropped soon afterwards.

Unnamed sources put that down simply to perceived lack of quality. The same logic was used to explain the other studios that then passed on releasing it. (Director Luca Guadagnino is an erratic talent; the film is now to be released by independent Neon.) Still, the impression of a mass Hollywood loss of nerve did match a landscape where every studio is now busy folding AI into its operations.

That list includes Universal and The Social Reckoning ’s distributor, Sony. Disney has lately advertised jobs bringing AI into its creative processes. Netflix is already well under way with that, using the technology in around 300 titles during the first half of 2026 alone. Kane Parsons, the wunderkind director whose May horror movie Backrooms became a box office sensation, has said the technology “defeats the purpose” of filmmaking. A24, the studio that funded it, now has an AI partnership with Google.

And of course, there is Paramount. Any day now, the studio looks set to finally seal the takeover of Warner Bros that will create a Hollywood behemoth. It will also give vast cross-industry power to Larry Ellison, owner of a controlling stake in Paramount Skydance, whose corporation Oracle has also driven much of the AI boom. Once the deal is done, every ticket to a “WarnerMount” film will be financially wrapped up with Oracle’s planned building of data centres worldwide.

Between them, he and Bezos will also be making a hefty proportion of all Hollywood product. It may be a long wait for the next big-league movie about flawed tech leaders.

Back in 1927, Fritz Lang ended Metropolis on a note of uplift. Ultimately, Joh Fredersen had a redemptive story arc. Real life follows its own script. Six years later, Lang fled Nazi Germany. Eventually, he settled in the US, making hard, sad, often brilliant films about moral grey zones and people’s helplessness in the face of the system.

Several are now owned by Warner Bros. As such, they will, in turn, shortly become the property of Larry Ellison. In 2026, it is perhaps where they belong.

‘The Social Reckoning’ is in cinemas from October 9; ‘Musk’ is in US cinemas from October 9; ‘Artificial’ is in US cinemas from December 25 and UK cinemas from January 22
