rows.title: Over 20 NHS trusts have ditched Palantir waiting-list tools, analysis shows
rows.content:
Amy Borrett and Laura Hughes in London

Published October 3 2026

More than 20 NHS trusts in England have stopped using Palantir’s waiting list tools, according to FT analysis that casts doubt on widely cited claims about the success of the controversial data project led by the US software giant.

NHS England claims that more than 300,000 patients have been flagged for removal from elective care waiting lists across 40 trusts realising benefits from two hospital co-ordination tools built using Palantir technology.

But FT analysis of freedom of information requests published on transparency website WhatDoTheyKnow found more than half of these trusts no longer used the inpatient or outpatient care co-ordination solutions to manage waiting lists.

The UK statistics regulator told the FT that, in response to the findings, it had opened a new investigation into NHS England’s claims in relation to the Federated Data Platform, the Palantir-built system that underpins the waiting list tools and is aimed at driving efficiencies.

The health service has already been scrutinised by the Office for Statistics Regulation after the FT uncovered a litany of errors in key datasets and revealed that it had quietly added a caveat to the claims on its website.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Palantir said in a statement: “These two tools are typically used most heavily when the software is first installed in a trust because their primary purpose is to clean up legacy data errors so that the trust has a clear picture of who needs to be treated.”

“This is a basic rule for any customer we work with: that before you start to use the software to make an organisation more productive, you make sure that you are working off accurate data,” the company added.

Ministers are searching for a British supplier in case they decide to replace Palantir, which is controversial because of its ties to the US and Israeli defence industries, amid growing pressure to trigger a 2027 break clause in the FDP contract.

The FT’s analysis of the FOI responses also uncovered fundamental flaws in another of NHS England’s key statistics: that 1.2mn patients have been removed from waiting lists using the FDP’s “referral to treatment” tool.

More than 60 per cent of the 31 NHS trusts included in this 1.2mn figure said they could not quantify the benefits of using the tool, while 6 per cent said they did not use it.

A further 16 per cent did not respond to the FOI requests, which were made by Medact, a health campaign group that opposes Palantir’s presence in the NHS.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

In their responses, many NHS trusts said it was not possible to directly attribute any waiting list removals to Palantir’s platform. One trust noted that staff were still responsible for processing discharges on existing hospital platforms with the aid of a number of inputs including the FDP.

Another NHS trust said that while the software helped with waiting list management, the removals “would be happening anyway” as staff could already access the information on existing systems.

The findings have amplified concerns that NHS England has misrepresented the data to present the contract, which was awarded in 2023 at a value of £330mn, in a more favourable light.

Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the House of Commons’ technology committee, said: “These overinflated numbers really show the Palantir contract should be cancelled. There are much better UK alternatives.”

NHS England has added disclaimers to a number of its key claims following the initial investigation by the statistics regulator, acknowledging that simple comparisons of performance before and after adoption do not prove the platform’s effectiveness.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Charles Tallack, former head of operational research and evaluation at NHS England, said the FT’s new analysis cast further doubt on the claims.

“By not accounting for what would have happened without the FDP, NHS England’s method overstates its impact,” he said.

The government has commissioned an independent evaluation of the FDP but the findings are not expected until 2029.

NHS England’s data, digital and technology committee has raised concerns about the “slow pace of delivery” across flagship technology programmes including the FDP, the NHS App and plans for a Single Patient Record.

According to board papers published this week, the committee found a “consistent experience of slower than anticipated pace and disjointed projects where we are falling short of our ambition”.

Critics have argued that Palantir’s tools are less good than some existing local systems, such as CIPHA, an NHS programme that uses technology to link health and social care data from more than 2,000 organisations. The software is used across almost 30 per cent of England, according to its supplier Graphnet.

The FDP could be delivered by a series of smaller businesses already providing data-sharing and management solutions to parts of the NHS, they have said, rather than relying on a single supplier.

One senior health service data expert said the FDP should be built by “a network of contracts, with multiple suppliers, orchestrated by a centre that understands the data and the services”.

NHS England said in a statement: “It is right that local NHS organisations are able to select — and test — individual tools in the Federated Data Platform depending on their needs. Nearly 140 NHS organisations across England have reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping join up and improve care for patients.”

Palantir added that the company’s “software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3 per cent reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 5.6 per cent improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days”.

The Office for Statistics Regulation told the FT that it did not regulate claims made by private companies.

rows.title: SJP overhauls controversial loan scheme to reduce disruption to customers
rows.content:
Emma Dunkley

Published October 3 2026

St James’s Place has overhauled a controversial loan scheme for its partner financial professionals to help mitigate disruption to clients when their adviser leaves the firm.

The UK’s largest wealth manager offers loans to partners — self-employed advisers operating within the SJP network — to help them acquire businesses and clients from other SJP advisers when they leave or retire.

The so-called Business Sale and Purchase scheme aims to provide a smooth transition for clients when they are handed over to someone else.

However, the scheme has come under criticism in recent years over cases where some clients who had been passed to new advisers had not received sufficient levels of service — despite paying fees.

SJP has now launched a digital tool so that advisers can access data about individual clients more quickly, helping them to serve clients better and to provide instant valuations of advisory businesses. Previously, a business valuation took about three weeks and could only be done twice a year.

“Through improved sharing of data, continuity of service to clients is assured during the sale process,” said Mark FitzPatrick, chief executive of St James’s Place. “This enhanced approach will allow ambitious partners to grow their businesses and make succession planning easier.

“It also manages many of the conflicts that could damage outcomes for clients,” he added, such as the inconvenience of moving to a new company’s infrastructure or a different charging structure.

The firm’s charging structure for clients was also revamped last year, with punitive exit charges removed for new customers.

SJP said that to improve the loan scheme’s transparency, it now issues a quarterly update so partners can see actual prices and terms agreed when a business is sold within the network.

Adviser succession planning is important for clients, who may not choose to follow their adviser to a new business and are instead passed to a different firm within the SJP practice.

The development comes as several partner firms have exited SJP in recent months, including Prospera and Wellesley.

Robin Powell, a financial consumer advocate, said that rather than necessarily creating a smoother transition for clients, the revamped BSP scheme and faster internal valuations mainly benefit SJP. “They keep assets and fees inside the firm at a moment when advisers are leaving for rivals.

“If this were really about client outcomes, SJP would be making it easier for clients to follow their adviser wherever they go, not just easier for the firm to reassign them internally.”

Rob Sanders, SJP’s chief client officer, said that clients can choose “who they are advised by, whether they choose to remain with SJP’s Partnership or go elsewhere”. The BSP overhaul is part of a broader strategy to revamp its tech under FitzPatrick.

rows.title: Tempted to go freelance? Here’s six financial tips for success
rows.content:
Claer Barrett

Published October 3 2026

Do you dream of becoming your own boss? Accountants tell me they are encountering more clients in their forties and fifties who are leaving senior professional roles because they want more autonomy and to build something for themselves.

For some, the switch to a freelance career has been prompted by a corporate restructuring, redundancy programme or the growing number of employers demanding a return to the office . Yet others feel they can do more and earn more with greater flexibility if they start something of their own.

“A lot of people are building out their personal brand and doing things in addition to their corporate career, which could be the first step towards starting their own business,” says Nicole Zalys, founder of Villiers & Co and better known online as The London Accountant.

If you’re weighing up a more entrepreneurial path, thinking about the financial side of your freelance life is vital — here are six points to consider:

What would you have to earn to replace the certainty of a monthly salary? Scrutinise your household expenses — what’s the bare minimum you’d need to earn (after tax) to meet these commitments? Many new freelancers I’ve helped in recent years confessed they only had a vague idea of this, but if you have a variable income, keeping a keen eye on the budget is non-negotiable.

Allowing money to intermingle makes it harder to know where you stand, project your income and, crucially, your tax liability. Not putting tax money aside is the easiest mistake to make, but Making Tax Digital means keeping separate records on approved accounting software a necessity.

Those generating more than £50,000 in revenue (not profit) from self-employment or property rental need to register and file quarterly updates to HM Revenue & Customs. From next April, this threshold will fall to £30,000.

Most digital banks offer free HMRC-compliant software with their sole trader or small business accounts, but scrutinise what else you’ll be charged for. Three words you need to understand? Payments on account. Once you generate a certain amount of income from self-employment, HMRC expects you to pay half of next year’s estimated tax bill in advance in January with a second payment in July.

This is the hardest thing for new freelancers to get right, but it’s the difference between succeeding and struggling, says Deborah Edwards, director of Harland Accountants. Even after researching what others charge, the temptation to undersell your services to get work can be hard to resist. She advises standing in front of a mirror and practising saying “My day rate is £X” to get used to it.

“You don’t have to charge the same price to everyone, but when you have negotiated a rate, agree a contract setting out what’s expected and beware of scope creep. If the client asks for something extra, say ‘Of course I can. Would you like me to put a quote together for you?’”

“Your fee isn’t just your ‘wage’: you’re paying your own tax and national insurance, and need to factor in the paid holiday and sick leave you would have had as an employee, as well as all those unbillable hours spent quoting, emailing, invoicing and sometimes travelling,” says private chef Philippa Davis .

Accountants can advise you on allowable expenses that you can offset against tax, which usually includes their fee. Deciding whether to set up as a sole trader or a limited company is an important question to discuss.

“You also need to talk about how you are going to draw an income or take money out of the company; how much tax you will probably have to pay and when and whether you should register for VAT,” Zalys says. Be aware that the £90,000 VAT threshold is measured over a rolling 12-month period.

Having limited liability status legally separates a business from its owner, offering protection for your personal assets. “If you have a higher level of risk, such as employing people or leasing a property, it’s definitely something to consider,” says Zalys.

“If you want to put your surplus capital to work, it’s possible to have a savings account in the name of your limited company and earn interest on it,” she adds. The Flagstone platform offers a good overview of different accounts and rates.

Be very careful about how you use directors’ loans. There are strict tax rules, and it’s very easy for the unwary to fall foul of these.

Just 16 per cent of self-employed people save for retirement, according to PensionBee. Locking money away inside a pension is a barrier for those with a variable income, but they could aim to set money aside in savings and make contributions on a quarterly or annual basis, says Maike Currie, vice-president of personal finance at PensionBee. “The ‘free money’ of tax relief from the government is a valuable incentive, especially for higher-rate taxpayers.” Limited company directors could offset their pension contributions against their taxable profits, thereby reducing their corporation tax bill.

Don’t forget about other benefits that employees often receive as standard, such as life insurance, health insurance, income protection or a critical illness policy. Yes, these will cost you, but the risk of not having protection in place could be greater.

My followers report that the biggest mindset shift from corporate life is that you can’t wait for the work to find you — you have to go out there and look for it.

“Don’t be afraid to put yourself and your business out there — it’s about being visible, memorable and not being afraid to stand out,” says Zalys. “The people who you end up gravitating towards and doing business with are the people who you remember.”

Invest time in building your professional network; join local groups (or set up your own) and be shameless — followers advise using the “Open to Work” banner on LinkedIn and contacting people you’ve previously worked with.

Finally, be aware that the freelancer’s life can be a lonely one. Building connections with a group of like-minded people for emotional support is something many followers tell me keeps them sane. You can share tips, recommend each other and collaborate, but most importantly, have each other’s backs if the going gets tough — as well as being there to celebrate the wins.

Claer Barrett is the FT’s consumer editor; [email protected] Instagram @ClaerB

rows.title: When £35 New Zealand Chardonnay meets £1,000 white burgundy
rows.content:
Jancis Robinson

Published October 3 2026

It takes something to put your small country’s relatively unknown wines up against world-famous archetypes that cost up to 28 times more in three blind tastings by accredited professionals in both hemispheres.

In this case that something was chutzpah, confidence and a billionaire backer with a taste for white burgundy. Brian Sheth, former president of Vista Equity Partners based in Austin, Texas, is now well able to afford grands crus retailing at about £1,000 a bottle.

He is the Sheth of Smith & Sheth, an ambitious wine producer formed in 2014 in Hawke’s Bay on the east coast of New Zealand’s North Island. With his particular interest in conservation and wildlife (and continuing to invest in tech and video games), Sheth found that he really appreciated the unsullied isolation of New Zealand, where he met fellow wine fanatic Steve Smith.

The forceful Smith, one of New Zealand’s impressive cohort of Masters of Wine, has enjoyed a storied career there at Villa Maria and in the 1990s set up the much-admired wine producer Craggy Range based on another American fortune, that made by the Peabody family from cement. Post-Craggy, in a move designed to prove that New Zealand wine is very much more than commercial Sauvignon Blanc, he organised tours for international opinion-formers of some of the country’s finest wine producers in 2023 (which I benefited from, pursued by Cyclone Gabrielle) and 2025.

The three blind tastings were held in Christchurch in July and in London and Burgundy last month, with tasters including 13 Masters of Wine (including two Burgundy specialists), four Master Sommeliers and some of Australasia’s and Europe’s most respected fine wine merchants.

I was away for the London one so joined Smith, Sheth and fellow tasters at one of Burgundy’s new luxury hotels, Les Sources de Vougeot, for one sunny morning devoted to blind tasting 10 of their New Zealand Chardonnays retailing at £35 to £95 and 14 white burgundies at £55 to more than £1,000 a bottle. Acknowledging Burgundy’s current sky-high prices, Smith pointed out in his briefing before the tasting that there had been similar comparisons in the past, but only with burgundies at the same prices as their New Zealand counterparts. “There’s no point in matching prices. If you don’t win that, you’re dreaming.”

With the six-month interval between grape harvests in the two hemispheres in mind, all the burgundies were 2023s picked before the rains that prejudiced that generous vintage, while the antipodean challengers came from the excellent 2024 vintage there.

The 24 wines were divided into four groups by supposed quality and style: the equivalents of Burgundy’s village wines; Chablis and the like; “premiers crus”; and “grands crus”. The burgundies had all been sourced via Farr Vintners in London and were chosen from producers particularly admired by Smith and Sheth, including Domaines Leflaive, des Comtes Lafon and François Raveneau, star of Chablis. The wild card, which stood out for its obvious ripeness, was the least expensive burgundy, a £55 wine made by Verget in the Mâconnais at the southern end of the region. But I thought the other Mâconnais wine made by Verget’s owner Jean-Marie Guffens under his own Domaine Guffens-Heynen label, a St-Véran, Clos de Poncetys, could easily have come from the Côte d’Or to the north (and was the tasters’ overall favourite in the “premier cru” group).

We were instructed to score each wine, and to say whether we thought it came from Burgundy or New Zealand. I’ve long sung the praises of New Zealand’s crisp, bright-fruited Chardonnays, generally much preferring them to the country’s more monotone Sauvignon Blancs, and know well that white burgundies can be much surlier in youth — so I don’t think I could be accused of automatically scoring the wines I took to be burgundies more generously than their antipodean counterparts. My favourites are in my list of recommendations.

I’m no fan of scores but needs must. For what it’s worth, I gave all these 10 recommended wines at least 17.5 out of 20 and six of the 10 turned out to be burgundies. But the only wine I scored 18.5 was a Smith & Sheth wine that was the tasters’ top wine overall and is currently unavailable commercially. Les Graviers is a tiny-production wine from its Omahu vineyard in Hawke’s Bay, just one barrique, so only 300 bottles to be launched next May.

It’s based on two selections of Chardonnay that came originally from top Burgundy vineyards co-fermented: one known as Wente in California and Mendoza in New Zealand, and the other based on a cutting Smith took, with permission on condition of the grower’s anonymity, from Le Montrachet vineyard in 1995. Smith’s then boss at Villa Maria insisted on exclusive use of it when it came out of quarantine but finally allowed Smith to plant it in 2017.

As for successfully identifying the origins of each wine, it was relatively easy in most of the groups, especially the grandest one, but I failed to match a single wine in the “Chablis” group with its actual origins — and was relieved to learn that my fellow Master of Wine, Tom Parker of Farr Vintners whose palate I respect, was similarly foxed. I suspect that the naturally high acidity (shared with that of Chablis) of New Zealand wines was a factor here.

In a 44-page introduction to the tasting, Smith pointed out that the Burgundian heartland of the Côte d’Or is much warmer than their three sites, in Hawke’s Bay, North Canterbury and Lowburn in Central Otago — especially as harvest approaches. Burgundy’s climate is (warming) continental whereas New Zealand’s is maritime and its especially bright light and unpolluted atmosphere are other aspects that add zest to NZ Chardonnay.

Much was made in this document of the geological parallels between the Côte d’Or and its antipode in New Zealand, especially the winery Smith and Sheth added in 2017, Pyramid Valley in North Canterbury which, unusually for New Zealand, boasts some of the limestone common in the Côte d’Or. I sent the text to Professor Alex Maltman, the most wine-minded of geologists. He was unimpressed.

Despite its ambitious nature, the whole exercise was a real triumph for New Zealand. The top-scoring wine in three of the four groups was one of Smith and Sheth’s, with Les Graviers (which was preferred to the two Côte d’Or grands crus) and Pyramid Valley’s Low Burn bottling from Central Otago in the “Chablis” group being particular favourites.

Sheth was there in both London and Burgundy to see this particular investment bear fruit. The private manager of his $3mn cellar, Summer Altice, came to Burgundy from her base in Los Angeles bringing various magnums of his grand cru burgundies for the celebratory meals after the tasting.

By coincidence, even more of the special qualities of NZ Chardonnay were demonstrated in another tasting in London later that same week. Paul Brajkovich hosted a showing of every single vintage of the most refined single-vineyard Chardonnay produced by his family at their Kumeu River winery outside Auckland. Of the 20 vintages of Kumeu River’s Hunting Hill Chardonnay from the superlative 2025, just released on export markets, back to 2006, not a single wine was tired (the Estate bottling is a steal at £190 a dozen in bond from Farr Vintners).

None was ruined by a dodgy cork (winemaker and Master of Wine Michael Brajkovich was an early adopter of screw caps ). And for much the same reason, none was remotely oxidised — unlike so many white burgundies made in the earlier years of this century.

Chardonnay is the most-planted white wine grape variety in the world. It is not too fussy about climate and terroir, so just about every wine-producing region has some, especially for traditional method sparkling wine, often labelled Blanc de Blancs if made exclusively from Chardonnay. But the regions that have established a widely acknowledged reputation for serious, refined, still Chardonnay, in — very approximately — the order that that reputation was established, are Burgundy; Limoux; Jura; Santa Barbara County and Sonoma Coast in California; Australia’s cooler wine regions; the Uco Valley and Patagonia in Argentina; coastal wine regions of South Africa and Chile; Willamette Valley in Oregon — and, of course, New Zealand.

Getting in on the act are Germany, England, Belgium and Canada, however.

rows.title: Can you survive a home renovation with your relationship intact?
rows.content:
Clara Baldock

Published October 3 2026

Squatting in a derelict kitchen, slurping pot noodles and donning shower caps to evade dust, it’s a miracle any whiff of romance remained. My husband and I had recently bought a shabby Victorian London home and, thinking ourselves practical types, we saw it as an exciting opportunity to put our stamp on the place.

Once the previous owners had moved out, taking with them the life-size Tardis (the time-travelling police box from Doctor Who ) that commandeered the dining room and a stack of festering rabbit hutches in the galley kitchen, we rolled up our sleeves and got stuck in.

There were the predictable stresses — budgets blown — and the unexpected ones: an infestation of fleas, caused by foxes sniffing around the half-built kitchen extension, which put two of the builders in hospital. There were the weekends and evenings dedicated to DIY (three letters that now make my husband shudder), the hours lost to YouTube tutorials and the stark reminder that Instagram’s glossy, flick-of-a-screen home transformations filter out the dirt, debt and marital spats. All the while, we were planning our wedding. It is not a combination I would recommend.

A recently updated study by Novuna Personal Finance found that more than half of homeowners reported disputes stemming directly from renovation decisions , and nearly one in five said a home improvement project had pushed them to the brink of splitting up — or ended the relationship entirely.

“It is an immutable fact of renovating that work always takes longer and costs more than you originally expected,” says Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell. She advises having a contingency fund of 10-25 per cent. “You need to agree on your approach to spending and borrowing. If one of you is more relaxed about debt, or more prone to overspending, you can end up in hot water.”

Environmental psychologist Toby Israel, author of Designing-Women’s Lives, adds that living in chaos heightens tensions. “When one’s space is a mess, life can feel a mess.” To help navigate this, she advises couples to carve out one tidy room, or create a “clean zone” wherever possible. Israel views the need for sanctuary as a matter of gender equality, too. “Even in today’s world, housework and childcare more often fall to women. My research shows that they often lack ‘a room of their own’ — a place where they can retreat and recharge,” she says. “When it comes to home style, men often defer to female partners, thereby stymying the opportunity to equally express their ‘self’ in their space.”

Unfortunately, an invasion of privacy is inevitable. During a renovation, you will temporarily acquire a third wheel: your builder. Our builder, my husband and I would eat sandwiches together in the unruly garden and squeeze into the front of his van for sundry trips to builders' merchants Selco. Even on the morning of our wedding, he still found a way to make his presence felt — calling about the precise pitch of the new roof before wishing us well.

“When there are people around in the house, there’s no privacy, less headspace and little time to talk — and when [couples] do talk, probably top of the agenda is the next decision on the renovation list,” says psychotherapist Joanna Harrison. Decision making is a common flashpoint. My pickiness and insatiable capacity for online trawling meant I dominated the design conversation. I obsessed over micro-details — agonising over brushed or antique brass for light switches — wearing my about-to-be husband’s patience thin, all while soliciting far too many other opinions.

Interior designer Emma Ainscough often finds herself mediating. “I’m regularly tasked with what feels like informal couples counselling over WhatsApp groups,” she says, noting that the master bedroom, bathroom and kitchen spark the most debate. Pink, she says, frequently kicks off arguments. “However, with heavy cabinetry and appliances, I find an earthy pink in the kitchen actually softens the scheme and creates a timeless, balanced look.”

So how do you survive a renovation as a couple? Harrison suggests regular check-ins to gauge how you are both coping, to accept friction and to approach financial conversations with curiosity. “Ask: what are you worried about?” And for those happy to jump into therapy speak: “What does spending money on this project mean to you?” She adds: “Relationships need updating as people grow and change. Doing up your house together can be a statement of investment — saying, this is how we want to live, and our home is a reflection not just of our ideas but of our whole relationship.”

Almost five years on, now that the dust has settled, it all feels worth it. My vision and my partner’s tenacity mean the Ikea “hack” wardrobes are still standing, the garden pavers — which he painstakingly chiselled into organic shapes at my behest — look lovely, and we glided through another wedding anniversary earlier this summer. The builder is still on speed dial.

rows.title: Students turn to lawyers to fight AI misconduct accusations
rows.content:
Josh Gabert-Doyon in London

Published October 3 2026

When Alice submitted an essay for her final year of university in May, she recognised that it “wasn’t the best thing” she’d ever written.

But she was surprised to receive an email from her Russell Group university accusing her of having used AI to write the coursework.

Alice — not her real name — described the experience as an “emotionally intense” ending to her music degree. Despite sharing her notes and early drafts of the essay with university administrators, she was told she would be questioned by a faculty misconduct panel.

Panicked that she would not complete her degree and waste tens of thousands of pounds in tuition fees, Alice turned to her university’s student services for support, which said they were too busy.

Instead, she sought legal advice — a move that has become increasingly common among students accused of AI misconduct as universities crack down on the abuse of the technology.

With the help of her lawyer, who charged more than £3,000, Alice had the cheating allegations against her dismissed.

Louise O’Driscoll, a solicitor specialising in education law who represented Alice, told the FT there had been a “notable increase” in similar cases this year.

However, she acknowledged that AI misconduct still “goes on a lot more than it probably comes to light”.

Daniel Sokol, a barrister at 12 King’s Bench Walk, described a “tsunami” of student enquiries from those facing accusations of AI misconduct.

He said his firm had received 300 requests related to the unauthorised use of artificial intelligence at universities in the first half of this year, roughly 40 per cent of total business enquiries.

The higher education sector is struggling with how to approach AI. Many universities are caught between wanting to prepare students for the workforce by encouraging AI use and having to police its widespread use in assessments.

The total number of students using AI in graded work is difficult to establish. However, a 2024 survey of more than 95,000 students at 20 public research universities in the US — led by Igor Chirikov at the University of California, Berkeley — found that about 9 per cent admitted to using AI to cheat.

“These are [accusations] that could haunt students for a long time after they’ve qualified,” Sokol said, noting many of his clients were students studying medicine and law. “You get innocent students being found guilty. Those are the biggest tragedies.”

Fighting a typical accusation of misusing AI at an internal misconduct panel will cost students between £2,000 and £3,000, Sokol said, although seeking testimony from forensic linguists or other experts can stretch the bills higher.

When it comes to their legal defence, education lawyers like Sokol and O’Driscoll have focused on ambiguities in universities’ policies on AI usage.

While many policies cover entire institutions, individual departments or lecturers may deviate in where they draw the line on misconduct, with some students unclear about what would constitute cheating.

For lecturers, the proliferation of AI-generated coursework has led to frustration.

Universities UK, the industry group representing higher education institutions, said that “both staff and students within the sector are alive to the potential risks posed by AI tools, particularly when it comes to exams and assessment”.

“Students must learn to use it honestly and well,” the group added.

Some universities have responded by simply softening the threshold of what constitutes AI misconduct. The University of Bath and Queen Mary University London have both published guidance using the term “poor academic practice” to distinguish certain forms of AI use.

Ciaran Donaghy, lead policy officer at the Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education, an independent body that works to improve standards in the sector, noted that a “lack of clarity” over how universities police AI was “fuelling anxiety” for students.

Donaghy noted that international students who speak English as a second language were at higher risk of being falsely accused. A 2024 study by a group of Stanford University academics found AI detectors disproportionately flagged writing by non-native speakers.

AI misconduct cases have also started to escalate from internal disciplinary cases to formal legal action. Sokol said he recently settled a case related to AI academic misconduct out of court with a university.

In the US, several high-profile cases have emerged, including that of a history student who successfully sued Adelphi University in New York after being accused of using AI to help with an assignment.

There are also concerns over the increasing reliance on AI-detection tools, which Sokol described as “flawed”. As the software has become integrated into universities’ digital submission systems, there have been more complaints of false positives.

Despite her experience, Alice, the music student, said she felt that universities were “trying their best” to deal with genuine AI misconduct.

And she offered a simple explanation for why she found herself accused. “I use AI day-to-day with emails and admin, kind of as a personal assistant,” she said. “If you’re at university right now, you’re going to pick up the language and the way that chatbots talk.”

rows.title: Can sing, can conduct, can dance: the many talents of Barbara Hannigan
rows.content:
Richard Fairman

Published October 3 2026

A group of dancers has formed a line across the stage, stretching out their hands. Two male dancers lift one of the women, spinning her round in the air, one of them sweeping her up on to his shoulders — and then she starts to sing. The music is complex, a modern electronic score, and the singer is hitting multiple high Cs as she continues to dance with the others. How can she do this?

Those who have followed Barbara Hannigan’s career to date just might have guessed it is her. The Canadian soprano is not just one of the world’s most in-demand singers, she has also built a serious career as a conductor — and now the 55-year-old is going one step further.

Hannigan has worked with dancers before, not least a couple of productions with choreographer Sasha Waltz, but nothing that will have prepared her for this upcoming multimedia show. Entitled La Mer and addressing the pollution of the seas, it is a full-scale dance evening, choreographed by Nanine Linning and presented by Scapino Ballet in Rotterdam and then on tour in the Netherlands and Spain, though without Hannigan or a live orchestra on the tour.

Here is the soprano in all her multitasking glory. The performance starts with her onstage as a silent observer. From there she goes down into the pit to conduct the Rotterdam Philharmonic Orchestra in Debussy’s La Mer and “Sirènes”. Then, finally, she is lifted out of the pit to join the dancers on stage, simultaneously singing and dancing through to the end. Beyond all of that, she is credited as the production’s music director.

Was she always an overachiever? “Our high school motto in Nova Scotia was ‘Strive for Excellence’,” says Hannigan. “I love being competitive with myself and it doesn’t matter if I win, or fall down, or don’t achieve everything I planned, only that I went for it. We had great music teachers and I still see my teacher from elementary school. All of us were inspired by her, not just the Hannigan kids, who were musical, but every kid in the class. She wanted us all to be the best and that sparked me.”

There were no dance lessons as a child. Her family only allowed one sport and one extracurricular activity, which for her was music. It was only when she was 19 that she signed up for a modern dance course and became involved with the contemporary music scene in Toronto, where composers and dancers mixed together (“that was my scene”).

From there to La Mer looks like a big jump. “I didn’t know what I was getting into until we started,” she says. “From the first day of rehearsal Nanine didn’t treat me as a singer, or a non-dancer, in any way. She makes the choreography and I have to do it. I am 30 years older than most of these dancers, but you can’t bring it down to the lowest common denominator. I have been training to be ready for this, I do a lot of cardio anyway and have my list of stretches and dance exercises.”

None of this would be possible with a singer who was not open to the physical challenges. Linning says Hannigan is the ideal colleague, as she allows physicality to inform her singing and vice versa. It helps that Linning has also directed five operas, so they are able to meet in a shared zone of understanding.

“In the beginning Barbara is playing a goddess, a seer, a leader, in a lament for what is broken,” says Linning, adding that, through the idea of transformation, she later finds a way to bring hope and vision. “We speak about climate change in this work, but also the duality of humanity. We all go to the oceans for rejuvenating, we live by them, we need them for food, but we are constantly dumping in them everything we don’t need. This piece is about giving the ocean a voice and at the same time reflecting on our behaviour as humans.”

The electronic score for the final section is by Cypriot composer Yannis Kyriakides, a fellow student when Hannigan was studying in The Hague. It is the first time he has written for her and she says she loves how flexible he is. Not every composer would be happy to raise the music by a fourth or spin it out at half the speed.

“This is the kind of collaboration I love,” says Hannigan. “George [Benjamin], who I adore, changed one note in [his opera] Written on Skin , only because I sang it wrong so many times that he began to like it. The last straw was when he cut his finger and I bandaged it for him, so he changed the note and wrote in my score, ‘Because you fixed my finger’.” What will musicologists studying the score in the future make of that?

Benjamin’s two full-length operas are only a couple of the prominent new works in which Hannigan has taken a leading role. She reckons she has, remarkably, given the premieres of over 130 contemporary pieces.

Nothing in her childhood seems to have prepared her for this testing speciality. The music in Nova Scotia, she says, was very limited. She didn’t hear a Mahler symphony until she moved to Toronto, because this was the pre-internet era and she was living in an area with little public transport, so “you stayed put and did your thing”.

That isolation, which she sees as a benefit, is something she recognises in Iceland, where she has just taken over as chief conductor and artistic director of the Iceland Symphony Orchestra — no small achievement for somebody who did not start conducting until she was 40.

“I was thankful for that,” she says. “I had so much experience standing beside conductors and watching what they say to players and how they handle the psychology. I see so many talented young conductors, but many do not get beyond the first 10 years, because they weren’t taught how to be authentic on the podium. An orchestra can kill a conductor. If the players are silly or chat, and you don’t understand why or you take it personally, it can stop the process.” Those sound like wise words.

Her concerts in Iceland start with a premiere in the first programme, more contemporary music and — no surprise — some music where she will sing and conduct at the same time. As for dancing, too? Possibly not just yet.

Scapino Ballet Rotterdam’s ‘La Mer’ has its premiere at the Nieuwe Luxor Theater in Rotterdam on October 9

rows.title: A Londoner’s guide to hating London
rows.content:
Bryce Elder

Published October 3 2026

London makes a man tired of living, as Samuel Johnson almost said. Maybe, had he ever ridden the travelator between the Jubilee and Northern lines at Waterloo Station, he’d have been more concise.

This past summer, for a couple of weeks, everyone on that route had no choice but to appreciate an audio art installation . The artist, Ain Bailey, lists with urgency the names of closed bars, nightclubs and record shops in between choruses of “Maybe It’s Because I’m a Londoner”, sung as ghostly overdubbed operetta.

Subtext, as the meme says, is for cowards — which is not to presume that many commuters were taking the message home. It would need a black-cab driver’s knowledge to recognise incantations of Candy Bar, Turnmills and Our Price as a eulogy for the capital’s lost community spaces rather than as a means to discourage loitering.

What’s most authentically London about the work is the intention. It’s a complaint. It’s a nearly seven-minute grouse, obscure in granularity, repeated on loop, about how things ain’t what they used to be.

We’re prone to this. Given time, even the biggest Johnsons, in their thrill for London’s immensity, will have made a list: the venues that failed us by failing; the transport pinch-points that were introduced for our inconvenience; the planning permissions granted and late licences denied, or vice versa.

Complaining about London is a national pastime. Andy Burnham’s elevation to prime minister has lent it purpose, forcing overdue conversations about devolved power and rebalanced spending, but the undercurrent of cultural stereotyping has been inescapable.

Burnham plays up to it, such as by claiming in a recent interview that his favourite London pubs are a tourist pit stop, a closed Wetherspoons and his former workplace local. We southerners took the bait, sneering at how these nondescript choices had sold London short. Northerners were quick to highlight our pretentiousness, self-regard and ignorance of value. No argument there.

But for all the talk of a north-south divide, there’s not much divergence of opinion here between Londoners and the self-identifying provincials. It’s just that their criticisms are too generalised. We hate at a PhD level.

An overpriced pint of beer in Covent Garden or a taxi to Stansted airport can become a visitor’s reference point for what’s wrong with the capital. Locals will grade by unpleasantness the streets around three dozen Tube stations, each calibrated against some half-invented past. Like supporting a football team into middle age, ours is an allegiance once guided by excitement, then replaced over time by extremely specific enmities.

We complain about crowds like they’re an invading force. We complain about the influencers whose hunger for promotable content has overwhelmed its availability. We complain about all the circumstances that conspire to make seat availability a luxury experience.

Our cynicism grows, so the city contracts. Each year we write off more territory as not worth the bother — Oxford Street and Leicester Square, then Camden Town and Clapham, Borough Market and Shoreditch. We’ll cite without irony the Yogi-ism about how no one goes there; it’s too crowded. We complain about how two-thirds of the city is at least an hour away yet in most respects looks exactly the same.

Harsh truths from the north won’t burst a Londoner’s bubble. You can’t out-hate a hater.

Or maybe none of that’s true. Maybe it’s just me. A capital city’s many frictions won’t be summarised by just one gripe list. Tiredness is the only universal. London is tiring, so we complain about being tired, and about being tired of being tired.

Johnson was on the right track. His London was a gathering point, not a museum. James Boswell’s biography of the archetypal Londoner gives hardly a word of description to where they went and what they saw. What they valued was the concentration of intellectual equals and admirers, as well as the choice of company that kept them safe from ever “falling in love indiscreetly”. Clubs, town houses and taverns held no interest in and of themselves. They were places where life happened. When life moved on, they moved on.

What brought them here is what keeps me here. London has the world’s highest concentration of Londoners. They’re the only reliably empathetic audience who won’t feel it necessary to tilt any complaint towards house prices and public spending-per-capita ratios. Having tired of London, their company is the only good reason to stay.

Nostalgia clouds this view. As we grow old, our tendency is to blame the city’s renewal for our growing apart from the life it holds. Defending cultural heritage against the developers is a good and noble cause. But by eulogising places, we choose to forget that all there ever is is people.

Bryce Elder is the FT’s City Editor, Alphaville
