rows.title: Private capital checks into Europe’s booming hostel market
rows.content:
Stephanie Stacey in London

Published October 3 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

The global giants of private capital are coming for Europe’s backpackers.

Over the past 18 months, investment firms including Brookfield and Apollo have made significant investments in the European hostel industry, which is growing faster than mainstream hotels.

The plan is to finance the expansion of standardised modern hostels and further professionalise an industry that has provided a cheap and cheerful refuge to travellers on a budget for more than a century.

Hostels are “the last space of the lodging sector that hasn’t really been touched [by institutional investors],” according to Andrew Heath, a vice-president at real estate adviser JLL. “People are looking and thinking: Can [hostels] be institutionalised? Can they be standardised and premiumised?”

Brookfield, which manages about $1tn in assets, acquired London-based Generator Hostels’ European business for €776mn last year.

That followed real estate private equity firm L&G Proprium’s purchase of another European chain, A&O Hostels, in 2023. A&O secured €874mn of financing from Apollo in April. Both A&O and Generator plan to double the size of their estates.

Some fear that the growth of private equity-backed “chain hostels” will undermine the charm of the historically shabby lodgings.

“What you compromise is that local, authentic atmosphere that so many travellers love,” said Evan Tzeng, founder of travel platform StayAltered, which works with independent accommodation providers.

In the 12 months to August, the number of large hostels in Europe — defined as those with capacity for more than 100 guests — grew 13 per cent to 83. While the total number remains small, the growth is outpacing that of hotels and other types of accommodation, according to figures from analytics company CoStar collated by JLL.

Lauren Okada Young, a managing director at Toronto-based Brookfield, one of the world’s largest property investors, said institutional investors were now “circling the [hostel] market and seeing that the economic model is quite profitable and attractive”.

Brookfield, she added, was drawn to the hostel sector because there was far greater scope for expansion than in the hotel market.

Generator’s “poshtels” aim to keep costs low while adding the modern design and amenities, including rooftop terraces and full-service cafés, more commonly associated with a boutique hotel.

“The sector is very fragmented so the ability to scale a platform here is interesting,” said Philipp Westermann, co-managing partner of L&G Proprium, which backed a management-led acquisition of A&O alongside StepStone Group in 2023.

Staffing costs — an increasingly significant burden for hospitality businesses — can be lower at hostels because they do not typically offer room service, while budget pricing makes them more resilient to economic turmoil, added Westermann.

Brookfield’s Generator plans to double its European estate to 30 hostels by 2030. Chief executive Xavier Mufraggi, a former boss of Club Med, said he was looking for properties that could fit a minimum of 500 beds because the model — which relies on maintaining high levels of occupancy — was only successful at “a critical size”.

Mufraggi added that Gen Z was a major growth market because they “want to travel more but they have less income than their predecessors”.

A&O, which has more than 40 hostels across Europe, is aiming to double its portfolio in the next five years. The company is opening what it said would be Europe’s largest hostel in mid-2027 after spending €40mn to convert a former office building into a 2,500-bed hostel in the heart of Berlin.

Redundant office buildings have in recent years been a source of growth for the hostel sector in Europe.

Converting large offices into hotels can be challenging because of the need to carve up a large space into individual rooms with their own plumbing and access to natural light. But hostels, with their variable dormitory sizes and less demanding clientele, are better suited to playing this “game of Tetris,” said A&O chief executive Oliver Winter.

Mufraggi said the biggest real estate opportunity for the sector was now in struggling mid-tier hotels, which can typically generate a better return for a hostel operator.

Mass market travel companies are also pushing into hostels. UK tour operator Jet2 launched its first hostel-based holiday packages in 2025 as part of an effort to reach younger and more price-sensitive customers.

rows.title: India throws month-long birthday bash for Narendra Modi
rows.content:
Michael Stott and Jyotsna Singh in Vadnagar and Andres Schipani in New Delhi

Published October 3 2026

Bearing water from the river Ganges, 500 motorcyclists are crossing India this month and heading to Vadnagar — where Prime Minister Narendra Modi was born 76 years ago.

Another 500 are riding in the opposite direction to Varanasi, the Hindu holy city which is Modi’s constituency, planting trees and cleaning streets in honour of his quarter of a century in public office, which will be celebrated October 7. He has led India for 12 years, after 13 years as chief minister in his home state of Gujarat.

Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party is using the twin celebrations for its revered leader to try to revive its fortunes after a summer of youth protests. Candle-lighting and prayer sessions across the country marked Modi’s birthday on September 17.

“Prime Minister Modi and his dedication to public service for 25 years are the inspiration for young people like me all over India,” said Deepesh Yadav, 32, a member of the BJP youth wing from Gujarat, as he passed through New Delhi after joining the motorbike rally.

“What he did in the past 12 years is automatically inspiring . . . now we must do something for Mr Modi.”

But the BJP cadres’ enthusiasm for their leader has less of an echo on the streets, where many of India’s 370mn youths are expressing anger over a broadening range of issues, including a lack of well-paid jobs and long-running sexual violence.

“Young people are not interested in the activities of mainstream politics, whether it’s birthday celebrations or whatever journeys the BJP organises,” said Eeshna Gupta, a 25-year-old opposition student leader in Delhi. “They are instead focused on their issues: we need jobs, social security, good education, and safety for women.”

Modi and his party’s youth-centric campaigns were “creating even more distance”, she added.

Now serving a third consecutive term as prime minister, Modi dominates India ’s political landscape like no other leader this century. As well as the national government, the BJP and its allies run 22 of India’s 31 states and territories with elected governments.

But mass protests over the summer by the upstart Cockroach Janta Party have cast a shadow over the celebrations in his name.

The CJP, which began as an online satirical movement but quickly morphed into a nationwide force, forced the exit in July of Modi’s education minister and close ally, Dharmendra Pradhan, over problems in the national exam system.

It launched more protests on Friday in Mumbai, where thousands gathered over allegations that the nominally independent election commission has improperly excluded tens of millions of voters from electoral rolls.

“Obviously, the government is under pressure,” said Pratap Bhanu Mehta, an Indian political scientist and former vice-chancellor of Ashoka University. “A lot of the accumulated problems of Indian society and the Indian economy are beginning to express themselves through protests.”

Modi biographer Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay said that while there was no denying the prime minister’s political achievements over a quarter of a century, the CJP protests had punctured his aura of invulnerability and “for the first time he was mocked at a mass level”.

“In the last two-months-plus, Mr Modi has not been able to reinvent himself,” Mukhopadhyay said.

Faced with this challenge to its leader and biggest electoral asset, the BJP is rallying its extensive grassroots operation to paint the premier as a dedicated and effective leader deserving of many more years in power.

Ram Madhav, a BJP national vice-president and former national secretary, emphasised the party’s commitment to seva , selfless devotion to others, and hailed Modi as an exemplar. “He is a very motivated type of leader,” Madhav told the FT. “He is not just doing his political duty. He thinks it’s a spiritual commitment to the welfare of the people.”

The mainly pro-government press has published birthday cover wraps with advertisements extolling Modi’s virtues. The celebrations even extended abroad, with the world’s tallest building, Dubai’s Burj Khalifa, illuminated in the colours of the Indian flag and a “Happy Birthday” message projected on to it above a photograph of Modi.

Madhav dismissed criticism that the party was too focused on its leader. “It’s not as if we’re creating a personality cult,” he said. “We are presenting [Modi] as an example of how a seva-minded politician should act.”

Modi’s birthplace in rural Gujarat has been a focus of the celebrations.

Passengers arriving at Vadnagar railway station snap selfies in front of the modest teal-coloured metal hut on the main platform, from which Modi says he helped his father serve tea as a boy chai-wallah . Outside, a giant kettle in a flower bed reinforces the message of his humble origins.

Still even in Vadnagar, where roads have been improved, a giant new archaeology museum built and public buildings associated with Modi’s life renovated, some residents are sceptical about the achievements of the town’s most famous son.

“There are better roads since Modi became PM and the town is a lot cleaner. Yes, the town has changed a lot but our lives haven’t,” said dairy farmer Vishnu Popat. “We are happy for Mr Modi and the celebrations but there are no jobs or business here. What about our children? How will they survive?”

Modi remains a formidable political operator, physically fit on a strict vegetarian diet with daily yoga exercises and no alcohol. After the youth protests, the prime minister summoned the 65-strong BJP national leadership for a meeting lasting more than four hours where he asked each to speak in turn and listened intently, participants said. Ministers have been ordered to hone their Instagram skills to project better to a youth audience.

Bhanu Mehta noted that with three years until India’s next general election, Modi and the BJP had “a lot of headroom to recover in the face of widespread social discontent and protest”.

But he said that despite Modi’s energy, the prime minister faced a fundamental contradiction in his efforts to address youth protests.

“He’s by instinct a centraliser. The power is centred in his persona. And these are governance challenges that you cannot solve by extreme centralisation,” he said.

rows.title: Chill out: Japan’s top vending machine maker now cools data centres
rows.content:
Harry Dempsey in Tokyo

Published October 3 2026

Japan’s biggest vending machine maker has reworked its refrigeration technology to offer power-hungry AI data centres an energy-efficient way to cool their servers.

Fuji Electric, which makes 80 per cent of Japan’s vending machines, has created a cooling system for data centres that it claims can cut energy consumption by 85 per cent, using a technology originally designed to chill sodas, teas and coffees.

The push is the latest by a Japanese industrial group to reinvent itself as a key supplier of components used in AI infrastructure, joining the likes of Panasonic, Mitsubishi Electric and Sumitomo Electric.

Cooling servers accounts for 30 to 40 per cent of data centres’ energy consumption, presenting a big opportunity for Japanese companies specialising in air conditioning and refrigeration.

Fuji Electric’s technology was born out of efforts to make vending machines more energy efficient after they became a symbol of waste following the Fukushima nuclear meltdown in 2011.

Shintaro Ishihara, Tokyo’s governor at the time, had gone as far as demanding a complete shutdown of vending machines to save energy as Japan faced a power crunch in the disaster’s aftermath.

That call prompted Fuji Electric and Toyota supplier Denso to develop a new cooling system. In 2015, a team of researchers created an ejector using a CO₂ refrigerant that did away with the need for a compressor and saved energy by 20 per cent, according to the company.

“Simply extending conventional technology wouldn’t have been enough,” said Hideto Shirai, who is leading efforts at Fuji Electric to sell the technology to data centres.

Most cooling systems deploy a compressor, which uses a large amount of electricity to turn a refrigerant into a hot, high-pressure gas. Fuji Electric’s ejector uses waste heat to drive refrigerant through a precisely shaped nozzle and raise its pressure through the movement of fluid.

However, the technology was never adopted inside vending machines because it was too costly to install when the machines only cost a few thousand dollars.

“We knew the technology was effective,” said Shirai. “But it was difficult to make it blossom inside vending machines. So the idea began: what if we applied it to a different industrial field?”

The Tokyo-based electrical equipment supplier is aiming to sell more than ¥10bn ($61mn) worth of ejector systems to data centres by 2030. It already sells ¥100bn a year in data centre-related components such as switchgears.

The company’s role as an AI “picks and shovels” supplier, as well as improving margins in its energy components business, has helped Fuji Electric’s shares rise almost 47 per cent in the past year. The company is valued at $13.9bn.

Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro, a research group specialising in data centre infrastructure, called the technology “promising” but said it was still “genuinely emerging”.

The data centre cooling market is shifting from traditional systems that use water and glycol or hydrofluoroolefin refrigerants towards direct liquid cooling, which circulates a liquid coolant directly to heat-generating components such as CPUs and GPUs.

Fuji Electric’s system could be used in direct liquid-based cooling systems. The ejector technology performs better in regions with high temperatures, creating a potential opening in parts of Japan, where summer heat can often exceed 35 degrees, and south-east Asia.

But Cordovil said a rival technology that uses waste heat — absorption chillers made by Japan’s Kawasaki, Ebara and Yazaki — had an edge over Fuji’s system for data centre adoption.

Ryo Harada, analyst at Goldman Sachs, expressed doubts about whether Fuji Electric would be able to access the large US data centre market.

“The technology may be compelling, but commercialisation is equally important,” he said. “Hyperscalers have largely locked in their next-generation data centre architectures for the next two to three years, so it is likely to take at least that long for new entrants to gain meaningful traction.”

rows.title: Two Iranian small-boat migrants charged with plotting attack on Jewish targets in Manchester
rows.content:
Robert Wright in London

Published October 2 2026

Updated October 2 2026

Counterterror police on Friday charged two Iranian men who arrived in the UK by small boat with terrorism offences over an alleged plot to attack Manchester’s Jewish community, in a plot that officers said might have been directed from Iran.

Salam Ahmadyan, 36, of Liverpool, and Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, were charged on the first anniversary of the attack on Manchester’s Heaton Park synagogue , which took place during Yom Kippur and left two worshippers and the attacker dead.

It also comes two days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran had a hand in Sunday’s alleged plot to target RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire. Tehran has categorically denied any involvement in the incident.

UK authorities have previously alleged that Iran had a role in multiple attacks on Jewish, Israeli and Iranian dissident targets in Britain.

The men were arrested in Manchester on September 20, hours before the start of this year’s Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. The men arrived by small boats in 2020 and 2023, according to the Home Office. Without saying which was which, the department said one had been granted asylum while the other had a live asylum claim.

Counter Terrorism Policing said on Friday: “They were both charged on Friday October 2 with engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts. It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot.”

The two men will appear in court on Saturday at Westminster Magistrates’ Court.

The charges allege that the men acquired instructions and equipment to assemble improvised explosive devices and conducted reconnaissance of potential targets.

Vicki Evans, senior national co-ordinator for CTP, said: “This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.”

She added: “I’m aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy Day period has caused a great deal of concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public.”

Referring to the RAF Fairford incident, when five people were intercepted by local police, Evans said the past week had brought “into sharp focus” some of the potential threats from Iran.

She added: “While this incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, is using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”

The men’s arrivals on small boat crossings are likely to further increase pressure on the government to be seen to be acting decisively to stop clandestine arrivals and to enhance security screening of people seeking asylum.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said on Friday evening that the latest developments would be “deeply distressing” to Jewish communities.

She added: “I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue. The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.”

Nigel Farage, leader of the anti-immigration Reform UK party who has long campaigned on the risk of terrorists arriving on small boats, accused the government of inviting “terror and horror into our communities”.

“We now have a state of national emergency on our borders, and this government is trying to open them to even more unknown individuals,” he added, referring to plans to reopen a resettlement scheme .

He suggested Mahmood “must resign” if she “disagrees”.

Additional reporting by David Sheppard

rows.title: US justice department will not reopen criminal probe of Fed’s Jay Powell
rows.content:
Ella Lee and Claire Jones in Washington

Published October 2 2026

The US Department of Justice will not reopen its criminal probe of Jay Powell over the Federal Reserve’s $2.5bn renovation project, after an investigation by the central bank’s watchdog cleared the former chair of criminal wrongdoing.

The long-awaited report from the Fed’s independent inspector general found “deficiencies in the management” of the project but stopped short of identifying “administrative misconduct”.

“Making mistakes and not having any sort of oversight over the folks doing billion-dollar projects isn’t necessarily a crime,” US attorney-general Todd Blanche said in an interview with Bloomberg Television on Friday.

The watchdog said in the report that at no time during its evaluation “did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred” that required a referral to the attorney-general.

Following the release of the report on Wednesday, Donald Trump revived his attacks on Powell, who has remained on the Fed’s Board of Governors after his term as chair ended in May. The president pointed to the blowout cost of the renovation as proof of Powell’s incompetence and suggested he should “be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY”.

Blanche told Bloomberg that he was satisfied with the report but did not think Powell had appropriately overseen the renovation project, which has run over budget by several hundred million dollars. Blanche also did not rule out future action if evidence of wrongdoing was uncovered.

The DoJ earlier this year dropped its criminal probe into Powell’s handling of the renovation after a group of Republican lawmakers refused to support Trump’s nomination of current chair Kevin Warsh until it was resolved.

However, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, raised the prospect of reopening it should the inspector general find evidence of wrongdoing.

Powell had vowed to remain at the US central bank as a governor until the DoJ investigation was “ well and truly over , with transparency and finality”.

The former chair, who was repeatedly criticised by Trump over his refusal to slash interest rates as the president desired, has the right to remain on the Fed’s board until early 2028.

The Fed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

rows.title: US backs down from fuel export ban threat as G7 agrees to release 100mn barrels
rows.content:
Ian Johnston and Henry Foy in Brussels, Malcolm Moore in London and Myles McCormick in Washington

Published October 2 2026

Updated October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

The US has backed down on a threat to stop exporting fuel to the world as part of a deal in which European countries agreed to release more diesel from their strategic reserves on Friday.

The decision comes as US President Donald Trump attempts to douse a surge in diesel prices for American industry and farmers ahead of November’s midterm elections , which will determine control of Congress.

G7 leaders said after a meeting on Friday that they would release 100mn barrels of crude and diesel, co-ordinated by the International Energy Agency, “in light of ongoing market pressures”.

In a joint statement, they did not give full details of the plan but said the release would be carried out over a four-month period, beginning “immediately”, and including a “substantial” release of diesel reserves within the first 20 days.

The intervention will take into account “commitments that have already been fulfilled” under a pre-existing 400mn-barrel pledge made in March, of which 325mn barrels have already been released, according to the IEA.

Three people familiar with the details of the release said 40mn barrels would come from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, while Europe would contribute about 50mn barrels of diesel, with the remainder coming from Asia.

The agreement comes after Trump had faced intense pressure from Republican legislators representing America’s agricultural heartlands to impose an export ban to ease the strain on farmers ahead of next month’s elections.

European negotiators — and the US oil industry — had raced to avert a suspension, which would have sent global fuel prices soaring.

“We’re not going to be doing the export ban,” Trump told reporters on Friday, describing Europe’s commitment to release diesel stocks as “a great thing”.

“Europe has a lot of diesel and they’re going to be making a major world contribution and so are we,” he said. “We’re going to have a lot of oil.”

Two diplomats familiar with the discussions said the White House had asked Europe to unlock at least 100mn barrels and threatened to go ahead with the ban on US diesel exports if European countries failed to meet Washington’s demand.

The joint statement included a commitment from the signatories — including the US — “to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions”.

Asked if Washington had ruled out a diesel export ban as part of the G7 release, the White House pointed to the pledge in the joint statement.

French President Emmanuel Macron said G7 members had agreed “not to take any measure to restrict the exchange of oil and energy products between partner countries”.

European diesel futures extended declines after the announcement, with the benchmark down 8 per cent to $1,337.75 a tonne, the lowest level since the start of September. Wholesale diesel for sale in New York harbour fell almost 2 per cent to $4.56 a gallon.

The G7 leaders said they would “convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary”.

The release is a big win for the US oil industry, which had lobbied hard against an export ban and encouraged the administration to lean on allies to dump stocks as an alternative.

“We welcome the administration’s efforts to secure a co-ordinated G7 release of 100mn barrels of crude and refined products, along with a commitment not to impose export restrictions between parties,” said Bethany Williams, spokesperson for the American Petroleum Institute, an industry lobby group.

Macron said on Friday that the release would “send a clear signal to markets”.

France had earlier proposed a plan in which Europe would release 50mn barrels of diesel and for IEA countries to unlock a further 50mn barrels of crude, according to several diplomats familiar with the matter.

In March, Europe committed to release 73mn barrels of refined fuels as part of a 400mn-barrel strategic stock draw co-ordinated by the IEA in response to the conflict in the Middle East.

The US has largely completed its share of that programme, but some European countries have not yet met their obligations, according to Fatih Birol, head of the IEA.

Diesel prices have been trading above $200 a barrel in the US, Europe and Asia for several weeks because of several shocks to the world’s refineries, including from the Iran war, Russia’s conflict with Ukraine and China’s decision to limit fuel exports.

Additional reporting by Sarah White in Paris and James Politi in Washington

rows.title: Italy and Greece seek leeway on EU fiscal rules
rows.content:
Paola Tamma in Brussels, Amy Kazmin in Rome and Eleni Varvitsioti in Athens

Published October 2 2026

Updated October 2 2026

Italy and Greece have asked Brussels for more fiscal wriggle room as surging fuel prices and rising inflation add to budgetary pressure on the bloc’s two most indebted countries ahead of elections next year.

Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis each wrote to the European Commission this week to plead for further room to manoeuvre under the EU’s fiscal rules, which are meant to limit a country’s annual deficit to 3 per cent of GDP.

Rising diesel and petrol prices, triggered by the war in Iran, have increased the cost of many national fuel price support measures, adding to mounting pressure on public finances around the world.

The EU’s fiscal rules were already adjusted in June to temporarily allow countries to spend up to 0.6 per cent of GDP until 2028 on energy investments that reduce dependency on imported fossil fuels.

This is part of a broader exemption allowing countries to spend up to 1.5 per cent of GDP on defence and energy, which both Italy and Greece are using, without the spending resulting in punitive measures.

The new requests made this week go further. Athens has asked for permission to exclude “temporary measures” from its net spending indicator, which analysts say are a reference to fuel subsidies.

Rome has requested that inflation be taken into account when assessing whether its budget complies with EU spending ceilings.

EU officials privately caution that markets may react negatively to granting additional flexibility under the fiscal rules.

Meloni sent a letter to Commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday requesting that the matter be discussed at a meeting of EU finance ministers next week.

In her letter, seen by the FT, she argued Italy should be permitted to use the additional tax revenues it collects as a result of inflation to limit the impact of higher prices for households and businesses without this breaching the fiscal rules.

Part of this extra revenue should be used “to dampen the increase in energy costs in a temporary and targeted manner”, she wrote.

The letter also appealed to Brussels to treat inflation as a mitigating factor if Italy’s 2027 budget projections exceeded the annual EU expenditure thresholds.

Unveiling Italy’s new financial planning document on Friday night, finance minister Giancarlo Giorgetti projected this year’s fiscal deficit would fall below 3 per cent of GDP, while growth would hit 1 per cent, up from 0.6 per cent forecast in April.

However, Giorgetti said Italy’s deficit would rise to 3.4 per cent of GDP in 2027, as Italy activates the so-called national escape clause and requests 0.6 per cent of GDP in additional leeway from the EU for additional spending on energy and defence for next year and 2028 — a total of €29bn in extra resources over the two years — provided parliament agrees.

The deficit would drop to 3.2 per cent in 2028 — still utilising the EU’s extra flexibility — then drop to 2.3 per cent in 2029.

Growth will remain below 1 per cent a year from 2027 to 2029, ranging between 0.8 and 0.9 per cent. Italy’s public debt is projected to peak at 138.5 per cent of GDP next year — when it will replace Greece as the EU’s most heavily indebted economy — before gradually declining.

Giorgetti confirmed that Italy had decided not to spend quite as much on defence over the next two years as it had originally been considering, given an economic context he described as “particularly complex”.

Since taking power in 2022, Meloni’s coalition has won accolades from debt investors and credit rating agencies for its fiscal prudence and restraint, cutting Italy’s fiscal deficit from 8 per cent in 2022 to 3.1 per cent in 2025.

However, Rome has spent an estimated €2.8bn this year on fuel excise tax cuts. Last week Italy’s state-controlled energy group Eni said it would put a temporary price cap on pump prices for at least one month to support the government’s efforts.

Mitsotakis has also pleaded with Brussels for greater flexibility, calling for more “breathing room” in a letter to von der Leyen on Wednesday, also seen by the FT.

He proposed allowing member states to use the additional tax revenues generated by higher prices to fund temporary support measures that would shield households and businesses from rising energy costs.

He also criticised the Commission’s recommendations to reduce energy demand as being “not politically acceptable”.

The intervention comes as the cost of living has emerged as a key concern for Mitsotakis’s government, which faces national elections in spring.

The Commission declined to comment.

rows.title: US economy adds just 29,000 jobs in September as hiring slows sharply
rows.content:
Myles McCormick in Washington and Kate Duguid in New York

Published October 2 2026

Updated October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

The US economy added just 29,000 jobs in September as hiring slowed sharply from the previous month, raising doubts over the resilience of the labour market and the outlook for interest rate rises.

Friday’s figure from the Bureau of Labor Statistics marked an abrupt reversal from the downwardly revised 133,000 jobs added in August and was well short of the 88,000 job gains anticipated in a Bloomberg poll of economists.

Hiring decelerated across multiple sectors, with healthcare, a big driver of job gains in previous months, slowing sharply. Employment in the financial sector continued to contract.

Payrolls for July and August were revised lower by a combined 60,000 positions. The July figure fell to a loss of 10,000 jobs. The unemployment rate climbed to 4.2 per cent in September from 4.1 per cent in August.

“Today’s soft payroll report demonstrates that the labour market is simmering, not boiling,” said Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist at Franklin Templeton.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The data came as the Federal Reserve weighs whether to raise interest rates further to tackle inflation after officials voted last month to increase borrowing costs for the first time in three years.

Treasury yields initially dropped following the report as traders lowered their expectations of additional rate increases.

Adam Schickling, senior economist at Vanguard, said the report “strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to remain patient”, adding that “the labour market has not deteriorated sharply, but there is also little evidence that it has meaningfully strengthened”.

The two-year Treasury yield, which moves with interest rate expectations, fell as much as 0.09 percentage points to 4.69 per cent immediately following the release of the data. It later recouped that move and sat 0.05 percentage points higher on the day at 4.84 per cent.

Market bets on an October rate rise fell from 29 per cent before the data was released to about 23 per cent. They had fallen sharply this week after senior central bank officials signalled that policymakers would probably need more time to consider the data before taking further action. As the Treasury sell-off resumed on Friday, traders attached a roughly 85 per cent chance to the prospect of interest rates being higher by the end of the year.

“For the Fed, this number should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike,” said Thomas Simons, chief US economist at Jefferies.

US stocks were higher on Friday, with the S&P 500 gaining 0.7 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 climbing 1 per cent to a record closing high.

Fed chair Kevin Warsh had pointed to the labour market being in “good shape” as a factor behind the central bank’s decision to raise borrowing costs by 25 basis points in the face of inflation he said had been “too high . . . for too long”.

Traders said that while Friday’s report should cause the central bank to re-evaluate that position, they still expected the Fed to raise borrowing costs further in the coming months.

“Overall the data pour a little bit of cold water on the narrative that rates should be running dramatically higher,” said Gennadiy Goldberg, head of US interest rates at TD Securities.

rows.title: Arctic sea routes boom as Gulf war and global warming divert shipping
rows.content:
Alice Hancock in London

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Shipping through the Arctic has reached record levels as melting sea ice and pressure on global chokepoints push shipowners to find alternative routes.

Voyages via the Northern Sea Route hit 133 last month, more than quadruple what they were in 2022, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence, and up 46 per cent compared with August.

Almost half of the transits were made by Russian-flagged ships. Voyages have also been made by Chinese ships seeking another way to European markets given the disruption in the Middle East and in the Red Sea. “It’s worth watching how the use of this route develops as government and operators increasingly look for alternative shipping lanes with less exposure to geopolitical disruption,” said Bridget Diakun, maritime intelligence and research director at Lloyd’s List.

The Chinese container ship Dubai Tower travelled from Qingdao to the UK port of Felixstowe via the Arctic in September, trimming its voyage time to 24 days as opposed to the 40 or more days it would take to sail via the Suez Canal or Cape of Good Hope.

Another ship belonging to the same company set out from Ningbo to Felixstowe using the same route on September 27.

September is typically the busiest month for Arctic sea routes as the ice is at its lowest ebb, allowing ships without icebreaker capabilities to transit.

The northern sea ice suffered its largest single-year winter decline in 2025 since satellite records began and has remained at historic lows since, according to University of Southampton researchers.

The lower sea ice and increased pressure on chokepoints such as the Bab al-Mandeb Strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, which is currently threatened by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, are making the Northern Sea Route more appealing to shipowners. The strait has become a vital route for Saudi Arabian oil exports since Iran throttled shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in response to US strikes on the Islamic republic.

Meanwhile the Panama Canal has suffered drought conditions this year.

Liquefied natural gas carriers often use the route to reach Russia’s Yamal and Arctic LNG 2 gas plants, but there was also an uptick in bulk cargo vessels that typically carry commodities like grains or iron ore.

The number of bulk carriers transiting the route was 29 in September, compared to 18 in August and a previous high of 12 in September last year.

A record number of crude oil tankers were also deployed on the route, Lloyd's List data showed.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The Northern Sea Route is broken up into 28 sections with different guidelines set by the Rosatom-controlled Northern Sea Route administration depending on the ice conditions. The Russian state-controlled company issues permits to sail through the area.

Insurance companies and environmentalists have warned that increasing use of the waterway could result in a major accident, with few search and rescue or clean-up capabilities in the region.

A major oil spill from the supertanker Exxon Valdez off the Alaskan coast in 1989 took at least four years to clean up, but residue from the accident is still lingering on nearby beaches. Romain Troublé, executive director of the Tara Ocean Foundation, said there was also a risk that even minor oil spills would accelerate global warming effects as black drops on the ice would absorb sunlight and increase melting.

“The people who will use this route are not only Russia and China . . . any companies that can go through this route in the future will have an impact on the Arctic,” he said. “If you and I are buying goods that are using this path, we are contributing to the dangers of it.”

There are also significant dangers for mariners given the unpredictable weather and harsh conditions.

Tom Mellor, head of technical partnering at the UK Hydrographic Office, the main provider of geospatial data to ships, said that navigational equipment could fail to work at far-northerly latitudes.

“Above or below that the world becomes much more curved and the display of that data requires a different methodology to make sure it is positioned correctly on that chart.”

“I wouldn’t want to go on board if you didn't have a proper system that was showing the chart correctly,” he said.

rows.title: Low-profile hedge fund smashes record for New York office rent
rows.content:
Zehra Munir and Amelia Pollard in New York

Published October 2 2026

A skyscraper in midtown New York has smashed rent records by leasing its top two floors to a low-profile hedge fund for up to $21.2mn a year.

Castle Hook Partners will move into the penthouse of 625 Madison Avenue, an office tower owned by real estate developer Related Companies, in the second half of 2029.

The fund’s willingness to pay between $350 and $400 per square foot in yearly rent for 53,000 square feet of space, according to people familiar with the matter, signals the boom at the high end of Manhattan’s office market is accelerating.

The previous reported record for office rent was set earlier this year when a private international family office signed a 10-year lease averaging $327.50 per square foot in a Midtown tower owned by the Soloviev Group.

While Related had originally planned to build a luxury residential high-rise on the site, purchased from SL Green in early 2024, it decided instead to tap into the “real premium” that exists for “new, properly amenitised, high-end office with incredible views”, Related chief executive Jeff Blau said in an interview.

A war for talent in the financial services and technology sectors, combined with a drive to attract workers back to the office, has resulted in a golden era for the city’s luxury offices .

The 53-storey high-rise overlooking Central Park has been designed by British architect Lord Norman Foster and will feature private dining facilities and wraparound terraces on its penthouse and “amenity floor”, said Blau.

Castle Hook, founded by Soros Fund Management alumnus David Rogers in 2016, is currently headquartered in the General Motors Building on Fifth Avenue. The firm counted legendary hedge fund manager Stanley Druckenmiller among its early investors and has kept a low profile on Wall Street. It manages about $11bn with 35 employees, according to its most recent regulatory filing.

The firm is among so-called global macro hedge funds — which trade macroeconomic trends in currencies, commodities, bonds and stocks — that have benefited from a volatile few years in markets. Macro funds were up 6.8 per cent for the year through the end of August, according to research firm PivotalPath.

Castle Hook has posted high returns in recent years. The firm reportedly gained about 50 per cent last year and made more than 60 per cent the year prior.

A spokesperson for Castle Hook did not respond to a request for comment.

The battle for talent among hedge funds has become fierce, with lavish offices and amenities emerging as ways to compete for top portfolio managers beyond huge cheques. Hedge funds and other financial firms were among the first companies to require employees to return to their desks after the pandemic.

Prominent hedge fund managers such as Bill Ackman and Dan Loeb have been among the loudest voices decrying New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s populist policies and their potential impact on the city’s real estate market. After Mamdani won the Democratic primary, some Wall Street executives privately warned his ascent would drive financial firms out of the city.

“People might have their views on where New York politics are, but I think people believe in the future of New York City,” said Related’s Blau.

Related’s building on Madison Avenue would be 67 per cent leased by the end of the year, mostly to financial services companies, said Stephen Winter, the company’s executive vice-president. Private equity firm General Atlantic will take five floors as the anchor tenant.

JPMorgan Chase’s headquarters, unveiled in 2025, features a state of the art health and wellness centre and 19 dining options, and has set the tone for new office amenities around the city.

The value of Castle Hook’s lease has not been previously reported. The 15-year tenancy agreement was reported earlier by the New York Business Journal.

rows.title: Treasuries are losing their moneyness
rows.content:
Brendan Greeley

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

The writer is the author of The Almighty Dollar: 500 Years of the World’s Most Powerful Money

In 1981 the economists Tom Sargent and Neil Wallace wrote a brief article for the Minneapolis Fed’s Quarterly Review, “Some Unpleasant Monetarist Arithmetic”. Unpleasant, that is, for monetarists. The ideas in the article have become the basis for considering one of the most important trade-offs in political economy: monetary dominance against fiscal dominance.

Under monetary dominance, the government is constrained as it spends money. It can’t sell more debt than the public demands. When the public stops demanding, interest on government bonds rises, and the government stops borrowing. This leaves the central bank a free hand to manage inflation by buying and selling government debt.

Under fiscal dominance, the government simply borrows what it wants, spends what it wants, and leaves the central bank with an unpleasant choice. It can buy bonds, bringing the government’s cost of interest down but risking inflation, as the Federal Reserve did during the second world war. Or the central bank can let the politicians fight it out with the market, risking collapse in the value of the bank’s own portfolio and . . . inflation.

It’s a useful model. But as Sargent and Wallace already hinted in their 1981 article, there’s a wormhole the government can slip through. If the demand for sovereign debt can’t be sated, then the government isn’t constrained. It can borrow and spend and borrow and spend. Its cost of debt remains low, and the central bank holds on to its own discretion to manage inflation.

Since about the time that article came out, the US has been slipping through exactly that wormhole. Washington was both fiscally dominant and not constrained by the cost of debt, a condition so solid and stable it seemed like the result of a physical law, and indeed as it continued it encouraged a new discussion. Were Treasuries debt or money? Did the Treasury sell its bonds, like a security? Or did it simply issue them, like currency?

Certainly Treasuries had what economists call moneyness. They were liquid like money. They were risk-free like money, a stylised fact that became an empirical truth. They were even referred to as money. Traders called them “cash,” historically a maddeningly flexible word that can accommodate anything in any century people think of as money. Commercial banks and the Fed haggled over whether Treasuries had the same secure status as America’s base money, the Fed’s own reserves.

It was difficult to find the limits of global demand for dollar-denominated assets with moneyness, which gave economists and politicians the luxury of treating Treasuries like they were both securities and money, a special phenomenon with its own properties.

The distinctions used to be clearer. In the 18th century, assemblies in the American colonies borrowed directly from their own colonists, paying their debts by issuing small-denomination, liquid bills — currency. Under the Constitution, however, this practice was forbidden. Alexander Hamilton followed by building a liquid market for federal debt, just like the one in the United Kingdom. The early American republic would sell its debt to investors for banknotes and silver, and not issue it to citizens as currency. The Hamiltonian system was built on the assumption that Washington’s debt is a bond, not money.

The idea of government debt as cash money lingered. During the Civil War, Confederate States began issuing their own currencies again, and the Union government began paying for things with greenbacks, paper slips tied to a vague promise that they would be bought back eventually with gold. Periodically during financial crises until the Great Depression, cities would pay for things with their own “hard-times money”, currencies that worked a lot like the old colonial bills.

Each time, however, the old Hamiltonian system reasserted itself: bonds were securities, sold to investors for the ready cash of banknotes and bank deposits. That appears to be happening again. As I write, yield on the US 10-year note is 5.25 per cent. It is not normal to have to add an as-I-write to the 10-year. Not normal, unless Treasuries are no longer special.

There are many explanations for the rise in yields on Treasuries. Yields are going up for government debt around the world. The US has no apparent plans to reduce deficits. A war has raised the price of gas, feeding into inflation. Debt for data centres is competing for cash. All of these are real, but they don’t completely explain the slope of the rise in Treasury yields right now.

One of the things that made Treasuries so money-like is that yields changed slowly, stabilising their value. It’s possible that after several decades, all of these problems together have suddenly eroded the money-like liquidity of US debt; the moneyness is getting squeezed out of Treasuries again.

Sargent and Wallace were always right. Under fiscal dominance, inflation is coming one way or the other, and the central bank has no good choices. America’s Treasuries are just bonds. The wormhole is closing.

rows.title: Stockpickers: AG Barr, Redcentric, Saga
rows.content:
Dan Jones , Investors’ Chronicle

Published October 2 2026

Rising costs and hard-pressed customers mean many consumer staples companies find themselves less essential than they had assumed.

In the US, staples now make up a record-low 4.6 per cent of the S&P 500, according to investment manager Bespoke Invest.

The sector’s ability to keep producing the steady, reliable growth on which its reputation was built is being called into question. Worries about the impact of weight-loss drugs on appetites have not helped.

UK businesses have rolled out turnaround strategies, with varying degrees of success. While investors had warmed to Unilever’s plan to focus on its core divisions, the proposed merger of its food business with sauces maker McCormick left some asking whether it had gone too far.

Diageo has pinned its revival hopes on a plan to cut costs and put more marketing resources behind bright spots, such as Guinness, while making a bigger push into canned cocktails. Its smaller peer AG Barr is already feeling the impact of pre-mixed drink competition, given that its cocktail brand Funkin saw sales struggle again in the first half of 2026.

But things look more positive for the group elsewhere. The Irn-Bru maker has diversified via a series of recent soft drink acquisitions and is making market share gains.

Another attraction is its valuation: a price/earnings ratio of just 11.6 times January 2027’s estimated earnings is near bargain-basement territory, according to FactSet.

The depressed valuation means the company is nowadays more akin to a smaller company than a mid-cap stock and there are recovery stories to be told in this part of the market.

Personal care business PZ Cussons and cleaning products manufacturer McBride have both seen their shares rebound, notably as their businesses stabilise. In AG Barr, investors who focus on larger companies may be missing out on another potential winner.

AG Barr has spent the past 18 months focused on diversifying its portfolio beyond the famous Irn-Bru for which it is known, writes Erin Withey . This has translated into a string of recent acquisitions, which the group is now bedding in.

Today, the Cumbernauld-headquartered company’s product lines span Rubicon juices, MOMA oat-based beverages, Boost energy drinks and, more recently, Fentimans and Frobishers premium mixers.

These purchases helped drive sales for the half-year to August 1 up by 8.5 per cent to £247mn. Adjusted pre-tax profit rose by 2.6 per cent to £36.1mn. The group ended the period with net bank debt of £47mn.

The shares trade near a 12-month low, and after a successful period of expansion into premium soft drinks, we think this could present a buying opportunity. AG Barr must now squeeze the most out of what it has bought.

In July, Redcentric’s share price dropped after it returned £90mn to its shareholders by acquiring 35 per cent of its issued capital at 160p per share, writes Arthur Sants .

The cash came from the sale of its data centre business. Most of this went back to shareholders, with the rest being used to pay down its debt.

This has left a more streamlined business. Redcentric used to own data centres as well as provide the managed service, but now it mainly just does the latter.

Management believes the company is at a turning point. It forecasts revenue growth to be flat in full-year 2027, but adjusted cash profit (ebitda) is expected to rise slightly.

Given that this is a business cutting its way to profit growth, its valuation does not reflect this. It trades on a forward price/earnings ratio of 13 times, according to FactSet analyst consensus.

Saga raised annual guidance and said it expects to deliver medium-term targets ahead of schedule, after the travel and insurance group delivered double-digit revenue growth in the first half of the year, writes Christopher Akers .

As profits and the state of the indebted balance sheet improve, the group’s goals for an annual underlying pre-tax profit of £100mn and leverage under two times are in sight before 2030.

Key earnings generator Ocean Cruise’s underlying profit climbed 38 per cent to £47.7mn.

River Cruise profit rose by 54 per cent to £6mn, helped by the launch of new ship Spirit of the Moselle, while holidays profit more than doubled to £6.6mn.

On the insurance side of the business, broking profit was up by 75 per cent to £15.9mn.

The shares trade on 13 times forward consensus earnings and have risen more than 165 per cent over the past year.

rows.title: Our healthy obsession with fitness trackers
rows.content:
The editorial board

Published October 2 2026

In 2014, Marc Benioff told the World Economic Forum in Davos that his friend, the computer magnate Michael Dell, had called him, worried that data shared from the Salesforce chief executive’s Fitbit monitor showed he had not been working out.

Benioff explained he had skipped the gym because he was suffering from a cold. But his enthusiasm for wellbeing wearables was infectious. Many more people have equipped themselves with Fitbits, Apple Watches, Whoop bands and other trackers since then.

Benioff and Dell have gone on to invest in Oura Health, maker of a fitness ring that promises in its initial public offering prospectus to “empower people to live healthier, longer”.

Oura this week delayed its flotation , which could have valued the Finnish-American company at about $16bn . The official reason was market uncertainty. But such is Oura users’ devotion to the $400 trackers that it is always possible executives and advisers synced their data that morning and decided to wait until their collective heart rates, sleep numbers and step counts heralded a more propitious outcome.

The company, and others like it, will be back. Some early leaders in the market, such as Jawbone, have dropped out or been absorbed by rivals, as Fitbit was by Google. But the runners still in the race are part of an overall market for consumer wearables forecast to generate $1tn in revenue between 2026 and 2032.

This is good news, and not just for investors. Healthy life expectancy is the metric that really matters for most people, and if we are to live longer, healthier lives then anything that nudges us to pay greater attention to our wellbeing is worth backing. Our health is our wealth, as the saying goes.

Silicon Valley’s billionaires are not the only ones banking on this connected future. In the US, Oura subscriptions and devices are already part of an insurance package for patients who share their sleep data with doctors, helping them detect, monitor and treat conditions such as obstructive sleep apnoea.

In the UK, insurer Vitality offers points to active customers who share fitness data which can help them qualify for lower premiums. Diabetes sufferers increasingly benefit from wearable glucose monitors, linked to apps. A 2022 analysis in The Lancet Digital Health of multiple studies of fitness trackers found that wearing one increased activity, to the tune of 1,800 extra steps per day.

The list of potential unwanted side-effects is long. As Benioff pointed out in 2014, the shared vital signs of listed company executives could become tradeable insider information. If insurers were to link protection too strictly to fitness goals, the unfit might be unable to buy cover at all.

The maxim “what gets measured gets managed” also has a flipside. Some important and hard-to-measure areas — mental rather than physical health, for instance — may be neglected, in an example of the McNamara fallacy, named after the bodycount-obsessed Vietnam-era US defence secretary Robert McNamara.

Fitness trackers can focus effort on restrictive targets , such as the quest to clock 10,000 steps daily, while some users’ cult-like dedication to hitting their goals (and bragging about it) could take a toll on their overall health, not to mention the patience of their friends.

Still, the gap is narrowing between fitness bands as faddish fashion accessories and as the serious healthcare tools some developers and doctors hope they can become. There is much further to go, but, to adapt the Chinese proverb, a journey of 1,000 miles begins with 10,000 steps.

rows.title: EU pushes Ukraine for further reforms to unlock funding
rows.content:
Paola Tamma in Brussels and Christopher Miller in Kyiv

Published October 2 2026

Brussels has rebuffed Ukraine’s request for additional financial support this year, demanding that Kyiv implement promised reforms before receiving further EU funding.

The decision comes as Ukraine grapples with intensified Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure, while its parliament struggles to pass the reforms required to unlock support from the EU and other donors.

This summer, Kyiv identified an additional $27bn in military needs and asked the European Commission to help cover the gap by bringing forward tranches from a €90bn EU loan agreed late last year .

That loan was intended to cover most of Ukraine’s financing needs in 2026 and 2027, allocating up to €45bn each year if certain reform milestones were met. However, only €15.7bn of this has been disbursed this year, partly due to delays in complying with reform requirements.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said further funding is urgently needed, in part to boost production of drones and interceptors as Moscow intensifies its aerial attacks on Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure ahead of the winter.

But Brussels rejected the request to frontload 2027 funding, instead pressing Kyiv to meet conditions that could unlock about €34bn in EU support this year.

In a joint statement on Thursday, Ukraine and the European Commission said they had “identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026. We have also reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release.”

The reforms Ukraine must deliver to receive the funds include the abolition of a VAT exemption for small parcels and the introduction of new taxation rules for digital platforms.

Both measures have passed in parliament, but include a controversial amendment that weakens the rules governing politically exposed persons (PEPs), which had been requested by the EU to strengthen anti-corruption efforts. That amendment, if signed into law, could threaten Ukraine’s compliance with the conditions attached to EU funding.

European commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos wrote a letter to the Speaker of Ukraine’s parliament, underscoring that additional financial assistance in 2026 was still available to Ukraine if it fulfilled the requested reforms.

“Avoiding any weakening of Ukraine’s framework on PEPs” was “essential”, they wrote in the letter, which was seen by the FT.

In an interview with the FT on Thursday, Zelenskyy pushed back against media reports of tense discussions with Commission president Ursula von der Leyen over reform conditions.

“We had a very good meeting with Ursula and with her team, and she understands that they have to help Ukraine,” he said.

Europe should help close Kyiv’s financing gap “because we are defending them”, he added. “They have to do it for them also, not only for us.”

He said he had told von der Leyen that wartime pressures meant reforms could not always proceed according to a normal timetable.

“We have to defend [ourselves] now, and some decisions, financial decisions, you can’t wait ,” he said. “Because it’s a question of our stability.”

The Commission is also assessing Ukraine’s yet-uncovered financing needs for 2027, which officials said could total about €70bn in military and budgetary support. The assessment is expected to be presented to EU leaders meeting in mid-October.

Ukraine is in discussions with the IMF about further disbursements from its $8bn programme, a review of which is due later this year. Those disbursements are contingent on funding agreements from the EU and Kyiv’s other allies that will help cover Ukraine’s financial needs in 2027.

rows.title: Investors seek refuge from bond rout in haven German debt
rows.content:
Emily Herbert and Ian Smith in London

Published October 2 2026

Updated October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

German government debt has emerged as the pre-eminent haven in the global bond rout, as concerns about an overheating US economy and fiscal worries elsewhere in Europe leave investors with few other places to turn.

The yield on 10-year Bunds has fallen 0.17 percentage points this week, even as borrowing costs have continued to rise elsewhere. French and Italian 10-year bond yields have risen 0.14 and 0.07 percentage points respectively this week, while US yields gained 0.07 percentage points over the week, even after a recovery following weak jobs data. Yields fall if the price of the bond rises.

“Demand for safety — Bunds — is on the up,” said Reinout De Bock, head of European rates strategy at UBS, amid a bond sell-off caused by an “[economic] cycle like no other with resilient growth, energy price risks and a broadening demand for capital”.

“Core Europe is emerging as the safe-haven allocation,” said Ales Koutny, head of international rates at asset management Vanguard, pointing to Germany but also the Netherlands and Switzerland, which have enjoyed almost as large falls in borrowing costs this week.

“First, it’s the historical benefit that they get from lower debt to GDP, better fiscal credibility and lower policy uncertainty,” he said. He added that the “amount of trade unwinds that we have seen has been wild”, as hedge funds have been forced to dump popular trades such as betting on Italian bonds outperforming Bunds.

Data pointing to powerful US economic growth has triggered a sharp sell-off in Treasuries in recent weeks, as investors have bet that the Federal Reserve will need to keep interest rates higher for longer to stop the economy from overheating. US government bonds posted their worst month since 2022 in September.

At the same time, a looming French budget and a fraught presidential election next year have brought investors’ attention back to the question of unsustainable debt piles in the region. Government bonds in Italy and Greece, both formerly the focus of market worries over debt, sold off in sympathy with French bonds on Thursday.

A big drop in German yields on Friday further drove up the additional interest rates that countries such as Italy and France pay on their 10-year debt relative to Germany’s.

France’s so-called spread over Germany hit 1.5 percentage points on Friday, its highest level since 2012, before narrowing later in the day to 1.4 points. Evelyne Gomez-Liechti, a multi-asset strategist at Mizuho, described 1.5 per cent as a “psychologically important” level.

The “violent” widening in Eurozone spreads on Thursday has “triggered an aggressive flight-to-quality bid into Germany”, she said.

There has been a particularly sharp move in so-called swap-spread trades, such as when investors buy French bonds and bet against euro interest rate swaps of the same maturity, typically using leverage.

The broader bond sell-off has sent the additional yield on five-year French bonds relative to the equivalent euro interest rate swaps surging to 0.8 percentage points, the biggest gap since 2011. That has led to losses for those betting on bonds against swaps.

Such idiosyncratic risks among several European countries had whittled down the options for investors looking to allocate outside the US, de Bock said.

“There has been rising demand for diversification” away from US Treasuries, he said. “People want to allocate into Europe” but there were “weak links, countries with higher deficits . . . the universe [of safer bond markets] is smaller than you thought”, he said.

De Bock said on Friday he was recommending that clients buy German debt and bet against Italian debt after the recent sell-off. He said he had previously used EU bonds, issued by the bloc as a whole, as the portion that clients should buy, but “I prefer to have a long that is really focused on the safest asset, which is Bunds”.

Investors were reassessing the risks around so-called peripheral Europe, including France, said Peter Schaffrik, global macro strategist at RBC Capital Markets.

“The market has figured out that for the slower-growing economies, these yield levels are unbearable; the economy can’t live with it,” whereas “Germany is still growing decently,” he added.

rows.title: The Ellison credit complex gets a bit more complex
rows.content:
Toby Nangle

Published October 2 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

We’ve joked before that Warner takeovers are the harbingers of financial apocalypse . So those of a superstitious disposition should mark next week — when the latest takeover is set to close — in their diaries, thanks to the willingness of bond investors to part with their cash.

But Paramount Skydance, the bond issuer and Warner Bros acquirer, is a big investment-grade company, isn’t it? And while $52bn is still a lot of corporate bonds for debt capital market teams to find homes for, big investment-grade companies seem like they sell large slews of bonds on a weekly basis.

S&P Global Ratings, 24th September:

We lowered our issuer credit rating on PSKY [Paramount Skydance] to ‘BB’ from ‘BB+’, as we expect leverage to increase when the acquisition closes shortly.

Wait, what? Double-B flat isn’t investment grade, it’s junk.

Luckily for investment-grade bond investors, Paramount Skydance didn’t let a little thing like being junk-rated get in the way of issuing a monster consignment of investment-grade rated bonds.

Somewhat unusually for a public debt transaction of this size, they threw in extra credit support in the form of a special first-lien charge. And as S&P Global Ratings explains in its ‘recovery rating’ report ($) :

Depending on the recovery assessment for a given debt issue, the issue rating is derived by notching up, down, or not at all from the issuer credit rating on the issuer of the debt.

The rating analysts reckon that, in the event of default, noteholders who have the benefit of this first-lien charge will recover 90–100 cents in the dollar. At least this is what they reckon if their 2031 default scenario comes to pass.

The 2031 default scenario imagines a world in which the company runs into difficulty, decides it needs to restructure its debt, but is still churning out $10.2bn of ebitda, giving it an enterprise value of around $63bn (after accounting for all the costs of bankruptcy administration).

Bondholders with the first-lien charge are close to having first dibs on this imagined $63bn enterprise value, and these dibs push the bond ratings up to BBB-, despite being issued by a BB-rated company. Nice.

Are there any other credit supports that help the company squeak over the IG rating line ($) ? Our emphasis:

Our ratings on PSKY reflects [sic] the commitment by the Ellison family , the company’s controlling entity, to take all steps necessary for it to deleverage below 3.75x on a net-debt basis (per the company’s definition) by 2028 and to 3.0x by 2029.

Of course.

David Ellison is the CEO of Paramount Skydance. He is also the son of Larry Ellison. And Larry Ellison, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index , is worth $187bn — largely based on the value of his holdings of Oracle Corp common stock. Having the owner of 40 per cent of the global AI hyperscaling heavyweight committed to taking all steps necessary to deleverage has got to be pretty reassuring to credit investors.

We checked in on how investors are pricing the global AI hyperscaler’s creditworthiness. We also threw the new Paramount Skydance bonds, and every other triple-B-rated US corporate bond in the ICE BofA corporate bond index into the chart.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Increasingly, it looks like two large issuers are being priced as having far higher risk credit premia than the rest. Both sit on the lowest rung of the investment-grade ladder, and both are Ellison family companies.

Moreover, as Chris Whittall of IFR noted today , the cost of insuring Paramount debt against default using credit default swaps has skyrocketed. And that Ellison family commitment doesn’t look like it has helped (h/t to Dec Mullarkey, who also flagged this correlation):

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Partly, this could be unhappy holders of the new PSKY bonds seeking to lay off risk. An IFR article ($) reports that the new 10-year bonds fell close to five points shortly after issuance, suggesting that maybe not everyone was in it for the long haul.

But, given its long history, the cyan Paramount CDS line most likely references obligations issued specifically by the Paramount subsidiary of Paramount Skydance to whom the commitment has apparently been given. S&P rates unsecured debt from this subsidiary a lowly single-B plus.

Still, if the new PSKY debt doesn’t look like it has been absorbed that well, at least we won’t be muttering about indices being gamed and passive bot-run funds getting stuffed. Because the weird timing of the bond deal all but guarantees that the victims have, so far, all been active human decision-makers.

As MainFT reported Wednesday , Paramount Skydance rushed to sell bonds to close the acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery “before a third-quarter deadline to avoid hefty penalty fees”. And this rush saw them sold on 30th September: not a great day for any wannabe corporate bond index constituent.

The cut-off for inclusion in Bloomberg indices — think the big US and Global Agg indices — is two business days prior to the last business day for the month, so Monday 28th September. For ICE BoA corporate bond indices , the cut-off for month-end rebalancing is three business days ahead of month-end, so Friday 25th September. And the iBoxx USD Liquid Investment Grade Maturity Indices require new issues to settle by the last day of the month. The new Paramount Skydance bonds settle on the 5th October.

So quasi-passive or actual index-replicating investors are unlikely to have piled in. And active managers needn’t have worried about any relative-to-benchmark performance cost of missing out on a deal that performed strongly, at least for the next month.

rows.title: Why does Anthropic’s IPO feel so weird?
rows.content:
Richard Waters

Published October 2 2026

For fast-growing tech companies, initial public offerings are an important rite of passage. From Google’s declaration that it wanted to “make the world a better place” to SpaceX’s ambition to “extend the light of consciousness to the stars”, they are a moment to capture the world’s imagination. The best IPO narratives fuse an idealistic vision of the future with a sense of inevitability about why this company will win.

Selling shares to the public for the first time is also seen as a milestone on the path to corporate maturity. There is an expectation that products have been honed and business models perfected.

Perhaps all of this goes some way towards explaining why the looming IPO of AI company Anthropic has felt so . . . weird.

Details from its draft prospectus leaked out this week, suggesting the share sale is close. If it hits the $2tn valuation investors are expecting, it would set a record for a new public company.

Compared to other blockbuster tech IPOs, though, the build-up to Anthropic’s stock market debut has felt discordant, even creepy. What other company, after all, would think to warn shareholders that its main product might go off the rails and resort to blackmail?

The most obvious cause of the weirdness has been the predictions from former and current employees that AI might lead to human extinction. Far from trying to stamp out such talk, CEO Dario Amodei agreed that the technology could cause “catastrophic damage” and regulation was urgently needed.

It isn’t only the doomerism that has struck a jarring note. Like the rest of its industry, Anthropic has struggled to convince the public that its technology is actually going to make the world a better place. AI executives such as Amodei like to talk about the economic “abundance” it will create and the diseases it will cure, but such utopian musings are out of tune with the wariness many people feel.

Then there are the mishaps. The extinction warnings relate to a future version of AI that might escape human control. Even at this stage, though, Anthropic can’t seem to keep a grip on the technology it is already building. Echoing problems at rival OpenAI, it confessed recently to three cases in which its AI had escaped on to the internet and hacked into other companies’ systems.

Ultimately, none of this may matter much to investors, given the company’s astounding growth. Even here, though, things are not straightforward. There is a lively debate among AI investors over whether makers of so-called frontier AI models like Anthropic will be able to maintain any kind of performance advantage. If not, it is likely to struggle to maintain pricing power and be forced into an overhaul of its business model.

To Anthropic’s critics, much of this reflects the immaturity of a five-year-old research lab that has, almost overnight, been propelled to global prominence.

Countering the extinction warnings, tech figures like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, former White House AI tsar David Sacks and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg argue that there is nothing inherently dangerous about developing more advanced AI or releasing the technology to a mass market. It just takes the same kind of engineering experience, product design and quality control that characterise other technologies — disciplines that Anthropic is still learning as it mutates from ambitious start-up into mature product company.

Before it sprang to wider attention, Anthropic was the product of a culture that seems singular even by the standards of Silicon Valley. Its founders were heavily influenced by a branch of the effective altruism movement known as long-termism, which is fixated on the risks of human extinction from technologies like advanced AI. To critics, that has led to a speculative and self-indulgent doomerism that overstates the more prosaic work needed to control AI.

This is certainly how things are seen in Washington. After a lunch at the White House this week, a number of AI executives — including Anthropic’s CEO — signed an “accord on super intelligence” that promises the kind of things you would expect from normal, mature companies: “Robust internal controls”, special board-level committees and outside audits to contain the risks.

It’s hard, though, to see this erasing the weirdness from the Anthropic IPO. Investors still need to grapple with voluminous warnings that take up fully a third of the company’s draft prospectus (including the one about blackmail). There are apparently so many things that could go wrong that Anthropic’s lawyers would be forgiven for suggesting the company instead issue a single, blanket statement: This technology will do crazy stuff we can’t even imagine yet.

Nor has the official line in Washington, exemplified by President Donald Trump’s insouciance, done anything to end the division in Silicon Valley. Technologists without an obvious axe to grind, like Bill Gates, have been sounding increasingly alarmed about AI, which they warn is much too dangerous to be left in the hands of private companies without serious external controls.

As its big moment on Wall Street nears, Anthropic’s unintended IPO narrative is hard to dispel: the hypergrowth AI company which, according to its own employees, might just kill us all.
