rows.title: Pedro Sánchez loses vote on Spanish housing reform
rows.content:
Barney Jopson in Madrid

Published October 2 2026

Spanish lawmakers have rejected Pedro Sánchez’s signature effort to address a ballooning housing crisis, in a major setback for the prime minister that could push him to call an early election.

Spain has been rocked by public anger over rising rents, which boiled over last week after an 87-year-old was evicted from her Madrid apartment because she could no longer afford it.

But Sánchez’s attempt to quell the fury with a legislative reform failed on Friday as his minority leftwing government could not corral enough support to pass the bill.

Junts per Catalunya, a Catalan separatist party whose votes helped Sánchez return to office in 2023, said it would not support the housing bill, arguing that it would reduce the supply of rental properties and drive up prices further.

The legislation included a prohibition on evictions until 2030 and a ban on the purchase of residential property by investors the government called “vulture funds”.

One of the EU’s few remaining socialist leaders, Sánchez has struggled to pass major legislative changes or a budget in his second term. The rightwing opposition — the conservative People’s Party (PP) and the populist Vox party — voted against the bill and renewed its calls for snap elections to break the gridlock.

Opinion polls carried out before Friday’s vote suggested the PP and Vox could secure enough votes to oust Sánchez and form a governing alliance.

But some analysts said the premier could still turn this defeat in his favour and mobilise his base, especially if he calls early elections. Pablo Simón, a politics professor at the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, said: “He has to call elections within nine months or so. So the question is: is he going to have a better moment than this in three or six months’ time? That is the question he will be asking himself. And the answer is probably no.”

The premier’s standing has been hit by an influx of thousands of unauthorised migrants into Ceuta, a Spanish African exclave, and by a series of corruption allegations, including charges against his wife, who denies wrongdoing.

Addressing the PP and Vox, Isabel Rodríguez, Spain’s housing minister, condemned them for opposing the bill. “Whilst people are protesting in the streets, you’re off to Miami or a vulture fund conference encouraging them to colonise us,” she said. The legislative push began when Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from her Madrid flat after her landlord introduced a rent increase she could not afford when a longstanding rent cap expired.

Following street demonstrations to support her at the weekend, hundreds of people set up a protest camp in central Madrid. The small company that owns her apartment subsequently struck a deal to let her return home.

rows.title: Tesla deliveries fall 2% as US consumers buy fewer electric vehicles
rows.content:
Kana Inagaki in London and Stephen Morris in San Francisco

Published October 2 2026

Tesla’s deliveries fell less than expected in the third quarter, as a recovery in European sales helped offset softening demand for electric vehicles in the US.

The US carmaker delivered 486,532 vehicles in the three months to the end of September, above analysts’ forecasts of 461,974 but down 2 per cent from 497,099 in the same period last year. Shares in Tesla rose nearly 4 per cent on Friday.

Tesla’s US sales have been suffering after President Donald Trump ended a $7,500 tax credit for EV purchases and cancelled federal emissions trading schemes that had become an important source of income for the carmaker.

The carmaker’s sales hit a record in the third quarter of last year as US consumers rushed to buy EVs ahead of the expiry of the tax credits.

Tesla does not provide a regional breakdown of its deliveries but quarterly sales in the US were likely to have fallen 31 per cent year on year to 123,880 vehicles, according to estimates by Cox Automotive.

Other US carmakers also reported lower sales for the third quarter. Ford said US sales for the period fell 6.6 per cent year on year to 509,764 vehicles as it phased out its Escape and Corsair models. General Motors reported a 6 per cent decline in US sales to 670,974 units due to a “much smaller EV market”.

Rising fuel prices have helped lift demand for EVs elsewhere, with sales in Europe continuing to recover following a consumer backlash against Tesla chief executive Elon Musk’s political activism last year.

New registrations in the UK and the EU increased 43 per cent year on year to 191,787 vehicles during the first eight months of 2026, according to European car industry body Acea.

Still, Tesla has faced intense competition from BYD and other Chinese manufacturers that are rapidly making inroads into the UK and other European markets.

The EU has also delayed a long-awaited vote on allowing Tesla’s supervised “Full Self-Driving” software across the bloc, from October to December at the earliest, though it is already allowed in certain member states.

Despite its name, FSD still requires humans to sit in the driver’s seat and pay full attention — unlike Google’s Waymo taxis. Musk has repeatedly promised that Tesla’s FSD software will be approved for fully autonomous driving soon, but it has yet to gain regulatory approval in any countries.

In a filing this week, Tesla said it had secured $30bn of new credit lines as Musk prepares to pivot the group from EV manufacturing to focus on autonomous driving, robotics and AI. In April, the company raised its guidance for annual capital expenditure from $20bn to $25bn.

In January, Musk discontinued Tesla’s premium S and SUV X models as the group shifted to the development of the Cybercab, a golden self-driving taxi, and a humanoid robot called Optimus. Both experimental products have started production, but are yet to generate any income through sales.

rows.title: Obama’s red herring
rows.content:
Edward Luce

Published October 2 2026

This article is an on-site version of our Swamp Notes newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Monday and Friday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

I am not among those who think Barack Obama should take on Donald Trump. Some have urged all the former presidents, including George W Bush, Bill Clinton, Joe Biden and Obama, to link arms and denounce Trump. What would happen then? My bet is that such a coming together would play straight into the hands of a president who claims he is the scourge of the establishment “uniparty”. Having spent their capital to no effect, or worse, the ex-presidents might find their accounts are empty. The same would apply to Obama. Though he has higher approval ratings (60 per cent plus) than anyone else in US politics, retired or active, that would buy little in today’s polarised arena. But he can have a real impact on the Democratic Party’s direction.

He could, of course, make the wrong kind of effect. At a recent event in New Hampshire, Obama said that Democrats should focus less on the “mechanical and instrumental and materialist” questions (chiefly economic) to tell a larger narrative about what brings Americans together. “What people are starved for at the moment is an ability to tell a moral, an ethical, story about how we live together,” Obama said. “All that stuff [the economy, inequality, power, AI] is important but there is an underlying moral foundation about how we see each other, that so often came out of a church, or a temple or a mosque . . . our leaders have to be able to speak that language in a serious way.”

It is hard to think of worse advice. Politicians should not aspire to be religious or spiritual leaders, though it is easy to see why Obama might think so. He shot to national prominence in 2004 with his Democratic convention speech saying there was no red state America, or blue state America, but the United States of America. He presented himself as a healer who delivered hope. Some might say that strategy worked. Having travelled with his 2008 campaign, I think there were other factors involved in his historic victory. He beat Hillary Clinton to the nomination on the strength of his opposition to the Iraq war and his superior ground game in states that hold caucuses. He defeated John McCain in the general election partly on the back of the Lehman Brothers-induced financial meltdown. Through both, he was a brilliant campaigner who packaged his story and biracial background to fit the larger moment.

We are living in a very different moment today. Moreover, Obama’s diagnosis does not really fit the facts. Far from focusing on the economy and other supposedly mechanical issues in the 2024 presidential election, Kamala Harris made her campaign about democracy. She made a larger bet on an ethical narrative that was repudiated. Her economic message was incrementalist and jumbled. Obama would have done it far better and might even have won. But when it boiled down to a choice, people voted for Trump because they thought he would put more money in their pockets. As Nancy Pelosi keeps reminding people, “democracy is saved at the kitchen table”. Obama’s second error is to presume he can be reproduced. He did tell a larger story about America. Reasonable people can disagree about how critical it was to his success. But both he and his moment were unique.

There is no doubt that Obama can move the needle. He helped persuade Joe Biden to drop his re-election campaign in 2024 after that disastrous debate. How people wish Obama had intervened sooner, though it might not have worked given Biden’s stubbornness. Likewise, Obama was probably decisive in persuading California’s voters last year to pass Proposition 50. That measure enabled Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, to gerrymander five extra Democratic seats in the state in retaliation for Trump asking Texas to do the same. The fruits of that could be critical in next month’s midterm elections. These are the kinds of practical interventions that can have a decisive effect. Talking about the arc of history bending towards justice once sounded good. Nowadays it sounds like pie in the sky.

I am turning this week to my colleague, Brooke Masters, the FT’s US managing editor based in New York. Brooke, it is easy for Washingtonians such as me to miss what people are thinking outside the Beltway bubble. Am I underestimating Obama’s national influence? He recently appeared with your mayor, Zohran Mamdani, a figure he clearly admires. Indeed, Mamdani’s ability to speak to the young and across some fairly improbable divides reminds me of the younger Obama. But their politics, and economics, are very different. From what you have seen of Mamdani, could he be the one who changes Democratic politics?

My column this week argues that the upcoming likely Republican midterm defeat will generate ripples, not earthquakes. “Loss of control of Congress — the switch to divided government — used to mean that the president’s room for manoeuvre would be roughly halved,” I write. “For the most part, however, Congress has been largely irrelevant in the last 20 months.”

I was both riveted and unnerved by this probing Ezra Klein interview with Bill Gates in the New York Times. Gates is a life-long techno-optimist. The vast risks of AI seem to have changed his mind.

Talking of AI, three cheers to Dan Drezner, dean of Tufts’ Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy, and author of a great Substack, who comes out swinging in defence of writing as an activity essential to thinking. I’m also with Joan Didion, who said, “I write to find out what I’m thinking”.

Hi Ed. I think you are being very clear-eyed about the limits of what Obama can accomplish in this election. His soaring oratory about unity resonated in 2008 in part because the economic situation seemed so dire. Today, voters feel financially squeezed and they are worried about the long-term problems posed by AI, but they aren’t nearly as scared.

Where I do think he can make a difference is on turnout.

The latest FT election poll shows Trump’s approval rating has fallen to the lowest level yet, but national disaffection does not guarantee a blue wave. I talked this week to canvassers in one bellwether congressional district, the 17th in the northern suburbs of New York City. It generally votes Democratic but elected a Republican to Congress in 2024. The door-knockers found potential voters are generally split and not particularly excited to turn out.

That tracks with history. Fewer than half of eligible voters usually vote in midterm elections, and the share has fallen as low as 36 per cent (in 2014). Given the efforts by the Trump administration and some states to make it harder to vote by mail, getting supporters to the polls is going to be absolutely critical in this election.

If Obama motivates Democratic voters who would not otherwise make the effort to take time out of work and stand in line, he can help change the outcome in closely fought states.

His enduring popularity with Black Americans means that he could play a particularly important role in states with close Senate races such as North Carolina, where 20 per cent of voters identify as Black, and Michigan (13 per cent) and Texas (13 per cent).

It is worth remembering that when midterm turnout set the modern record of 49 per cent during Trump’s first term in 2018, Democrats gained 40 seats and flipped control of the House of Representatives, but they still lost seats in the Senate.

rows.title: I’m even more bullish about stocks than a year ago
rows.content:
Stuart Kirk

Published October 2 2026

Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.

A year ago, I wrote that greed would be my fourth-quarter investment strategy . We were in a bubble, I reckoned, but it had a way to go. Besides, US stock returns had been positive 80 per cent of the time in the last three months of the year since my mum was at kindergarten.

So much for that. By the end of October I had sold every equity fund in my portfolio and ran a 100 per cent cash position for the next five months. Does being greedy make sense again now? Will I ignore my advice regardless?

Part of the reason I threw my shares out of the pram was how well they had performed in 2025 up to that point. Everything felt too perfect. I was up 17 per cent since January, comfortably ahead of the S&P 500 – even though I had no US stocks.

This year, my portfolio has risen in value by 11 per cent, in line with the S&P 500 in dollars, but four percentage points behind in pounds. I will take that every time, of course. But it doesn’t seem as frothy and overheated as this time last year.

Yes, there’s been SpaceX, the frothiest and most overheated company listing in the history of finance. And the size and growth in borrowing to fund the artificial intelligence boom is off the charts — $340bn by the hyperscalers alone next year, according to Goldman Sachs.

So what do I mean when I say that equities feel less exuberant to me than 12 months ago? And does that necessarily make them more attractive? As an investor you want the va-va-voom. You just don’t want to overpay.

For earnings, that is. And one of the most extraordinary developments since my column a year ago is how much more profit I receive for my money. In every one of the markets I’m invested in, forward price-to-earnings ratios are lower today.

I read once about a hedge fund manager who used to scream at analysts: “Don’t bring me stocks on eight times price-to-earnings ratios and tell me they’re cheap. Show me something that you think is undervalued on 50 times!”

Like Nvidia, I suppose. In 2023, its forward price-to-earnings ratio was exactly that (its trailing multiple was 180 times). I would have told my boss it was ridiculously expensive and only a moron would buy it.

It turns out it was cheap — as defined by the fact that Nvidia’s share price subsequently sextupled. And indeed its earnings grew by even more, such that the consensus forward price-to-earnings has dropped to just 19 times, according to Capital IQ data.

It grew into its valuation, as the pros say — and then some in Nvidia’s case. A milder version of this is what has been going on in equity markets more broadly. In the US, Japan and Latin America, forecast earnings are a third higher than a year ago. For the UK, it’s 27 per cent. LatAm earnings will nearly double.

Thus, if I had known last October that US profits would be what they are forecast to be this year, the 25 times forward price-to-earnings back then was actually closer to 18 times. Japan’s was 13 rather than 17. The FTSE 100’s was more like 11 than 14.5 times.

The surge in earnings didn’t come until long after I sold out of equities. It was only after Iran kicked off that profits began accelerating almost everywhere. But you need to look at a long-run chart to appreciate just how unusual this is — especially in the US.

So much so that not only are forward price/earnings ratios lower today than a year ago for every stock market I own but they are all — save the US — beneath the levels they dropped to when I bought back into equities as missiles were flying over the Gulf.

Even the S&P 500’s ratio is only a smidgen higher — 21.3 times today compared with 20 in late March. And yet the index is up by a fifth. Asia ex-Japan has performed even better, while its price/earnings ratio fell by as much as the US’s rose. It’s a similar story, to a lesser degree, for the UK.

If investors are receiving way more profits per share compared with the price of each share versus a year ago, it goes without saying that we should be more bullish today — right? Other things being equal, I suppose so.

Any expected-return calculation takes current values as a starting point. The higher the valuation relative to the past, the lower the expected returns — and vice versa. Share prices can veer off trend for years, though. I’ve been waiting for some ratios to mean revert for decades.

But history shows that the future performance of equity markets has tended to be better the lower the valuation is now. In that case, if I were happy to own stocks when I wrote my end-of-third-quarter review a year ago, I should be keener still.

And I am. There are risks aplenty, of course. There always are — even if the young ’uns out there believe a rocky investment landscape is a new phenomenon. What is different, however, is that whereas last time a re-rating (down) in valuations was the risk, today I would argue that missing out on earnings is the worry.

What does that come down to? Three things: whether your mum thinks using ChatGPT is useful or not (demand); whether the price of compute plummets due to intense competition (supply); and whether AI can stay unregulated without a rogue agent spurring a worldwide backlash.

For now I’m hopeful, especially given the resilience of equity markets to rising bond yields. But you know how long my bullish moods can last now, don’t you?

The author is a former portfolio manager. Email: [email protected]

rows.title: Paris Fashion Week confronts luxury’s crisis of desire
rows.content:
Elizabeth Paton

Published October 2 2026

Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.

Front row conversations dissecting the state of the industry in Paris can feel rather heavy these days. Most of the starry creative hires made by big heritage houses a year ago, with a handful of notable exceptions, have failed to generate the magic — and sales momentum — hoped for in brand C-suites. Budgets are tighter, and some designers may be on the move again already, decisions that have a wider ripple effect across studios, head offices and people’s daily lives. A sharp luxury slowdown in China is another cause for concern. And it is heaping the pressure further on creatives to make people dream about and spend again on goods they do not aspire to in the way they once did.

It is interesting to see how designers respond to the moment. Some keep clients fully front of mind, like Daniel Roseberry, who built a subterranean velveteen nightclub for his latest Schiaparelli ready-to-wear show based on sexy deconstructions of the “Schiap jacket” — to the delight of his couture clients, many of whom sat at tables drinking champagne in support. Others opt for shock factor, like Matières Fécales, which shut down Place de la République, a square famous for public demonstrations, for its show titled “The 99 per cent”. Featuring 99 non-Caucasian models of different ages and sizes, it was a personal and political rallying cry from co-founders Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran to those they feel are left behind by the system. It generated a huge outpouring of support on social media — even if critics asked whether such fashion statements empower the masses if it’s only the 1 per cent who can afford to own the garments.

Pushing the boundaries of possibility comes in many forms. At Anrealage, Kunihiko Morinaga offered incredible colour-changing skirts and dresses via rippling 3D-printed scales, LED lights and E Ink paper scales, playfully stretching ideas of what clothes can or should be. Here are some other takeaways from the biggest shows of the week.

This season it was all about glamour at Dries Van Noten. Julian Klausner, the brand’s creative director since 2024, explained backstage that he and his team took cues from the little flourishes that made them feel glamorous when walking down the street: a cinched waist, a sparkling brooch or bold pops of colour. This brought to mind 1950s movie stars, which on the runway translated to movie poster prints inspired by the era splashed across dresses, skirts and car coats. Like Prada before it this season, this felt like an homage to skirts: a nod to the hyper-femininity of the 1950s, perhaps, but also reworked to relish the style’s versatility. Almost all falling to the knee, they came dripping in Indian crystal embellishments or with paper-bag waists, cargo pockets or with gauzy layers over stencilled prints. Matched up with everything from cropped jackets (everywhere at the moment) and sweater vests, and layered up with plenty of cocktail jewellery, it felt contemporary, fun and, most importantly, wearable.

Every so often, a fashion show transports you to another dimension. Such was the case at Rick Owens on Thursday, where the grand colonnades, reclining statues and supercharged fountain jets of the Palais de Tokyo plaza were recast as an otherworldly set, one where models in long stone-coloured ceremonial gowns strode their way down a huge ramp to electronic music that thudded like a heartbeat. The inspiration this season was, in fact, stones: from “elegant stoicism” to “stone-throwing, which I’ve made my life’s modest mission to oppose” and “the stone thrown aside during Christ’s resurrection,” read Owens’ show notes.

Some dresses had a sturdy, quilted quality like armour, while others in gossamer silk rippled in the breeze. Rompers with sharp edges, worn with crystalline rope boots, then acted as a turning point to tougher, more industrial layered looks including sulphur-dyed denim skirts and biker jackets, before closing with a series of strange structured head-to-toe harnesses, which Owens called his version of a négligée. Owens has been described by The New York Times as “fashion’s patriarch of freaks” — a title he would relish. His weird and wonderful universe feels ever more invigorating than the bulk of the industry mainstream.

Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, founders of The Row, have long let their chic, minimalist clothes for very, very rich women do the talking. The duo rarely give interviews; famously, they also don’t allow guests to use social media at their Paris show. Logo-free, the brand’s calling card has generally been “if you know you know” when you see their clothes in the street. It hasn’t held them back, per se; their €5,000 Margaux bag has cult status and their €1,000 rubber flip flops spawned endless imitations.

Lately, however, there has been a quiet shift in the script, including (whisper it) advertising in glossy magazines, with a volume shift on the runway too. Amid the neat, neutral tailoring this season were even more beautiful and colourful fabrications than usual, bringing new verve: opulent vintage-esque materials in reds and turquoise, or broderie anglaise, elegantly fashioned into wrap tops and slips, next to floral ribbon belts, and fraying straps and hems. Bohemian, almost, until you remember the wild price tags.

The general consensus on the front row of the Chloé show on Thursday morning was that this would be the last from creative director Chemena Kamali. Rumour has it that she will take over from Anthony Vaccarello at Saint Laurent; and though this is not confirmed, her exit could prove an issue for parent group Richemont, which already has another vacant creative director spot to fill at Alaïa, where it is yet to find a replacement for Pieter Mulier who decamped to Versace. Anyway, back to business — and to the runway, where the show notes began: “May the love poured into this collection endure forever.” This collection certainly cycled through house archetypes; plenty of broderie anglaise dresses, cape-like outerwear in block colours (worn with fun fisherman’s hats), sorbet-hued, barely-there lingerie and vast floaty gowns. A romantic ode, then, and one that got a standing ovation. But that was likely more of a farewell gesture than directed at the clothes themselves, which felt more dutiful than truly spirited.

Pierpaolo Piccioli inherited a complex challenge when he took the reins at Balenciaga last year; a house with its own distinct heritage and even starker contemporary codes courtesy of Piccioli’s predecessor Demna. Thus far, his collections have yet to offer a cohesive view of what Balenciaga should be today. His Thursday show, however, was a step in the right direction. This season, he was motivated by the idea of putting couture-like cuts and techniques on everyday pieces of clothing, which included T-shirts with cascading trains, denim cut on the bias, peplum white-collar shirts, voluminous oversized cargo trousers and blazers finished with trailing ribbons. There were too many ideas at play. But Piccioli is also working hard to make his mark here. A coral-inspired textile totem structure at the centre of the runway was a nod to the coral necklaces he wears every day — and a personal touch.
